Each row of the page shows the same thing in the sun and in the shade, and the sun side changes from row to row. Level 1 has two pairs, Level 2 four. Level 3 has three pairs and two thermometers for the water: read the cup thermometers, then show each child the line to color up to.
note.watch: Right: in every row, the circle beside the thing in the sun is red and the one beside the thing in the shade is blue. Check that children look for the sun or shade label, not the side of the page. On Level 3, the sun thermometer is colored higher and is the one circled. If a pair felt the same on a cloudy day, say so and test again on a sunny day. No answer key.

K:sun-warms.routine: Set out two of each: a pail of sand, a bottle of water, a rock, and a ball. In the morning, put one of each in full sun and one in the shade of a tree or a building. After about an hour, children feel each pair with the back of a hand; a grown-up touches first, because a dark rock in strong sun can get hot. Then pour each bottle into a cup and stand a thermometer in each cup for a few minutes to read the water.

K:make-shade.title: Make Shade for an Ice Cube
K:make-shade.objective: Children build a small shade from paper, cloth, craft sticks, and cups to keep an ice cube from melting in the sun, then compare which shade kept its ice cube the longest.

note.mistake: Children think a shade must wrap the ice cube, or that any cover works, even clear plastic that lets the sunlight through. They think the ice melts because of the wind, not the sunlight.
note.words: Ask: "Which ice cube is melting fastest? Why?" Say: "A shade blocks the sunlight, so the ice under it warms more slowly." The page shows paper, a plate, an umbrella, a leaf, and an empty box for something else. Level 1: children circle what they will use, draw their shade over the ice cube, and after the test color how much ice was left: all, half, or none. Level 2: they color the result for two shades. Level 3: they also draw a better shade for next time.
note.watch: There is no answer: the results come from your test. A right page shows a shade drawn over the ice cube and a result that matches what happened. Ask, "Did your shade keep the sunlight off? How do you know?" Compare each result with the ice cube with no shade. A shade that let light through, such as thin paper, is a good result to talk about: "What would block more light?" On Level 3, ask what the better shade changes: bigger, thicker, or another material.

K:make-shade.routine: Set out ice cubes of one size, paper plates, construction paper, cloth scraps, craft sticks, paper cups, tape, leaves, and a small umbrella. Each group builds a shade that stands over its ice cube on a plate. Put all the plates in full sun at the same time, plus one ice cube with no shade to compare with. Check every 10 to 15 minutes and watch which ice cube melts fastest.

K:natural-made.title: Natural or Made by People?
K:natural-made.objective: Children sort real things (a rock, a leaf, a pinecone, a cup, a crayon, a paper bag) into natural and made by people, and tell how people change the land to get what they need, such as cutting trees for wood and paper.

note.mistake: Children think a wooden chair or a paper bag is natural because wood comes from trees. They call anything found outside natural and anything inside made by people, so a flower in a classroom pot is "made by people."
note.words: Ask about each thing: "Did people make it, or did it come from nature?" Say: "People cut down trees and made wood and paper from them. The tree is natural; the paper bag was made by people." Ask: "What else do people change to get what they need?" (fields for food, roads, houses). Say: "When people cut trees, they can plant new ones." Day 2, the page: the two groups are printed Natural and Man-made. Read "Man-made" and say, "That means made by people." Children draw a line from each picture to its group. Name every picture first. Level 1 has four pictures, Level 2 six, Level 3 eight.
note.watch: Right: the flower, the rock, the leaf, the mountain, and the sun are natural; the house, the chair, the car, the ball, the cup, and the book are made by people. Ask, "Who made it?" A child who puts the chair or the book with natural because "it is made of wood" or paper is thinking well: agree that it came from a tree, then ask, "Who made it into a chair?" No answer key.

K:natural-made.routine: Put real things on a tray: a rock, a leaf, a pinecone, a stick, a plastic cup, a crayon, a paper bag, and a wooden block. Children pick up each one, say whether people made it or it came from nature, and sort the things into two baskets. Then hold up the stick beside the wooden block and the paper bag, and talk about how people make wood and paper from trees.

K:recycling.title: Recycle, Reuse, and Keep Earth Clean
K:recycling.objective: Children sort clean, empty things by what they are made of and into the class recycling and trash bins, find one thing they can use again, and help pick up litter around the school.

note.mistake: Children think everything goes in the recycling bin, food scraps and plastic spoons too, and that recycled things just disappear. They think a clear or yellow jar is plastic.
note.words: Ask, "What is it made of?" Say what your town takes: many US towns put paper, plastic, glass, and metal in one recycling cart, and a plastic spoon or a toothbrush goes in the trash. The page sorts things by material into five bins: paper, plastic, glass, metal, and compost (food scraps). Read the bin names. Every thing on the page is one a US recycling cart or a compost bin takes, empty and clean. Children draw a line from each thing to its bin. Level 1 has six things, Level 2 eight, Level 3 nine. Another page of the same lesson asks children to circle the bin in each row.
note.watch: Right: paper, an envelope, a notebook, a cereal box, and a box to paper; the water bottle and the shampoo bottle to plastic; the jars (honey, jam) to glass; the can to metal; fruit, vegetables, bread, and a leaf to compost. A child who says "in our town paper and cans go in one cart" is right too: the five bins are the sorting the recycling center does. No answer key.

K:recycling.routine: Bring clean, empty things: a cereal box, a can, a glass jar, a plastic water bottle, a banana peel, a plastic spoon. Children say what each is made of, sort them into the school's recycling, compost, and trash bins, and find one thing to use again. Then take a short litter walk: everyone wears gloves, children pick up paper and wrappers, a grown-up picks up anything sharp or broken, and everyone washes hands.

1:road-signs.title: Road Signs on the Way to School
1:road-signs.objective: Children match the road signs they pass on the way to school (STOP, YIELD, a pedestrian crossing, a school zone, DO NOT ENTER, a traffic signal ahead) to what each one tells drivers and walkers, and point them out on a walk around the school block.

note.mistake: Children think signs are only for drivers, that YIELD means the same as STOP, and that the walking-person sign means it is safe to cross without looking. Many think first graders may cross alone once they know the signs.
note.words: Teach the shapes and colors: STOP is a red octagon, YIELD a triangle point down, the school sign has five sides, the walking-person and traffic-light signs are yellow diamonds, and DO NOT ENTER is a red circle with a white bar. Say: "Signs help drivers and walkers. Even at a crosswalk, we stop at the curb and look left, right, and left again, and first graders cross with a grown-up." The page: children draw a line from each sign to what it means. Read every meaning aloud; the sentences are long for first-grade readers. The page is one level.
note.watch: Right: STOP, every car must halt here, then look; YIELD, slow down and let the others go first; the school sign, a school is near; the walking-person sign, a marked place where people cross; the traffic-light sign, a traffic light is coming; DO NOT ENTER, no car may drive into the street from this side. Ask, "Who is this sign for?" On the walk, a sign children spot on their own counts more than the page. No answer key.

1:road-signs.routine: Take the class on a walk around the school block with at least one more grown-up. Children walk in pairs on the sidewalk, and the class crosses only at a crosswalk, with you, after everyone stops at the curb and looks left, right, and left again. At each sign, stop and say its shape, its color, and what it tells drivers and walkers. Back in the room, children make the sign shapes from colored paper.

1:healthy-habits.title: Brushing Teeth, Stopping Germs, and My Habit Chart
1:healthy-habits.objective: Children sort the steps of brushing teeth, choose the ways that stop germs, and keep a habit chart at home for a week.

note.mistake: Children brush for a few seconds and only the front teeth. They think sharing a cup is kind, and coughing into a hand polite.
note.words: Say: "Brush two times a day for two minutes. Germs are too small to see." On Brushing Teeth, children circle before, during, or after for six pictures; on Stop the Germs, they circle the healthy picture in each row. The habit chart goes home: children check each habit they did each day for a week (send a second copy for a second week). Each page is one level.
note.watch: Before brushing: toothpaste on the brush, teeth with spots; during: the outsides, insides, and chewing tops; after: the clean tooth. Germs: the elbow cough, soap and water, each child with his or her own cup, the tissue in the trash. Never ask about home: a chart with few checks needs encouragement, not blame. No answer key.

1:healthy-habits.routine: Brush a big egg-carton model of teeth with a large toothbrush while the class counts: outsides, insides, and chewing tops. Children copy the motions in the air; we never share toothbrushes. Then practice: cough into the elbow, throw a used tissue away and wash hands, and label a cup with your name.

1:ask-a-grown-up.title: Medicines Only from a Trusted Adult
1:ask-a-grown-up.objective: Children learn that medicines and vitamins help only when a trusted adult gives them and are never candy, circle the things only a grown-up may give or use, and practice saying "I need to ask a grown-up first."

note.mistake: Children think gummy vitamins are candy, and that if medicine helps, more is better. They think medicine is fine if a friend or an older child gives it, and that a cleaner in a cup is a drink.
note.words: Say: "Medicine can look like candy. Only a trusted grown-up gives it to you." Say: "If you find pills or a bottle, do not touch it. Tell a grown-up." Read the sentence at the top of the page together. Children circle in red each thing only a trusted grown-up may give them or use, and put a check in the box under each food and drink. Level 1 has six cards; Level 2 has eight, with a spray cleaner; Level 3 has eight and the sentence "I ask a grown-up first." to trace and say.
note.watch: Right: the medicine, the gummy vitamins, the shot, and the spray cleaner are circled in red; the carrot, milk, bread, banana, and apple are checked. Ask about the vitamins: "Why do they need a grown-up?" Keep it plain: many homes keep medicine, and that is fine when a grown-up stores and gives it. For grown-ups, the Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222. No answer key.

1:ask-a-grown-up.routine: Show photos side by side, never real medicine or cleaners: pills next to candy, gummy vitamins next to gummy bears, a spray cleaner next to a sports drink. Children guess which is which and find how hard it is to tell. Then a puppet offers a child "candy" that is really vitamins, and children practice the answer: "I need to ask a grown-up first." Last, practice what to do when you find pills or a bottle: do not touch, and tell a grown-up.

1:myplate-groups.title: MyPlate: The Five Food Groups
1:myplate-groups.objective: Children sort foods into the five MyPlate food groups (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy) and find where each group sits on a MyPlate picture, with milk, yogurt, and cheese in the dairy cup.

note.mistake: Children put eggs in dairy because they are near the milk in the store, and cheese in protein. They think one food group is the "good" one, or that a food they like must be a fruit.
note.words: Say: "MyPlate shows the five food groups. Fruits and vegetables fill half the plate. Milk, yogurt, and cheese go in the dairy cup." Say: "All five groups help us grow; we need foods from each one." Ask: "Where does an egg go? Why?" Level 1: children draw a line from each of five foods (one from each group) to its part of the plate. Level 2 has ten foods. Level 3: children first write the group names on the plate from the word bank, then draw the lines.
note.watch: Right: the pear, orange, banana, apple, and strawberry are fruits; the lettuce, carrot, celery, and broccoli vegetables; the bread, oatmeal, cereal, and toast grains; the ham, egg, and fish protein foods; the milk, yogurt, and cheese dairy. A child who says cereal has milk is right that the milk is dairy; the cereal itself is a grain. On Level 3, accept any consistent labeling: the lines must go to the labels the child wrote. No answer key.

1:myplate-groups.routine: Lay out five hula hoops or large paper plates labeled fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy, beside a MyPlate picture. Children sort clean, empty food packages and food pictures cut from grocery store flyers into the five groups and tell why. If you use real food, check your allergy list first.

1:myplate-lunch.title: Build a MyPlate Lunch
1:myplate-lunch.objective: Children find the times in a school day when they eat or drink (breakfast, snack, lunch, a drink after recess) and build a lunch with a food from each MyPlate group and water or milk to drink.

note.mistake: Children think a good lunch must be big, or must have every food they like. They forget the drink, or think the drink does not matter. Some think a lunch from home is wrong if it looks different.
note.words: Say: "A MyPlate lunch has a food from each group and water or milk to drink." Ask: "Which group is missing from your plate?" Never comment on what a child eats at home or whether he or she had breakfast; every family's food can fit on a plate. The page asks, "Circle the times you eat or drink on a school day," then children cut out one food for each part of the plate and glue it on. Level 1 has four parts with picture hints; Level 2 adds the dairy cup and has no hints; Level 3 adds writing each food's name and circling water or milk.
note.watch: Each part of the plate should hold one food from its group; there are more cards than parts, so children choose. The circled times are each child's own: any circles are right. On Level 3, invented spelling is fine. If a child says he or she did not eat breakfast, listen kindly and let the school know quietly if needed. No answer key.

1:myplate-lunch.routine: Give each child a paper plate, a paper cup, and food pictures cut from grocery store flyers, or let small groups use play food. Each child builds a lunch with one food from each group, sets a picture of water or milk in the cup, and tells a partner what is on the plate. Talk about the times in a school day when we eat or drink. If you use real food, check your allergy list.

1:habit-to-grow.title: Which Habit Will I Grow?
1:habit-to-grow.objective: Children check which healthy habits they already do (brushing teeth twice, washing hands, drinking water, moving their body, going to bed on time) and choose one habit to do more for the next two weeks.

note.mistake: Children think healthy means doing everything perfectly, and that one missed day means they failed. Some choose a habit they already do every day, so it cannot grow.
note.words: Say: "A habit is something we do again and again. Small steps every day help a habit grow." Ask: "Which habit would you like to do a little more?" The page: children color the sun next to each habit they did yesterday, then circle the one habit they will do more. Level 1 has three habits; Level 2 has five; Level 3 adds the sentence "Every day I will ___."
note.watch: There are no right or wrong answers on this page: the suns are each child's own honest check. The circled habit should be one the child wants to do more; accept any choice. Never compare children's suns or charts. A child with few suns needs encouragement, not blame: what happens at home is not up to a first grader alone. On Level 3, the sentence should name the circled habit. No answer key.

1:habit-to-grow.routine: Play habit charades: a child acts out brushing teeth, washing hands, drinking water, jumping, or yawning and climbing into bed, and the class names the habit. Then each child chooses one habit to grow and draws it on a small card to take home. For two weeks, at morning meeting, children who did their habit show a thumbs-up; there is no thumbs-down.

1:health-helpers.title: Health Helpers at School and in Town
1:health-helpers.objective: Children visit the school nurse's office, name the health helpers in town (doctor, dentist, pharmacist, firefighter, paramedic) and what each does, and practice asking their teacher to see the nurse when they feel sick or get hurt.

note.mistake: Children think only women are nurses and only men are doctors or firefighters. They think firefighters only put out fires, and that a pharmacist gives medicine to children directly.
note.words: Say: "Health helpers keep us safe and healthy. At school, the nurse helps when you feel sick or get hurt: ask your teacher first." Ask: "Who would help if someone was badly hurt? Who gives medicine to your grown-up?" Level 1: children draw a line from each of three helpers (a doctor, a nurse, a firefighter) to the helper's name. Level 2 adds the pharmacist behind a pharmacy counter and the sentence "When I feel sick or get hurt at school, I ask my teacher to see the ___." Level 3 adds "A ___ keeps people healthy by ___."
note.watch: Each helper goes to its own name; the pharmacist stands behind a counter with medicine shelves and an Rx sign. Say that men and women do every one of these jobs. The sentence on Levels 2 and 3 is "nurse"; if your school has a health aide, or the office helps instead, accept that answer too. On Level 3, accept any true sentence, such as "A doctor keeps people healthy by checking them when they are sick." No answer key.

1:health-helpers.routine: Visit the school nurse's office. The nurse shows a few tools (a thermometer, a bandage, an ice pack) and tells when children should come. Back in the room, children practice asking: "May I please see the nurse? My stomach hurts." Then show photos of a doctor, a dentist, a pharmacist, a firefighter, and a paramedic, and the class says how each one helps people stay healthy.

1:whole-body-listening.title: Listen with Your Whole Body
1:whole-body-listening.objective: Children practice whole-body listening (eyes toward the speaker, quiet hands and feet, ears open, a calm body), repeat back what a partner said, and use the skill to follow a safety direction the first time it is given.

note.mistake: Children think listening means only being quiet, or staring hard at the speaker. Many hear the first words of a direction and stop listening. Some repeat their own idea instead of the partner's.
note.words: Say: "We listen with our whole body: eyes toward the speaker, ears open, mouth quiet, hands and feet still." Say: "In a fire drill or on a field trip, listening the first time keeps us safe." Some children listen best while moving a little or without looking at a face; that is okay, and the page is a help, not a test. The page: children color the sun next to each body part that listened. Level 1 has eyes, ears, and mouth; Level 2 adds hands and feet; Level 3 adds "My partner said ___."
note.watch: There are no wrong answers on this page: the suns are each child's own check, and an honest uncolored sun is fine. On Level 3, the sentence should tell one thing the partner really said; accept the main idea, not the exact words. Watch the "Teacher says" game for children who follow a direction the first time, and name it: "You heard it the first time." No answer key.

1:whole-body-listening.routine: Show a whole-body listening picture card. Read a short story with one direction hidden in it ("When you hear the word blue, touch your nose"), and see who catches it. Partners take turns telling about their weekend while the listener repeats one thing he or she heard. End with a "Teacher says" game with safety directions: line up, freeze, walk to the door, hands to yourself.

1:fire-safety-911.title: Fire Safety and Calling 911
1:fire-safety-911.objective: Children practice getting out and staying out, crawling low under smoke, and stop, drop, and roll, tell what a smoke alarm sounds like, and learn to call 911 only in a real emergency, saying their name and address.

note.mistake: Children think hiding under a bed or in a closet is safe in a fire, or that they should go back for a pet or a toy. They think 911 is for a lost toy or a small scrape. Some are scared of firefighters in masks and hide from them.
note.words: Say: "Smoke rises, so the clean air is low: crawl." Say: "Call 911 only in a real emergency: a fire, or someone badly hurt or very sick." Say: "Firefighters may look scary in their masks. They are there to help you; go to them." Level 1: children write 1, 2, 3 under stop, drop, and roll, circle 9 and 1 on the phone, and write their name. Level 2 adds "I live at ___." Level 3 adds "I call 911 only when ___."
note.watch: Right: stop 1, drop 2, roll 3; the 9 and the 1 are circled. Check addresses privately, send the page home for a grown-up to check, and never post addresses in the room. If a family has no fixed address, accept the name of the place where the child lives and a grown-up's phone number, and follow your school's privacy rules. On Level 3, accept "there is a fire" or "someone is badly hurt." No answer key.

1:fire-safety-911.routine: Tell the class first, then press the test button on a smoke alarm so children know its sound; for children sensitive to loud sounds, play a recording. Practice crawling low on the rug to the door, getting out, and going to the class meeting place. Practice stop, drop (cover your face with your hands), and roll over and over until the fire is out. Say the rule together: "Get out and stay out. Never go back for a toy or a pet." Then each child calls you on a toy or paper phone and says, "My name is ... I live at ...". Never dial 911 to practice.

1:say-no-go-tell.title: Say No, Go Away, Tell a Trusted Adult
1:say-no-go-tell.objective: Children practice what to do when something feels uncomfortable or unsafe (say "No!" in a strong voice, go away, tell a trusted adult) and act it out for calm playground scenes.

note.mistake: Children think telling is tattling, or that they will get in trouble for telling. They think they must keep a secret when someone asks them to. Many think only strangers can make them feel unsafe.
note.words: Say: "If something feels unsafe or uncomfortable, say No! in a strong voice, go away, and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault." Say: "We never keep a secret that makes us feel unsafe. If the first grown-up does not listen, tell another one, and keep telling until someone helps." Level 1: children write 1, 2, 3 under the steps, trace the three steps, and draw themselves saying No! Level 2: children write who they can tell at school, at recess, and at home. Level 3 adds "If the first grown-up does not listen, I ___."
note.watch: Right: say No! 1, go away 2, tell a grown-up 3. Accept any trusted adult in each place: the teacher, the recess aide, the nurse, a family grown-up. On Level 3, accept "tell another grown-up" or "keep telling." If a child tells you something worrying, listen calmly, thank the child for telling, do not promise to keep it a secret or ask leading questions, and follow your school's reporting rules. No answer key.

1:say-no-go-tell.routine: Teach the three steps with hand signs: a flat hand for No, walking fingers for Go, and a hand beside the mouth for Tell. Small groups act out calm scenes from picture cards: an older child pushing, a dare to climb the fence, and a grown-up they do not know asking them to leave the playground. After each scene, the class decides which trusted adult to tell: the teacher, the recess aide, or a family grown-up.

1:help-a-friend.title: Helping a Friend Stay Healthy
1:help-a-friend.objective: Children list ways to help a friend make healthy choices (a reminder to wash before lunch, an invitation to play, sharing a spot in the shade, getting a grown-up when a friend is hurt) and practice one kind reminder in a friendly voice.

note.mistake: Children think helping a friend means bossing or telling on them. They think only grown-ups can help someone stay healthy. Some think getting a grown-up when a friend is hurt is tattling.
note.words: Say: "Friends help each other stay healthy. A friendly voice and the word let's invite a friend to join you." Ask: "Which reminder would you want to hear?" Say: "When a friend is hurt, getting a grown-up is a big help." Level 1: children trace "Let's wash our hands!", circle one way they helped a friend this week, and draw it. Level 2: in each of three scenes, children circle the reminder a friend would listen to, then draw one way they helped. Level 3 has the three scenes and "A friendly voice works better because ___."
note.watch: Right on Levels 2 and 3: "Come sit with me in the shade!", "Let's get a drink of water!", and "Let's wash our hands before lunch!"; the bossy ones end in "Now!" or "Hurry!" or say "Get out of the sun!" On Level 1, any true way the child helped is right. On Level 3, accept "a friend wants to listen" or "it feels kind." No answer key.

1:help-a-friend.routine: Fill a class chart, "How can I help a friend be healthy?", and sketch a quick picture beside each idea. Pairs act out one reminder, "Let's wash our hands before lunch!", once in a bossy voice and once in a friendly voice, and the class says which one a friend would listen to. During the week, each child draws one way he or she helped a friend on a sticky note for the chart.

1:five-senses.title: Our Five Senses
1:five-senses.objective: Children sort things by the sense they use for each, name the body part that does it, and say "I can hear ..." sentences about sounds they find in the classroom.

note.mistake: Children mix up smell and taste, and think we touch only with our fingers. Because we can see almost everything, some draw every line to the eye.
note.words: Say: "Scientists use their senses to observe. Each sense has its own body part." For each picture ask, "Which sense do you use MOST for this?" On Sort by Sense, children draw a line from each picture to a sense box; each box shows its word and its body part, so read the five words together. On Which Sense?, children circle one body part in each row. Each page is the same at every level.
note.watch: The pictures change from copy to copy. Right: candy, cookies, and other foods go to taste; drums, guitars, bells, and other things that make sounds to hear; flowers to smell; the sand, rock, and feather to touch; things we look at or through (a star, lights, a flashlight, binoculars) to see. A child who says "I can see the sand too" is right; ask, "Which sense tells you it is rough?" No answer key.

1:five-senses.routine: Set up five stations, one sense each: shake a bell in a closed box (hear), sniff a cotton ball with a drop of vanilla (smell), feel sandpaper and a feather in a paper bag (touch), look at a leaf with a magnifying glass (see), and taste an apple slice only with families' permission and after checking allergies (taste). Then children listen with eyes closed for one minute, and you write the sounds they heard: "I can hear the clock."

1:weather.title: Weather Words and the Weekly Forecast
1:weather.objective: Children write the weather word for each symbol, read a five-day forecast, and decide which day is best for outdoor recess and which day needs a raincoat.

note.mistake: Children think a forecast is a promise, so they are upset when it is wrong. They read every cloud as rain, and mix up the rain and storm symbols. Some think one cold week means it is always cold where they live.
note.words: Say: "Weather is what the air outside is like today. A forecast tells what the weather will probably be." On Write the Weather Word, children find each symbol's word in the bank and write it, one letter in each box: "Count the boxes. The word has that many letters." On Read the Weekly Forecast, the five days have one symbol each; read each question aloud, children find the symbol, then circle the day under it. Each page is the same at every level. Ask the class questions too: "Which day is best for recess? Which day needs a raincoat?"
note.watch: Right on the word page: sun, cloud, rain, storm, snow, and rainbow, each matching its number of boxes. On the forecast page, the days change from copy to copy; check that the circled day has the symbol the question names. For recess, accept a sunny or a cloudy day with a reason. A child who circles the day before or after has lost track of the column: have him or her point from the symbol straight down. No answer key.

1:weather.routine: On Monday, print a five-day forecast for your town from a local TV station or weather.gov and post it on the Calendar Wall. Read it together and choose the best day for outdoor recess and the day that needs a raincoat. Each morning, a weather helper looks outside and posts the real weather beside the forecast. On Friday, the class compares the two: "Was the forecast right every day?"

1:sun-earth-moon.title: Sun, Earth, and Moon
1:sun-earth-moon.objective: Children read facts about the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon and check which one each fact is about, then put pictures of the Moon in order as its lit part grows and shrinks.

note.mistake: Children say the Moon makes its own light, that it really changes shape, and that the Sun goes around the Earth. They do not believe the Sun is a star, because it looks so different from the stars at night.
note.words: Say: "The Sun is a star. It makes its own light and heat. The Moon has no light of its own; sunlight shines on it. The Moon does not change shape: we see more or less of its sunny side." On Sun, Earth and Moon, children read each sentence, with you as needed, and check one box: Level 1 has six sentences, Level 2 eight, Level 3 ten. On Moon Phases in Order, say: "The white part is the part we see lit by the Sun. A wedge that gets wider means the lit part grows." Children write 1 to 5 in each row. That page is one level.
note.watch: Right: covered in craters, goes around our planet, shape seems to change, and the smallest are the Moon; big oceans, air we can breathe, a planet, and its turning gives day and night are the Earth; makes its own light, a star, the biggest, and the hottest are the Sun. In the growing row, the dark moon is 1, then the thin sliver, the half, the almost-full moon, and the full moon 5; the shrinking row starts at the full moon. No answer key.

1:sun-earth-moon.routine: Darken the room and set a lamp without its shade on a table as the Sun; nobody touches the hot bulb. In small groups, with room to turn, each child holds a foam ball on a pencil at arm's length, a little above the head, as the Moon, and faces the lamp. Children turn slowly in a circle and watch the ball's lit part grow from a thin sliver to a full circle and shrink again.

1:animal-classes-coverings.title: Animal Groups and Body Coverings
1:animal-classes-coverings.objective: Children sort animals into mammals, birds, and reptiles by their body coverings (fur, feathers, scales) and tell how each covering helps.

note.mistake: Children say a penguin is not a bird because it cannot fly, and that a bat is a bird because it flies. They think a turtle has no scales because of its shell. Some sort by where an animal lives or by its size.
note.words: Say: "Mammals have fur or hair. Birds have feathers. Reptiles have dry scales." Then: "Fur keeps a mammal warm. Feathers keep a bird warm and help most birds fly. Scales protect a reptile's skin." On Sort the Animals, children draw a line from each animal to Mammals, Birds, or Reptiles; on Animal Coverings, to Fur, Feathers, or Scales. Both pages have 6 animals on Level 1, 9 on Level 2, and 12 on Level 3.
note.watch: In the first copies, the mammals are the wolf, sheep, panda, zebra, pig, dog, giraffe, cat, fox, rabbit, and lion; the birds the seagull, owl, penguin, woodpecker, duck, swan, peacock, and parrot; the reptiles the snake, tortoise, turtle, chameleon, iguana, gecko, and alligator. A pig has short, bristly hair even when you cannot see it, and its babies drink milk: it is a mammal. The turtle's shell is covered with big scales. The fish on Level 3 of the coverings page has scales but is not a reptile. No answer key.

1:animal-classes-coverings.routine: Pass around a feather, a scrap of fake fur, and a toy lizard or a photo of snakeskin, and let children feel and describe each one. Then test fur: fill two cups with warm (not hot) tap water, wrap one in the fake fur, and leave the other bare. After 15 minutes, children touch both cups: the wrapped one is still warmer.

1:body-parts.title: Parts of Our Body and Their Jobs
1:body-parts.objective: Children label the parts of the human body, tell the job of each part, and compare our parts with an animal's: our hands grab like a monkey's, our eyes face forward like an owl's.

note.mistake: Children mix up the shoulder and the elbow, and call the whole arm "hand" and the whole leg "foot," so they write "arm" for the shoulder tag. When spelling, they skip letters and leave boxes empty.
note.words: Say: "Every part of our body has a job." Ask: "What would be hard without your elbows? Without your knees?" The page has a figure with six numbered tags; children find each tag and write the part's name, one letter in each box. The page has no word bank, so leave the sticky notes from the tracing in sight, or write the words on the board. Say: "Count the boxes. The word has that many letters." The page is one level.
note.watch: In the first copy the six parts are the ear, mouth, shoulder, arm, hand, and knee; other copies choose other parts, so check each tag on the figure. A word is right when it names the tagged part; accept a letter or two off when the child says the word and the boxes count. Ask about two parts, "What job does it do?" A child who writes "leg" for the knee tag is close: point to the bend and ask what it is called. No answer key.

1:body-parts.routine: Trace one volunteer's body on a long sheet of butcher paper. Children take turns writing a body word on a sticky note and sticking it on that part, and the class says the part's job: "Hands hold things. Legs walk and run. Ears hear." Then show photos of a monkey holding a branch and an owl looking straight ahead, and children compare: "Our hands grab like a monkey's. Our eyes face forward like an owl's." Hang the tracing for the lesson.

1:habitats-needs.title: Where Animals Live and What They Need
1:habitats-needs.objective: Children match animals to the habitats where they find food, water, and shelter, and tell what each animal needs.

note.mistake: Children think an animal chooses where it likes to live, as people do. They think every water animal can live in any water, and that whales and dolphins are fish. Some think a savanna is a zoo.
note.words: Say: "A habitat is the place where an animal finds what it needs: food, water, and shelter." Ask: "Could a whale live in a pond? Why not?" On Animal Habitats, four pictures are labeled A, rainforest; B, savanna; C, pond; and D, ocean; children write the letter under each animal. That page is one level. On Where Do Animals Live?, children draw a line from each animal to Land or Water: Level 1 has 6 animals, Level 2 8, Level 3 10.
note.watch: Right on the habitats page: the toucan, macaw, and gorilla A; the lion B; the beaver and dragonfly C; the whale and octopus D. On the land page (the animals change from copy to copy): the cat, dog, lion, horse, and elephant land; the fish, dolphin, whale, shark, jellyfish, and octopus water. A child who says "a dolphin breathes air" is right: it comes up to breathe and still lives in water. Ask about one animal, "What does it eat there?" No answer key.

1:habitats-needs.routine: Lay four large sheets of paper on tables labeled rainforest, savanna, pond, and ocean, with a photo or a drawing of each. Children place toy animals or animal photos where each one lives and tell where it finds food, water, and shelter: "The beaver eats bark, drinks from the pond, and lives in a lodge." Then walk the schoolyard: a grown-up lifts a log or a rock, rolling it toward himself or herself; children look but never reach under it. Put it back gently.

1:plant-parts.title: Parts of a Plant
1:plant-parts.objective: Children dig up a weed or a bean plant, wash the roots, find the roots, stem, leaves, and flower, and label each part and its job on a diagram.

note.mistake: Children think plants eat soil through their roots and that roots are the bottom of the stem. They call every colorful part a flower, and do not know that the pod is a fruit or that the beans inside are seeds.
note.words: Say: "Roots take in water and hold the plant in the soil. The stem holds the plant up and carries water. Leaves use sunlight to make the plant's food. The flower makes seeds, and the fruit holds the seeds." Ask about the celery: "How did the color get to the leaves?" (Up the long celery stalk, which carries water the way a stem does.) The page: children write the name of the part each numbered tag points to. Level 1 has four tags and a bank (leaf, stem, flower, roots); Level 2 six tags and a bank that adds seed and fruit; Level 3 six tags and no bank.
note.watch: Check each tag against the drawing: the fruit is the green pod, and a seed is one bead inside it; the leaf tag sits on a leaf, and the roots tag sits in the soil. On Level 3, write the six words on the board for children who need them. Accept invented spelling when the part is right. Ask about one part, "What is its job?" No answer key.

1:plant-parts.routine: With gloves, pull up a few small weeds from the schoolyard (ask first) or bean plants the class grew. Shake off the soil, swish the roots in a tub of water, and lay each plant on a paper towel. Children look with magnifying glasses and point to the roots, stem, leaves, and any flowers. Open a pea pod to find the seeds. Then stand a celery stalk with leaves in a cup of water with food coloring; the next day the leaves show the color. Wash hands afterward.

1:life-cycles.title: Life Cycles in Order
1:life-cycles.objective: Children put the life cycles of a chicken, a butterfly, a frog, and a plant in order and tell what the young looks like at each stage.

note.mistake: Children think a caterpillar and a butterfly are two different animals, and that a tadpole is a fish. They put the stages in a line and stop at the grown-up. Some put the hen first and the egg last.
note.words: Say: "A life cycle is the way a living thing grows and changes. When it is grown, it has young, and the cycle starts again." Ask: "Does the caterpillar look like its parent? What changes?" On The Life Cycle of a Chicken, children write 1, 2, and 3 under eggs in a nest, a chick, and a hen; that page is one level. On Butterfly Life Cycle, Level 1 prints the egg as 1 and the butterfly as 4, and children write 2 and 3; on Level 2 only the egg is printed, children write 2 to 4, and the last box asks what comes after the butterfly; Level 3 prints no numbers.
note.watch: Right: the eggs 1, the chick 2, and the hen 3; the egg 1, the caterpillar 2, the chrysalis 3, and the butterfly 4. The box after the butterfly is 1: the butterfly lays eggs, and the cycle starts again. A child who writes 5 sees a line, not a cycle. Call it a chrysalis; a moth spins a cocoon. No answer key.

1:life-cycles.routine: Act out the butterfly life cycle together: curl up small as an egg on a leaf, crawl and munch as a caterpillar, hold still wrapped in arms as a chrysalis, then stretch and flap as a butterfly that lays eggs again. Then hand out large stage cards for the chicken, the frog, and a bean plant. Small groups stand in a circle in the right order and walk around once, to show that the cycle starts again.

1:materials-recycling.title: What Is It Made Of?
1:materials-recycling.objective: Children sort clean recycling into paper, cardboard, plastic, glass, metal, and wood by how each one looks and feels, and draw three things their family recycles at home.

note.mistake: Children decide by color or shine: anything clear is glass, and anything shiny is metal. They call a cardboard box paper, and think a thing is made of what is inside it, such as a jar of jam being "jam."
note.words: Say: "Look and feel, then test. What is it made of?" Ask: "Does it bend? What sound does it make when you tap it?" On What Is It Made Of?, eight things are numbered; children write the material from the bank (plastic, paper, cardboard, glass, metal) on each line. Read the bank together. On Three Things I Recycle, children draw three things their family recycles at home and write what each one is; it can go home to finish with a grown-up. Each page is one level.
note.watch: Right in the first copy: the bolt and the saucepan are metal; the spoon is plastic; the notebook and the sheet of paper are paper; the honey jar and the jam jar are glass; the box is cardboard. Other copies add a toothbrush, comb, glue, shampoo, or sunscreen tube (plastic), an envelope or a letter (paper), and a can (metal). Cardboard is thick, stiff paper; the box is cardboard. On the drawing page, accept any thing the family recycles. No answer key.

1:materials-recycling.routine: Bring clean, empty things: a newspaper, a cereal box, a plastic bottle, a glass jar, a can with taped edges, and a wooden craft stick. Children tap each one with a pencil (metal rings, glass clinks, plastic thuds) and try to bend it (paper bends), then sort the things onto trays by material. A grown-up handles the glass; anything chipped or broken stays out.

1:sink-float.title: Sink or Float? Predict and Test
1:sink-float.objective: Children predict and then test whether objects sink or float, find that some heavy things float while some light things sink, and use the results to choose materials for a raft.

note.mistake: Children think heavy things always sink and light things always float. They change their guess after the test so it looks right.
note.words: Say: "Scientists make a guess, then test it. A wrong guess teaches us something." Ask: "The pumpkin is heavier than the nail. Why does it float?" On Sink or Float?, children draw a line from each object to the group they THINK it belongs in, before the test (4, 6, or 8 objects on Levels 1 to 3). On the experiment page, each object has two tanks: children color the top ring (floats) or the bottom ring (sinks) in My guess before the test and in The test after it, and the star if they were surprised (4, 6, or 7 objects).
note.watch: In water: the leaf, feather, apple, lemon, banana, duck, boat, ball, pumpkin, pine cone, pencil, and log float; the rock, bolt, nail, key, fork, hammer, pliers, and scissors sink. The first page is a guess, so any line is fine there. On the experiment page, check that The test matches what the class saw, and that the guess was not changed. No answer key.

1:sink-float.routine: Fill a clear tub with water, lay out towels, and test the things on the pages: a pine cone, a leaf, a rock, a bolt, a nail, metal scissors, a ball, a small pumpkin, a toy boat, a wooden pencil, a block of wood, and an apple. Children predict with a thumbs-up (float) or a thumbs-down (sink), then watch. Let them hold the pumpkin and the nail: which is heavier? A grown-up handles the nail and the scissors.

1:vibrations-make-sound.title: Feel the Buzz: Vibrations Make Sound
1:vibrations-make-sound.objective: Children pluck rubber bands, tap a drum with rice on it, twang a ruler, and hum with fingers on their throat, and find that every sound came with something shaking.

note.mistake: Children think the sound comes from hitting, not from shaking. They expect to see every shake, so humming "does not count." They do not notice that the sound stops when the shaking stops.
note.words: Say: "Sound is made when something shakes back and forth very fast. That shaking is called a vibration." At each station ask, "What shook? Did you feel it, see it, or both?" Then: "Hold the ruler still. What happened to the sound?" The page: at each station children circle "I felt it shake," "I saw it shake," or both. Level 1 has three stations; Level 2 has four and a box to draw the part that moved; Level 3 adds the sentence "The sound came when the ___ shook."
note.watch: The page records what each child noticed. Usually children see the rubber bands, the rice, and the ruler shake, and feel their throat shake. Either circle, or both, is right when it is true for that child. The part that moved: the rubber band, the drum top, the end of the ruler, or the throat; on Level 3 accept any of them. On Day 3, a tighter band or a shorter ruler end makes a higher sound, because it shakes faster. No answer key.

1:vibrations-make-sound.routine: Set up four stations: rubber bands stretched around an open shoebox to pluck; a drum made of plastic wrap pulled tight over a bowl with a rubber band, with a spoonful of rice on top to tap; a ruler held flat on a desk with one end sticking out to twang; and a spot to hum with fingertips resting lightly on the throat. Small groups visit every station. On Day 3, groups try one change: a band stretched a little tighter, or a shorter ruler end. What happens to the sound? Rubber bands stay on the box, never snapped at anyone.

1:sound-moves-things.title: Sound Makes Things Move
1:sound-moves-things.objective: Children bang a pan near a drum with rice on it, dip a ringing tuning fork into water, and rest a hand on a speaker playing music, and find that sound can make things vibrate.

note.mistake: Children think the wind from the pan moved the rice, or that the pan must touch the drum. They think sound is only something we hear, not something that can push. Some draw the "with the sound" picture the same as "before."
note.words: Say: "Sound travels through the air as vibrations, and it can make other things vibrate too." Ask: "The pan did not touch the drum. What made the rice jump?" Try a soft bang and a loud bang. For each test, children draw the thing before the sound and with the sound, then circle what happened. Level 1 has two tests (the pan and the tuning fork); Level 2 adds the speaker; Level 3 adds the sentence "The sound made the ___ move."
note.watch: The page records the class's tests. A right drawing shows the rice still before and jumping with the sound, the water flat before and splashing with the sound. On the speaker row, children circle what their hand felt. If nothing moved, bang louder or closer and test again; record what really happened. On Level 3, accept the rice, the water, the speaker, or my hand. No answer key.

1:sound-moves-things.routine: Hold a metal pan close to the plastic-wrap drum with rice on it, without touching it, and bang the pan with a wooden spoon; warn the class before each bang. Then strike a tuning fork (borrow one from the music room) on a rubber eraser and dip its tips into a clear cup of water. Last, each child rests a hand on a small speaker playing music. Keep the bangs short, and wipe up spilled water.

1:cup-telephone.title: Cup Telephones
1:cup-telephone.objective: Children build a cup-and-string telephone, test it with the string tight, loose, and touching a chair, and find the string must be tight to carry a whisper.

note.mistake: Children think the sound travels through the air between the cups, so a loose string should work. They shout instead of whispering, so they hear each other without the telephone.
note.words: Say: "Your voice makes the cup bottom vibrate. The string carries the vibrations to the other cup, and it gives them back as sound." Ask: "What changed when the string was loose?" Say: "Whisper, so you only hear it through the string." The page: children circle the cups and the string the class used, then circle "I heard it" or "I did not hear it" for each test. Level 1 has two tests (tight, loose); Level 2 adds a drawing of our telephone and the chair test; Level 3 adds one change that made the telephone work better.
note.watch: The class's results decide. Most groups hear the whisper with the string tight and not with it loose or touching the chair. A group that heard a little through a loose string can circle "I heard it": ask, "Was it as clear as with a tight string?" On Level 3, accept any change the class really tried, such as pulling the string tighter or keeping it off the chair. No answer key.

1:cup-telephone.routine: Each pair gets two paper or plastic cups and about 15 feet of string or yarn. A grown-up pokes a small hole in each cup bottom with a pencil. Children push the string ends through, tie a big knot inside each cup, and walk apart. One whispers into a cup while the other listens. Test with the string pulled tight and hanging loose; on Day 3, test it touching a chair and try one change of your own. Keep string away from necks.

1:see-with-light.title: We See Only with Light
1:see-with-light.objective: Children peek through a hole into a closed shoebox with a toy inside, then open a flap in the lid, and explain that they could see the toy only when light shone on it.

note.mistake: Children think we can see in total darkness if we wait, or that cats can. Some think our eyes send out light. If light sneaks in through a gap, they say they saw the toy in the dark.
note.words: Say: "We see a thing when light shines on it and bounces into our eyes. No light, no seeing." Ask: "What was different when the flap was open?" The page shows the box twice, flap closed and flap open. Level 1: children circle "I saw it" or "I did not see it" for each box. Level 2 adds a box to draw what they saw through the hole. Level 3 adds the sentence "I could see the toy when ___."
note.watch: Right: with the flap closed, children did not see the toy; with it open, they did. A child who saw something with the flap closed is telling the truth: light got in through a gap. Tape it, test again, and talk about it. On Level 3, accept "the flap was open" or "light came in." No answer key.

1:see-with-light.routine: Make a peep box: a shoebox with a small toy inside, a hole the size of a pencil in one end, and a flap cut in the lid on three sides so it can open. Tape the box shut so no light gets in. Each child looks through the hole with the flap closed, then again with the flap open while a friend shines a flashlight in. Shine the light into the box, never into eyes.

1:light-through-materials.title: Does Light Go Through?
1:light-through-materials.objective: Children shine a flashlight at wax paper, plastic wrap, cardboard, a clear cup, thick cloth, and foil, and sort each one: lets all light through, lets some through, or blocks it.

note.mistake: Children think foil lets light through because it is shiny, or that clear things are "nothing." They judge by color instead of by looking at the spot on the paper.
note.words: Say: "Some materials let all the light through, some let a little through, and some block it." Teach the words clear (all light), cloudy (some light), and blocks (no light). Ask: "Look at the paper. Is the spot bright, dim, or gone?" Level 1: children color the box for all light, some light, or no light for four materials. Level 2 has six materials. Level 3: children write clear, cloudy, or blocks from the word bank, then test one more thing from the room, draw it, and write its name.
note.watch: Right: plastic wrap and the clear cup let all light through (clear); wax paper lets some through (cloudy); cardboard, foil, and thick cloth block it. A thin cloth may let some light through: accept what the class's cloth did. On Level 3, the extra material and its word must match the test. No answer key.

1:light-through-materials.routine: Dim the room and tape a sheet of white paper to the wall. Pairs hold each material between a flashlight and the paper: wax paper, plastic wrap, cardboard, a clear plastic cup, a folded towel, and foil. They look at the paper: a bright spot, a dim spot, or no spot at all. Then they sort the materials onto three trays: all light, some light, no light. On Day 3, each child tests one more thing from the room. Never shine the flashlight into eyes.

1:mirrors-bounce-light.title: Mirrors Bounce Light
1:mirrors-bounce-light.objective: Children use a small unbreakable mirror to bounce a flashlight beam onto a paper star on the wall, and find that a mirror sends light off in a new direction.

note.mistake: Children think the mirror makes its own light, or that light goes through it. They think it does not matter which way the mirror is turned. Some draw the path from the star back to the flashlight.
note.words: Say: "Light travels in a straight line until it hits something. A mirror bounces the light off in a new direction." Ask: "Which way did you turn the mirror to reach the star?" Level 1: children trace the dashed path from the flashlight to the mirror to the star, and color the star when their real light lands on it. Level 2: in each room, children circle the one mirror of three that is turned the right way. Level 3: children draw the path with arrows through two mirrors, then choose a mirror in a second room.
note.watch: Right on Level 2: when the star is below the light, the mirror slanted like \; when the star is above, the mirror slanted like /. A mirror standing straight up sends the light back. Test any argued room with a real mirror. On Level 3, the arrows go from the flashlight to the lower mirror, up to the top mirror, and across to the star. Check that every arrow points the way the light travels. No answer key.

1:mirrors-bounce-light.routine: Tape a paper star on the wall. Pairs get a flashlight and a small unbreakable plastic mirror. One child shines the light at the mirror, held on a desk; the other turns the mirror slowly until the spot of light lands on the star. Then move the star and try again. Never shine the light, or its bounce, into anyone's eyes.

1:shadows-near-far.title: Shadows
1:shadows-near-far.objective: Children hold toys in a flashlight beam, see that a shadow forms where something blocks the light, and find that the shadow grows when the toy moves closer to the flashlight.

note.mistake: Children think a shadow is a reflection with the toy's colors, or a thing that can come off. Many think the shadow gets bigger when the toy moves closer to the wall.
note.words: Say: "A shadow forms where something blocks the light. The closer the toy is to the light, the bigger its shadow." Ask: "Where was the toy when the shadow was biggest?" Level 1: children draw a line from each of four toys to its shadow. Level 2: three toys, then a drawing of a toy near the light and its shadow on the wall. Level 3: three toys, then two drawings (near the light and far from it), a circle on the bigger shadow, and the sentence "The shadow got bigger when ___."
note.watch: A shadow matches its toy by outline, not by color: point to the shape. On Level 3, the drawing with the toy near the light has the bigger shadow, and the sentence says "the toy was near the light" or "the toy was close to the flashlight." No answer key.

1:shadows-near-far.routine: Dim the room and shine a flashlight at a wall from a desk. Children make hand shadows, then hold small toys in the beam. One child moves a toy slowly from near the flashlight toward the wall while the class watches the shadow change, and a helper marks the shadow's size with tape: once with the toy near the light, once far from it. Keep the flashlight pointed at the wall.

1:light-messages.title: Send a Message with Light
1:light-messages.objective: Children invent a flashlight code with a partner, test whether a classmate across the darkened room can read it, and change the signal until it works every time.

note.mistake: Children flash too fast to count, so two flashes look like one. Partners forget to agree on the code before they start. Some think a wrong message means they failed, when it shows what to change.
note.words: Say: "People send messages with light: a lighthouse, a traffic light, a car's turn signal." Ask: "What made the message hard to read? What can we change?" The page: children color one circle for each flash of their code and draw their signal light, then for each test circle the message they sent, the message their friend read, and "right" or "wrong." Level 1 has yes and no and two tests; Level 2 adds come here and three tests; Level 3 adds one change that made the message easier to see.
note.watch: A test is right when the message sent and the message read are the same. The code circles must match the code the pair used. A wrong result is useful data: ask what the pair changed next. On Level 3, accept any change the pair really tried. No answer key.

1:light-messages.routine: Pairs invent a code: for example, one flash for yes, two for no, three for come here. Dim the room. One child stands across the room and flashes the light at the floor near the partner's feet; the partner says the message out loud. Switch roles. On Day 3, pairs change what did not work (slower flashes, a pause between them, a brighter light) and test again. Never shine the light into eyes.

1:shadow-through-day.title: My Shadow Through the Day
1:shadow-through-day.objective: Children trace the shadow of a stick in the morning, near noon, and in the afternoon, and find that the shadow moves and changes length because the Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west.

note.mistake: Children think the shadow is longest at noon, or that it disappears at noon. They think the shadow points toward the Sun, and that the Sun really moves around the Earth.
note.words: Say: "We face south. East is on our left, and west is on our right." Say: "The Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west, because the Earth turns." At midday, say out loud: "The shadow is short, but it does not go away. In most of the United States the Sun is never straight overhead." The page calls the midday trace "near noon." Level 1: the Sun is drawn in each picture, and children draw the stick's shadow and circle when it was shortest. Level 2: children draw the Sun and the shadow. Level 3 adds "The Sun seems to move from ___ to ___."
note.watch: Right: in the morning the Sun is low on the left (east) and the shadow is long on the right (west); near noon the Sun is high and the shadow is short; in the afternoon the Sun is low on the right and the shadow is long on the left. The shadow always points away from the Sun. The shortest shadow is near noon. Level 3: from east to west. No answer key.

1:shadow-through-day.routine: On a sunny day, stand a stick upright in a can of sand or soil on the blacktop, in a spot that gets sun all day. The class stands facing south. At about 9:00, at midday when the Sun is highest (about 12:00, or about 1:00 p.m. during daylight saving time), and at about 2:30, a child traces the shadow with chalk and writes the time beside it. Children may point to the Sun, but never look straight at it.

1:moon-journal.title: Moon Journal
1:moon-journal.objective: Children look at the Moon every few days for a month, record its shape, and find that the shapes change in a pattern that repeats and can be predicted.

note.mistake: Children think the Moon comes out only at night and that its shapes change in no order. They color the dark part instead of the bright part. Some think the Earth's shadow makes the shapes.
note.words: Say: "The bright part of the Moon is the part lit by the Sun. The shape we see changes in a pattern that repeats about every month." In the Sun, Earth, and Moon lesson the moons showed the bright part white; here we color the bright part, so the journal looks like the Moon we see. The new Moon is the dark one; we cannot see it. Level 1: eight boxes, every few days; children write the day, color the bright part, or circle "cloudy" or "not in the sky." Level 2: a numbered circle for every day; circle 1 is the first day of the journal, weekends included; X means clouds hid the Moon, and a dash means it was not in the sky. Level 3 adds a guess for the next shape, then the Moon they saw, and "the same" or "not the same."
note.watch: Check that children color the bright part. Over about two weeks the bright part grows from a thin sliver to a full Moon, then shrinks again; in the United States it grows on the right side. Accept a rough shape. Cloudy days are real data. On Level 3, a guess is good when it follows the pattern. No answer key.

1:moon-journal.routine: Start the journal about a month before this lesson, near a new Moon (a Moon calendar shows when), and send a note home asking families to look for the Moon with their child in the evening. After the full Moon, look in the morning sky too: before school or at morning recess the class can often see it toward the west. Hand out the page on the first day and keep it in folders. On Day 3 of the lesson, children compare their journals and guess the next shape. Looking at the Moon is safe; looking at the Sun is not.

1:day-night-sky.title: Stars Come Out at Night
1:day-night-sky.objective: Children compare the day sky and the night sky and explain that the stars are in the sky all the time, but we see them only at night because the bright Sun hides them in the day.

note.mistake: Children think the stars go away or turn off in the day. They think the Moon is only in the night sky, and that the Sun is not a star.
note.words: Say: "The stars are always in the sky. In the day, the Sun is so bright that we cannot see them. The Sun is a star too: the closest one." Ask: "Our flashlight stars were there all the time. Why could we not see them with the lights on?" Level 1: children draw what they can see in the day window and the night window, using the pictures of the Sun, the Moon, and stars. Level 2: the same, without the pictures. Level 3 adds the sentence "The stars are still there in the day, but ___."
note.watch: Right: the Sun in the day window and stars in the night window. The Moon may go in either window: we see it at night and on some days. On Level 3 accept "the Sun is too bright" or "the sky is too bright to see them." No answer key.

1:day-night-sky.routine: Poke small holes in a sheet of black paper and tape it over the end of a flashlight. Turn the flashlight on in the bright classroom and shine the "stars" on the ceiling: they are hard to see. Then turn off the lights and close the blinds: the stars are easy to see. Later, go outside on a morning when the Moon is up and look for it. Never look straight at the Sun.

1:daylight-hours.title: How Long Is the Day?
1:daylight-hours.objective: Children color a bar for the hours of daylight on the 21st of each month from September on, and find that the days are shortest in December and grow longer again.

note.mistake: Children think the days are the same length all year, or that winter days are short because it is cold. Some read the clock time of sunset as the length of the day.
note.words: Say: "Daylight is the time from sunrise to sunset. In our winter the days are short, and in summer they are long. The shortest day is around December 21." Ask: "What happened to the bars from September to December? And in January?" Level 1: children color the bars for September to December from the class chart and circle the month with the shortest day. Level 2 adds January and a box to write each month's hours. Level 3 adds a dashed guess for April. On every level, if months are the same, children circle all of them.
note.watch: The bars must match the class chart. In the northern half of the country December is the shortest bar. In much of the South and Southwest, November, December, and January round to the same hour: children circle all of them, and you may show the minutes from the table, where December 21 is still the shortest day. The April guess is good when it is longer than January; color the real bar when April 21 comes. In Alaska a December bar can be under 7 hours: leave it empty and write the number. No answer key.

1:daylight-hours.routine: Look up the 21st of each month, from September on, on a sunrise-and-sunset table for your town (it shows past dates too), even when the 21st falls on a weekend or in winter break. Round the day length to the nearest hour and add it to a class chart. If you start late, look up the past months together. Level 1 needs September to December; Levels 2 and 3 also need January 21. Add April when it comes.

1:animal-parents.title: Animal Parents and Their Young
1:animal-parents.objective: Children read about animal families, record what parents do (feed, carry, keep warm, protect) and what babies do (call, follow) to help the young survive, and find that some animals, like sea turtles, never care for their young.

note.mistake: Children think every animal takes care of its babies, and that only mothers do. They think babies just wait to be cared for and do nothing to help. Some think a robin carries its chicks.
note.words: Say: "Parents help their young survive: they feed them, carry them, keep them warm, and protect them. Babies help too: they call when they need something and follow their parents." Say: "A sea turtle lays her eggs in the sand and swims away. The babies find the sea by themselves." The page: children circle what each parent and each baby does, as the book or clip showed. Level 1 has the cat and the kangaroo. Level 2 has four families and asks which parent never takes care of its babies. Level 3 has three families, a sentence for each ("The parent ___ so the baby ___."), and the same question.
note.watch: Circles should match what the class read or saw. A cat feeds, carries (by the neck), keeps warm, and protects; kittens call and follow. A kangaroo carries its joey in a pouch. Penguin parents keep the chick warm on their feet and feed it. Robin parents feed and keep chicks warm but do not carry them. The sea turtle is the parent that never takes care of its babies. No answer key.

1:animal-parents.routine: Read short picture books or watch short clips about animal families: a cat and kittens, a kangaroo and a joey, penguins, robins, and sea turtles. After each one, the class adds to a two-column chart: what the parent did and what the baby did. On Day 3, read about the sea turtle, finish the chart, and act it out: a "baby" calls, and a "parent" comes to feed or protect it.

1:design-like-an-animal.title: Copy an Animal: Design a Helper
1:design-like-an-animal.objective: Children study an animal part (a duck's webbed feet, a bird's beak, a beaver's teeth) and design something for people that copies how it works.

note.mistake: Children copy how the animal looks instead of how its part works: tongs shaped like a bird's head. They think an invention must be big or have a motor.
note.words: Say: "Engineers copy how an animal's body part works to solve a problem for people." Ask: "What does this part do for the animal? What could it do for people?" Level 1: children draw a line from each animal part to the invention that copies it, then draw one invention. Level 2: children circle one animal part (a woodpecker's beak, a toucan's beak, or a whale's body shape), draw an invention that copies it, and finish "It helps people ___." Level 3 adds "My ___ works like a ___ because ___."
note.watch: Right on Level 1: the duck's webbed feet go with the paddle, the beaver's front teeth with the saw, and the toucan's beak with the tongs. On Levels 2 and 3, accept any invention that copies how the part works: a woodpecker beak like a hammer or a drill, a toucan beak like tongs, a whale's shape like a submarine or a boat. Ask, "How does it work like the animal's part?" No answer key.

1:design-like-an-animal.routine: First, children paddle in a tub of water with fingers spread, then with a plastic sandwich bag over the spread hand, like a webbed foot, and feel which pushes more water. Then each child makes beak tongs from two craft sticks and a clothespin and picks up pom-poms or dry beans. On Day 3, pairs build a model of their own invention from craft sticks, paper, tape, and clothespins, and show the class how it works.

1:like-parents.title: Like Their Parents, but Not Exactly
1:like-parents.objective: Children compare young animals with their parents and find how each young animal is like its parent and how it is different.

note.mistake: Children expect a baby to be a tiny copy of its parent, so a gray cygnet "cannot be" a swan's baby. They think size is the only difference, or call every clue different.
note.words: Say: "Young animals are like their parents in many ways, but not exactly." Ask: "What does the foal have that its mother has too? What is different?" The page: for each parent and young, children circle each clue that is the same for both and cross out each clue that is different. Level 1 has the horse and foal; Level 2 adds the sheep and lamb and the hen and chick; Level 3 has two pairs and the sentence "The ___ is like its parent because ___, but different because ___."
note.watch: Right: size is different for every pair; has four legs, has a mane, has wool, has two legs, and has a beak are the same; color is different for the hen and the chick (a white hen, a yellow chick). On Level 3, accept any true pair of reasons, such as "The lamb is like its parent because it has wool, but different because it is smaller." No answer key.

1:like-parents.routine: Show photos of animal parents and their young: a dog and puppies, a cat and kittens, a swan and gray cygnets, a horse and a foal. Pairs take one photo, find one way the young is like its parent and one way it is different, and tell the class; write the words on a two-column chart, alike and different. On Day 3, each pair compares a second photo. Keep the comparisons to animals; do not ask children to compare themselves with their own families.

1:seedlings-and-parent.title: Young Plants and Grown Plants
1:seedlings-and-parent.objective: Children compare bean seedlings with a grown bean plant and with each other, and find that young plants of one kind are like their parent but not exactly alike.

note.mistake: Children think a seedling is a different plant because its first leaves look different from the grown plant's. They expect all the seedlings to be exactly the same size.
note.words: Say: "A young plant is like its parent, but not exactly the same. Young plants of one kind are not all the same either." Say: "A bean seedling's first leaves are single leaves. Later leaves grow in threes, like the leaves of our grown plant." The page shows our grown bean plant. Level 1: children draw one seedling, count its leaves, and circle "same" or "different" for leaf shape, size, and color. Level 2 has three seedlings. Level 3 adds the sentence "My seedlings are different from each other because ___."
note.watch: The page records what children see. Size is different. Leaf shape is different while the seedling has only single leaves; accept "same" once its leaves come in threes. Color is usually the same green; a seedling that got less light can be paler. Accept a careful leaf count. On Level 3, accept any true reason ("one is taller," "it has more leaves"). No answer key.

1:seedlings-and-parent.routine: Plant the grown bean plant 8 to 10 weeks before this lesson (bush beans flower in about 6 weeks and make pods in 7 to 8) in a big pot in the sunniest window; if you have none, use a large photo of a grown bean plant. Two or three weeks before the lesson, each child plants a bean seed in a clear cup of soil and keeps it watered. Children set their seedling beside the grown plant, measure both with a paper strip, and count the leaves. Wash hands after handling soil.

1:design-a-raft.title: Design a Raft
1:design-a-raft.objective: Children sketch a raft that will carry ten pennies across a tub of water, choose floating materials, build it, and label how its shape and parts keep the pennies dry.

note.mistake: Children think more material always makes a better raft, and pile the pennies on one side. They build first and plan after, or plan a raft from materials that sank in the float check.
note.words: Say: "Engineers plan before they build. Your raft must carry 10 pennies and keep them dry." Ask: "Which materials floated? How will your raft keep the water off the pennies?" Level 1: children check the materials they used and color the raft drawn on the page. Level 2: children draw their own raft and label two parts that keep the pennies dry. Level 3: children draw it, label three parts, and finish "My raft will float because ___."
note.watch: The page records each group's plan. The checked materials should match what the group used. Good labels name parts that matter, such as "sides," "corks under it," or "flat bottom"; invented spelling is fine. On Level 3, accept a reason tied to the test, such as "corks and foam float." Keep the plans for the next lesson's test. No answer key.

1:design-a-raft.routine: Give each group craft sticks, a foam tray, corks, plastic straws, clear packing tape, a metal washer, and 10 pennies. First, test each material in a tub of water: does it float? Groups then sketch a raft from the materials that floated, and build it on Day 2. On Day 3, they set it gently in the water, add the pennies, and see whether the pennies stay dry. Label each raft with the group's name, let it dry on a paper towel, and retape loose sticks before the test. Keep pennies away from mouths.

1:test-two-rafts.title: Test Two Rafts
1:test-two-rafts.objective: Children load two rafts with pennies one at a time, record how many each held before water came over the top, and tell one strength and one weakness of each raft.

note.mistake: Children count the penny that sank the raft, or drop pennies on one side. They decide which raft is better by how it looks, or test one raft more gently than the other.
note.words: Say: "A fair test treats both rafts the same way: the same water, the same pennies, one at a time." Ask: "Which raft held more? What made it work?" Level 1: children draw each raft and color one circle for each penny it held, with a "+ more" box after 20. Level 2: a tally mark for each penny and the total. Level 3 adds one good thing and one thing to fix for each raft, and the better raft circled (or both, if they held the same).
note.watch: The circles or tallies must match the class count, and the total must match the tallies. The better raft held more pennies. A good thing and a thing to fix should fit what happened: "the sides kept water out," "it tipped, so add corks at the corners." No answer key.

1:test-two-rafts.routine: Both boxes on the page say "our raft": each group tests two rafts of its own. Raft A is the raft the group built in the last lesson; at the start of this lesson the group builds Raft B with one change (more corks, sides, or a foam-tray base). Test both in the same tub: a child adds pennies one at a time, in the middle, while the class counts aloud, and stops when water comes over the top or the raft tips; the raft held the pennies before that one. Count the pennies back into a cup.

2:three-ways-healthy.title: Healthy in Body, Feelings, and Friendships
2:three-ways-healthy.objective: Children sort healthy actions into three parts of being well (my body: sleep, food, moving; my feelings: calming down, talking about a worry; my friendships: playing fair, including others) and name one thing they already do for each part.

note.mistake: Children think being healthy means only food and exercise. They think a worry should be kept inside, that some feelings are bad, or that telling a grown-up a worry is tattling.
note.words: Say: "Being healthy means taking care of my body, my feelings, and my friendships." Say: "All feelings are okay. What we do with them can help us." Ask: "Which part does this help?" Level 1: children cut out six cards and glue each under my body, my feelings, or my friendships. Level 2 has nine cards. Level 3 adds "Write one more thing you do under each part."
note.watch: Right: sharing crayons, inviting a friend to play, and taking turns in a game help my friendships; telling a grown-up a worry, a deep breath to calm down, and drawing to feel better help my feelings; sleeping at night, running fast, and eating an apple help my body. If a child says running with friends helps friendships too, agree, and ask which part the card shows most. On Level 3, accept any true thing the child does. If a worry a child shares makes you concerned for his or her safety, follow your school's reporting steps, and never promise to keep it a secret. No answer key.

2:three-ways-healthy.routine: Lay three hoops on the floor with signs: my body, my feelings, my friendships. A child acts out an action without words (yawning and lying down, taking a slow breath, sharing crayons, inviting someone to play), the class guesses it, and the actor stands in the hoop it helps. Practice one calm breath together: smell the flower, blow out the candle. End in a circle: each child names one thing he or she already does for one part, or passes.

2:healthy-habits-why.title: Why We Do Healthy Habits
2:healthy-habits-why.objective: Children match each habit to what it protects (washing hands keeps germs away, brushing teeth twice a day keeps teeth strong and stops cavities, sleep rests the body and the brain, moving makes the heart and muscles strong, sunscreen and a hat keep skin from burning) and explain one habit in a full sentence.

note.mistake: Children think water alone washes germs away, or that hands are clean if they look clean. They think brushing once a day is enough, and that sleep is only for when they feel tired.
note.words: Say: "A habit is something we do again and again. Each healthy habit protects us." Ask: "Why do we do this one?" Ask children to answer in a full sentence: "We wash our hands because …" The page has five habits and five reasons; children draw a line from each habit to the sentence that tells why we do it. The page is one level.
note.watch: Right: the sun hat and sunscreen go to "We do not get burned on sunny days."; running to "It makes us fit, fast and strong."; washing hands to "It gets rid of the germs we picked up when we touched things."; sleeping to "Our body and brain rest and get ready for a new day."; brushing teeth to "It keeps our smile clean and bright." The rows change from copy to copy. Current practice: scrub with soap for 20 seconds; brush twice a day for two minutes. No answer key.

2:healthy-habits-why.routine: Put a drop of hand lotion and a pinch of ground cinnamon on one child's hands as "germs." Children shake hands around the circle and look: the "germs" spread to many hands. Two children rinse with water only, and two scrub with soap for 20 seconds (sing "Happy Birthday" twice), then compare. Last, everyone jogs in place for a minute and feels the heart beat faster. Check for skin allergies first, and keep hands away from eyes until everyone has washed.
