note.watch: Right: a bad dream at night and a headache at home, a parent; a friend who cannot swim well, the lifeguard; a stomachache at school, the school nurse; lost in a store, a store worker at the checkout; a fire in a building, call 911; a classmate left out again and again and a worry at school that will not go away, the school counselor. "A parent" means any grown-up who cares for the child at home. No answer key.

3:who-can-help.routine: Children practice asking for help clearly: who you are, what happened, and what you need ("Excuse me, I can't find my grown-up. Can you help me?"). Act out short scenes with a pretend lifeguard, school nurse, and store worker. Practice a pretend 911 call on an unplugged phone (your name, where you are, what happened), and talk about what an emergency is: 911 is only for emergencies. If the first grown-up cannot help, keep asking.

3:investigation.title: A Fair Test: One Change at a Time
3:investigation.objective: Children plan a fair sink-or-float test that changes only one thing, keep everything else the same, run it, and write a lab report with their question, prediction, results, and conclusion.

note.mistake: Children change two things at once (a bigger orange and no peel), so they cannot tell which change mattered. They think heavy things always sink, and they write what they expected instead of what happened.
note.words: Say: "In a fair test, we change only one thing and keep everything else the same." Ask: "What is the one thing you changed? What stayed the same?" The page is a lab report: children check one question ("Does an orange float with its peel? Does it float without its peel?" or "How many cubes can a clay boat carry before it sinks?"), write what they think, draw what happened in the two tanks and describe it, then finish "Now I know that ___." The page is one level.
note.watch: An orange with its peel usually floats, because the peel is full of tiny air pockets; without its peel it usually sinks. A clay boat carries cubes until the water comes over its sides. "I think" is right as a guess even when the test shows something else; "I learned" must match what happened. Keep the reports: the later investigations use the same steps. No answer key.

3:investigation.routine: Give each group a tub of water on towels, two oranges, and modeling clay with a cup of plastic counting cubes. Day 1: groups choose a question and list what they will keep the same (the same tub, the same water, the same orange). Orange groups float one orange with its peel, then peel the other and float it. Clay-boat groups add cubes one at a time and count until the boat sinks. Day 2: groups run the test again and finish the report.

3:balanced-forces.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
3:balanced-forces.objective: Children play tug-of-war with a rope and a stuffed animal in the middle, push a box from both sides, and find that equal pushes or pulls in opposite directions leave it still while unequal ones make it move; they show each case with force arrows.

note.mistake: Children think a thing that is not moving has no forces on it, so a book on a table has none. They think a force is needed to keep a moving thing moving, and that the bigger child always wins.
note.words: Say: "A force is a push or a pull. It has a size and a direction." Say: "Balanced forces do not change how an object moves, so a still object stays still. Unbalanced forces make it start to move, stop, or change speed or direction." Level 1: three pictures with arrows; children circle "balanced" or "unbalanced" and "stays still" or "starts to move." Level 2 has six pictures, and children draw the arrows. Level 3 adds "The book does not fall because the table ___."
note.watch: Right: the rope with both pulling equally hard, the book on the table, and the bag on the hook are balanced and stay still; the box with one child pushing much harder, the wagon, and the kicked ball are unbalanced and start to move. Level 3: the table pushes up on the book as hard as gravity pulls it down, and "The two forces on the book are balanced (equal), so it stays still." A longer arrow means a stronger force. No answer key.

3:balanced-forces.routine: Tie a stuffed animal to the middle of a rope and tape a line on the floor under it. Day 1: two children pull gently and equally, then one pulls harder, while the class watches the animal; no wrapping the rope around hands, and everyone stops on "stop." Day 2: two children push an empty box from opposite sides, first equally, then one harder. Day 3: children draw force arrows for each case on the board, a longer arrow for a stronger force, and act out a book resting on a table.

3:predict-the-swing.title: Predict the Swing
3:predict-the-swing.objective: Children build a pendulum from string and a washer, count its swings in 15 seconds several times, find the count stays the same for the same string, and use the pattern to predict the count for a shorter string before testing it.

note.mistake: Children count each move to one side as a swing, so their counts double. They think a heavier washer or a harder push changes the count, or that one count is enough.
note.words: Say: "One swing is over and back." Say: "Scientists repeat a test and use the middle count, so one mistake does not fool them." Ask: "What changed? What stayed the same?" Level 1: three counts for the 12-inch string, "Were the three counts close to each other?", and a drawing. Level 2 adds the 6-inch string, the middle count, and a prediction ("close" or "not close"). Level 3 adds the 9-inch string, a bar graph, "When the string is shorter, it swings ___ times," and "A 3-inch string would swing about ___ times."
note.watch: The class's counts decide. Expect about 13 or 14 swings for 12 inches, about 15 or 16 for 9 inches, and about 19 for 6 inches; counts from the same string should be within a swing or two. Shorter string, "more" swings. The 3-inch prediction should be more than the 6-inch count (it is about 27). The middle count is the middle one of the three put in order. No answer key.

3:predict-the-swing.routine: Gather string, metal washers, tape, rulers, and a timer. Groups tape the string to the edge of a table so the washer hangs without touching anything, and measure from the tape to the washer. Use the same washer for every string, and each time pull it out to the side the same small distance and let go without pushing. Day 1: count the swings of a 12-inch string for 15 seconds, three times. Day 2: predict, then test a 6-inch string. Day 3: test a 9-inch string, find the class pattern, and test a 3-inch string against a prediction.

3:friction.title: Friction Slows It Down
3:friction.objective: Children roll a toy car down the same ramp onto carpet, tile, and sandpaper, measure in inches how far it travels on each, and explain that friction is a force that slows a moving object.

note.mistake: Children think the car stops because it "runs out of push," not because a force slows it. They push the car on one try, or start it from different spots.
note.words: Say: "Friction is a force that pushes against a moving thing and slows it down. Rough surfaces make more friction." Ask: "Was it fair? What stayed the same?" Level 1: one try on the tile floor and the carpet, "The car went farther on," and a drawing of the ramp. Level 2 has three surfaces, three tries each, the middle distance, and "The car went farthest on ___ because ___." Level 3 adds a bar graph, rounded to the nearest 10 inches, and "Friction is a force that ___."
note.watch: The class's measurements decide. Usually the car goes farthest on the tile floor and much shorter on carpet; sandpaper is often in between. A good reason names friction: "the carpet made more friction." Level 3: "Friction is a force that slows a moving object." For the graph, 85 inches rounds to 90; past 160, color to the top and write the number on the bar. No answer key.

3:friction.routine: Set a board on one book as a low ramp on a tile floor. Children start the same toy car at the top of the board every time, let it roll without a push, and measure in inches, with a yardstick or tape measure, from the end of the board to the front of the car. Then lay a carpet square at the foot of the ramp, then a sheet of sandpaper, and test the same way, three tries on each surface. Last, each child rubs a hand over each surface and tells which feels roughest.

3:static-electricity.title: Balloon Tricks: Static Electricity
3:static-electricity.objective: Children rub a balloon on a wool sweater or scarf, bring it near bits of paper, a thin stream of tap water, and another rubbed balloon, and record which things move without being touched.

note.mistake: Children think the balloon is sticky, or that the paper moves because of wind. They think a force can only act when things touch.
note.words: Say: "Rubbing gives the balloon an electric charge. A charged balloon can pull or push some things without touching them." Ask: "What changed when we rubbed it?" Level 1: three tests; children circle "moved toward," "moved away," or "did not move." Level 2 adds a prediction for each test and "a balloon we did NOT rub," then "What happened when we did not rub the balloon?" Level 3 adds "When I rubbed the balloon, ___. This happened because ___."
note.watch: Usually the paper bits and the stream of water moved toward the rubbed balloon; the two rubbed balloons moved away from each other; the balloon nobody rubbed did not move the paper. That balloon is the comparison: it shows the rubbing made the difference. On a humid day the tricks can fail; that is a real result. Level 3: "it got an electric charge from rubbing." No answer key.

3:static-electricity.routine: Check for latex allergies first and use non-latex balloons if needed. Tear tiny bits of paper, and turn a faucet on to a thin, steady stream. Children rub a balloon on a wool sweater or scarf for 10 seconds and hold it close to the paper, then to the water, then to a second rubbed balloon hanging from a string, without touching. Repeat with a balloon nobody rubbed. Dry days work best. Pick up every piece of a popped balloon right away.

3:what-magnets-pull.title: What Do Magnets Pull?
3:what-magnets-pull.objective: Children predict and test which classroom objects a magnet pulls, and find that magnets pull things with iron or steel in them but not every metal (aluminum foil, a penny, and a brass key are not pulled).

note.mistake: Children think magnets pull all metals, or anything shiny. They think a magnet will pull a penny because it is metal.
note.words: Say: "Magnets pull things that have iron or steel in them. Many metals are not pulled." Ask: "Is it metal? Was it pulled?" Level 1 has six objects, each with what it is made of; children circle a prediction and a result. Level 2 has twelve objects, then children sort them into "pulled" and "not pulled." Level 3 adds "Does a magnet pull all metals? My evidence: ___."
note.watch: Pulled: the washer, the paper clip, the bottle cap, the safety pin, the scissors, and the nail. Not pulled: the aluminum foil, the penny (copper and zinc), the brass key, the button, the eraser, and the wooden spoon. Level 3: no; the foil, the penny, and the brass key are metals that were not pulled. A prediction is right as a guess; the result must match the test. If one of your objects surprises you, the test decides. No answer key.

3:what-magnets-pull.routine: Gather a bar magnet for each pair and a tray of objects: a ball of aluminum foil, a penny, plain steel washers (not stainless steel), paper clips, crimped metal bottle caps, a safety pin, steel scissors, a nail, a plastic button, an eraser, an all-wood spoon, and a brass key. Test every object yourself first. Pairs predict, then touch the magnet to each object and sort it into "pulled" and "not pulled." Keep magnets away from computers, tablets, and phones, and out of mouths.

3:magnet-distance.title: Magnet Force from a Distance
3:magnet-distance.objective: Children measure in inches how close a paper clip must be before a magnet pulls it, test whether the pull works through paper, cardboard, and water, and find the force gets weaker as the distance grows.

note.mistake: Children think a bigger magnet is always stronger, or that the pull stops at a sharp edge. They think a magnet cannot pull through paper or water.
note.words: Say: "A magnet can pull without touching. The pull gets weaker as the distance grows." Ask: "Where did the clip start to move?" Level 1: one measurement, then a prediction and a result for a sheet of paper, cardboard, a plastic cup of water, and a thick book, and a drawing of one test. Level 2 measures a small and a big magnet three times each, with the middle distance and "Which magnet pulled from farther away?" Level 3 adds "When the clip is farther from the magnet, the pull is ___. I know because ___."
note.watch: Print the page at 100%: its ruler is true to scale. The class's measurements decide. A bigger magnet is not always stronger, so "small," "big," or "the same" can all be right. The pull goes through the paper, the cardboard, and the water; a thick book may stop a weak magnet, which is a real result, not a wrong one. Level 3: "weaker," because the clip did not move until it was close. No answer key.

3:magnet-distance.routine: Tape a ruler to each table and lay a magnet at 0. Use classroom bar magnets, not tiny strong ones, keep them away from computers, tablets, and phones, and count them back in: small magnets are dangerous if swallowed, so none go home. Day 1: slide a paper clip slowly toward the magnet and mark where it starts to move, to the nearest half inch, three times. Day 2: repeat with a small and a big magnet. Day 3: hold paper, cardboard, a cup of water, and a thick book between magnet and clip.

3:magnet-problem.title: A Problem Magnets Could Solve
3:magnet-problem.objective: Children list everyday problems a magnet could help with (a cabinet door that swings open, a box of steel and aluminum cans to sort, a lost needle), choose one, and write what a good solution must do and what limits it has (materials, size, time).

note.mistake: Children jump to building before they know what the solution must do. They mix up criteria and constraints, and think a solution can have no limits.
note.words: Say: "Criteria are what the solution must do. Constraints are our limits: the materials, the money, the time, and the size." Ask: "How will we know it worked?" Level 1: children circle one problem, circle what a good solution must do and our limits, and sketch the problem. Level 2: children write the problem, "A good solution must ___," and "We can only use ___." Level 3 asks for two criteria and two constraints.
note.watch: Good choices for the door: "holds the door shut" and "still opens easily"; for the cans: "pulls out only the steel cans"; for the needle: "finds the needle fast"; "is safe for small hands" fits all three. The Level 1 limits ("costs very little," "uses only things in our classroom") are constraints, not things the solution must do. Constraints name real limits, such as one magnet, tape and cardboard, one class period. No answer key.

3:magnet-problem.routine: Show the three problems for real: a cabinet door that swings open, a box of clean, empty steel and aluminum cans with taped edges, and a straightened paper clip hidden in a rug square as the lost needle (never a real needle). Children try each one with their hands, then talk in groups: what would a good solution have to do, and what are the limits? List the criteria and constraints on chart paper. Keep the chart for the next lesson.

3:compare-magnet-solutions.title: Design and Compare Magnet Solutions
3:compare-magnet-solutions.objective: Children sketch two or three solutions to their magnet problem, score each against their criteria and constraints, build the best one, and test it.

note.mistake: Children choose the design they like best or a friend's, not the one that meets the most criteria. They think a test that shows a problem means the group failed.
note.words: Say: "Engineers compare their ideas against the criteria before they build." Say: "A test that shows a problem is useful: it tells us what to improve." Ask: "Which criteria does this sketch meet?" Level 1: two sketches, why each is good, which one to build, and how the test went. Level 2 has three sketches and a chart of three "must do" rows and two "our limit" rows, with a check under each solution that meets each one. Level 3 adds "After the test, we would improve it by ___."
note.watch: The chosen solution should have the most checks, or the "because" must say why not. "When we tested it" tells what really happened, against a criterion: "the door stayed shut." An improvement should fix what the test showed. Every group's answers are its own. No answer key.

3:compare-magnet-solutions.routine: Each group takes out its problem and criteria chart from the last lesson. Set out magnets, cardboard, tape, string, craft sticks, and paper cups. Day 1: each child sketches a different solution, and the group shares them. Day 2: the group scores each sketch against its criteria, a check for each one met, and builds the best one. Day 3: the group tests it against each criterion, improves it, and tests again. Keep magnets away from computers, tablets, and phones.

3:weather-data.title: Our Weather Data: Tables and Graphs
3:weather-data.objective: Children put two weeks of the class's daily high temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, rain or snow, and cloud cover into a table and a bar graph, and compare them with the class's data from the fall.

note.mistake: Children think one cold day means winter has come, or that the weather on a date is the same every year. They read a bar graph by its color instead of by the line at the top of the bar.
note.words: Say: "Weather is what the air is like on one day. Data from many days shows a pattern." Ask: "How have the highs changed since the fall?" Level 1: five days, then "The warmest day was day ___. Its high was ___ °F." Level 2 has ten days, a bar graph (round each high to the nearest 10 degrees), and "In the fall, our warmest high was ___ °F. Now it is ___ °F." Level 3 adds two highs changed to °C, read across a °F and °C thermometer.
note.watch: Every answer is the class's own data. The bars must match the rounded highs: 64 °F rounds to 60, and 65 °F rounds up to 70. "Now our days are ___ than in the fall": warmer or colder, as the data shows. On Level 3, read across the thermometer: 70 °F is about 21 °C, and 32 °F is 0 °C. No answer key.

3:weather-data.routine: Plan ahead: in the first weeks of school, start the class weather log. Each school day a helper writes the date, the high in °F (from the National Weather Service for your town, or an outdoor thermometer read at about 2 p.m.), rain or snow, and the clouds: clear, partly cloudy, or cloudy. Keep the fall pages. Day 1: children copy the last two weeks of the log into their tables. Day 2: they round the highs and graph them. Day 3: they compare the graphs with the fall.

3:seasons-weather.title: What Weather to Expect Each Season
3:seasons-weather.objective: Children graph the average monthly high temperature and rainfall for their town or a US city from a table, and describe the typical weather of each season from the graph.

note.mistake: Children think summer is hot and dry everywhere and every winter is snowy. They mix up the weather on one day with the usual weather of a season.
note.words: Say: "These are averages from 1991 to 2020: the usual weather, not one day." Ask: "Which months are warmest? Which are wettest?" Level 1: four months (Jan, Apr, Jul, Oct); children graph each high rounded to the nearest 10 degrees and write two words from the word bank for each season, with a drawing. Level 2 graphs all twelve months (January and February are done for you). Level 3 adds "The warmest season is ___," "The wettest season is ___," and how they differ.
note.watch: Bars: Jan 50, Apr 60, Jul 80, Oct 60; on Levels 2 and 3 also Feb 50, Mar 50, May 70, Jun 70, Aug 80, Sep 70, Nov 50, Dec 50. Words that fit: winter cold or cool and rainy; spring cool or mild; summer warm, sunny, and dry; fall cool and rainy. Level 3: summer, highs about 70 to 80 °F; winter, about 16 inches of rain in all (6 + 4 + 6). No answer key.

3:seasons-weather.routine: Find Seattle, Washington, and your own town on a US map. Read Seattle's table of monthly highs and rain together. Pour water into a clear container up to 6 inches to show January's rain, and into another up to 1 inch for July's. Then children act out Seattle's year: shiver for the coolest months, fan themselves for the warmest, open a pretend umbrella for the rainiest. If you can, find your own town's averages too and compare.

3:water-cycle.title: The Water Cycle
3:water-cycle.objective: Children mark the water level in an open cup each day as water evaporates, see water condense on the outside of a cold glass (water from the air, not from inside the glass), and label evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection on a water-cycle diagram.

note.mistake: Children think the water in the cup disappeared or that the Sun used it up. They think the drops on a cold glass leaked through it, and that clouds are made of steam or smoke.
note.words: Say: "Water evaporates into the air as a gas we cannot see. When it cools, it condenses into tiny drops: that is what a cloud is." Say: "The water goes around and around: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection." The page has a diagram with four numbers; children write each word from the word bank on the line with the same number. The page is one level.
note.watch: Right in the first copy: 1 evaporation (the arrow rising from the water), 2 condensation (the cloud), 3 precipitation (the rain), and 4 collection (the water on the ground). The class cup should show the level dropping a little each day. No answer key.

3:water-cycle.routine: A week ahead, fill a clear cup with water, mark the level with tape, set it in a sunny window, and mark the level each day. On the day, fill a dry glass with ice water and a few drops of food coloring; children dry the outside and watch drops form. The drops are clear, not colored, so the water came from the air, not from inside the glass. Then children act out the cycle: rise as vapor, huddle as a cloud, fall as rain, and pool as a lake.

3:climates-of-the-world.title: Climates Around the World
3:climates-of-the-world.objective: Children read climate graphs for places such as northern Alaska, Miami, the Sahara, and the Amazon rain forest, compare their typical temperatures and rainfall across the year, and sort them into hot and dry, hot and wet, and cold.

note.mistake: Children think weather and climate are the same thing, or that one cold day changes a place's climate. They think every hot place is a desert.
note.words: Say: "Weather is what the air is like on one day. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years." Ask: "What do the bars show about this place all year?" Level 1 has two places: children write each place's letter from the map and circle "hot and dry," "hot and wet," or "cold." Level 2 has four places. Level 3 adds "Weather is ___. Climate is ___."
note.watch: Right: Utqiagvik is cold ("In winter the high is below 0 °F"); Miami is hot and wet; Tamanrasset in the Sahara is hot and dry, with almost no rain; Manaus in the Amazon is hot and wet. The map letters change from level to level, so check each place by where its dot is: the far north of North America, the tip of Florida, the middle of northern Africa, and northern South America. No answer key.

3:climates-of-the-world.routine: Find each place on a globe: Utqiagvik in northern Alaska, Miami in Florida, Tamanrasset in the Sahara, and Manaus in the Amazon rain forest. Day 1: read the temperature bars together and act each place out (shiver, fan yourself). Day 2: read the rain bars, and fill a tall vase to about 12 inches to show Manaus's wettest month beside an almost empty cup for Tamanrasset. Day 3: sort the four places by climate and talk about how weather and climate differ.

3:weather-problem.title: Define a Weather Problem
3:weather-problem.objective: Children choose a weather hazard of their region (a flood, high wind, a blizzard, lightning), describe a problem it causes for the school, and write the criteria a solution must meet and its constraints.

note.mistake: Children describe the weather instead of the problem it causes, or jump straight to a solution. They think a solution can stop the storm itself, not just reduce the damage.
note.words: Say: "We cannot stop a storm, but we can reduce the damage it causes." Say: "Criteria are what the solution must do; constraints are our limits." Level 1: children circle a hazard, circle what a good solution must do, and sketch the school and the hazard. Level 2: children write the hazard, the problem it causes, "A good solution must ___," and "We are limited by ___." Level 3 asks for two criteria and two constraints.
note.watch: Good choices match the hazard: a flood, "keeps water out of the school"; high wind, "keeps the playground safe"; a blizzard, "keeps the path to the door clear"; lightning, "protects people outside." "Is strong enough for a storm" fits most. On Level 1, "costs very little" and "uses only things in our classroom" sit under "Circle our limits:": they are the constraints. Keep the pages: the next lesson tests designs. No answer key.

3:weather-problem.routine: Talk about the weather hazards of your region: floods, high wind, blizzards, lightning. Show photos you have previewed so they do not frighten; some children may have lived through a storm. Walk the schoolyard and look for places a hazard would cause trouble: a low spot where water pools, the path to the door, things that could blow away. Review the safety rule for each, such as "When thunder roars, go indoors." Groups choose one hazard and list the problems it causes.

3:reduce-weather-damage.title: Which Design Reduces the Damage?
3:reduce-weather-damage.objective: Children test model solutions such as a wind barrier in front of a fan or a model house on stilts in a tray that floods, compare the results, and make a claim with evidence about which design best reduces the hazard.

note.mistake: Children test each design differently (more water, a closer fan), so the results cannot be compared. They choose the design they like best, not the one the evidence supports.
note.words: Say: "A claim is what we think is true. Evidence is what we saw in our test. Reasoning tells why the evidence supports the claim." Level 1: children draw the house before and after the test, circle whether it stayed dry and stayed standing, and write what they would change. Level 2 tests two designs and circles the one that worked better. Level 3 adds a claim, evidence, and reasoning, and circles a real design that works like theirs.
note.watch: The class's tests decide: the better design kept the house drier or standing under the same test. On Level 3, a wall of clay along the water is like "a levee (a wall of earth along a river)," and blocks in front of the fan are like "a row of trees to block the wind." A house on stilts is like "a house raised on posts." No answer key.

3:reduce-weather-damage.routine: Each group builds a small model house (a milk carton or a paper cup) in a plastic tray. Flood groups pour the same cup of water each time; for wind groups, a grown-up runs a fan on low at the same distance each time, with the fan and its cord well away from the water trays. Day 1: test the house with no protection. Day 2: build two designs, such as stilts of craft sticks, a wall of clay, or a barrier of blocks, and test each the same way. Day 3: compare and write the claim.

3:life-cycles-compare.title: Butterfly and Frog Life Cycles Compared
3:life-cycles-compare.objective: Children compare the butterfly and frog life cycles, sort facts into true for one, the other, or both, and find that every life cycle includes birth, growth, reproduction, and death.

note.mistake: Children think a caterpillar and a butterfly, or a tadpole and a frog, are different animals. They think a tadpole is a fish, and that the two life cycles have nothing in common.
note.words: Say: "Every life cycle has birth, growth, reproduction, and death, even when the young look very different from the grown-up." Ask: "Is it true for the butterfly, the frog, or both?" The page has eight sentences; children put a check under the butterfly, the frog, or both when the sentence is true for that animal. The page is one level.
note.watch: Right in the first copy: "The grown-up catches insects to eat." frog; "The grown-up has six legs." butterfly; "It hatches from an egg." both; "Its young has no legs at first." frog (a caterpillar has legs); "The grown-up drinks nectar from flowers." butterfly; "Its young swims with a tail." frog; "Its young looks very different from the grown-up." both; "It spends one stage as a chrysalis." butterfly. The sentences change from copy to copy. No answer key.

3:life-cycles-compare.routine: Show photos or a short video of a butterfly's and a frog's life cycles. Lay stage cards for each in two circles on the floor, and children walk each circle saying the stages aloud. Then talk about all living things: they are born, grow, have young (reproduce), and die. Children name another animal and tell its stages, such as a chicken: egg, chick, and adult hen.

3:flower-parts.title: Flowers Make Seeds
3:flower-parts.objective: Children take apart a grocery-store flower, find and name the petals, sepals, stamens, and pistil, and explain that a flower is the part of the plant that makes seeds so new plants can grow.

note.mistake: Children think flowers are only for looks, and that every colorful part is a petal. They think seeds come from the soil, not from the flower.
note.words: Say: "A flower is the part of the plant that makes seeds. Pollen from the stamens reaches the pistil, and seeds grow at the base of the pistil." Ask: "Which part protected the bud? Which part makes pollen?" The page shows a flower with four numbered parts; children write each part's name on its line and cross out the word in the word bank that is not a part of a flower. The page is one level.
note.watch: Right in the first copy: 1 sepal, 2 stamen, 3 pistil, 4 petal; "roots" is crossed out, because roots are a part of the plant but not of the flower. The numbers change from copy to copy. No answer key.

3:flower-parts.routine: Buy grocery-store flowers with big parts, such as lilies or alstroemeria, one for each pair; in these flowers the three outer parts that look like petals are the sepals. Pairs gently pull the flower apart with their fingers and tape each part onto paper with its name: sepals, petals, stamens (stalks tipped with pollen), and the pistil in the middle. With a hand lens, they look inside the base of the pistil for tiny bumps that can become seeds. Pollen stains, so cover the tables; wash hands after.

3:mealworm-life-cycle.title: Raise Mealworms Through Their Life Cycle
3:mealworm-life-cycle.objective: Children keep mealworms in oats with a slice of carrot, observe them every few days for several weeks, record each stage with a dated drawing and length in inches, and build a model of the darkling beetle's life cycle.

note.mistake: Children think a mealworm is a worm; it is the larva of the darkling beetle, an insect. They think the still pupa is dead, and that the beetle is a different animal.
note.words: Say: "A mealworm is a larva. Like a butterfly, the darkling beetle has four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult." Ask: "What changed since last time?" Level 1: four dated drawings, each with its stage circled, then the life-cycle ring. Level 2 has eight rows and adds the length in inches, to the nearest quarter inch. Level 3 keeps the date, length, and stage without drawings, and adds "A mealworm is a ___, like a caterpillar," "Both life cycles have ___ stages," and one way they differ.
note.watch: The ring, round the arrows from the eggs: larva, pupa, adult beetle. Level 3: "larva"; "four" stages: egg, larva, pupa, adult; a difference: a butterfly pupa is a chrysalis, or the adult is a beetle, not a butterfly. A larva grows longer; a pupa does not eat and hardly moves. The eggs are too small to see easily. No answer key.

3:mealworm-life-cycle.routine: Plan ahead: about six weeks before, buy 20 regular mealworms at a pet store (not giant mealworms or superworms, which may never become pupae) and keep them in a plastic tub with an inch of oats and a slice of carrot, no water dish; change the carrot when it dries. Hand out the page then: twice a week children measure one mealworm in inches (and draw it on the Level 1 and 2 logs). Day 1: compare the log. Day 2: find larvae, pupae, and beetles in the tub and finish the log. Day 3: build a clay or paper-plate model of the life cycle. Wash hands after; never release them outdoors.

3:traits-from-parents.title: Traits from Parents
3:traits-from-parents.objective: Children compare photos of parent animals and their young and a litter of puppies, record traits passed from parents (ear shape, fur color) and how the young differ from each other, and analyze the data in a table.

note.mistake: Children think the young look only like the mother, or that brothers and sisters look the same. They think a trait a parent got during its life, such as a scar, passes to its young.
note.words: Say: "Young animals get traits from both parents, so brothers and sisters can look different from each other. That is called variation." Ask: "Where did this puppy get its ears?" Level 1: children circle each dog's fur color and ear shape. Level 2 adds spots, then "Which traits came from the parents?" and "Are all the puppies the same?" Level 3 adds a cat family and asks why variation matters.
note.watch: Right in the first copy: mother brown, floppy ears, no spots; father white, pointed ears, spots. Puppies: 1 brown, pointed, no spots; 2 white, floppy, spots; 3 brown, floppy, spots; 4 white, pointed, no spots; 5 brown, floppy, no spots. Every trait came from a parent; the puppies are not all the same ("no"). Cats: mother gray, white paws; kitten 1 gray, white paws; kitten 2 brown, no white paws; kitten 3 gray, no white paws. Variation matters because some young may survive better if things change. No answer key.

3:traits-from-parents.routine: Find photos of parent animals with their young: a dog with a litter of puppies, cats and kittens, horses and a foal. Do not ask children to compare themselves with their own families. Day 1: in pairs, children list traits they can see, such as fur color, ear shape, and spots, for each parent and each young animal. Day 2: they make a class table of which young share each trait with the mother, the father, or both. Day 3: they look at how the young differ from each other and why it matters.

3:traits-environment.title: Traits the Environment Changes
3:traits-environment.objective: Children compare two bean plants of the same kind grown with plenty and with too little water and read about a dog that gets heavy from too much food and little exercise, and explain that the environment can change traits such as height and weight.

note.mistake: Children think the short plant is a different kind of bean, or that every trait comes from the parents. They think a change from the environment, such as Max getting heavy, passes to his puppies.
note.words: Say: "Some traits come from the parents. The environment, such as water, light, food, and exercise, can change other traits, such as height and weight." Ask: "Was this trait there from the start, or did the environment change it?" Level 1: children cut out four cards and glue each under "a trait from the parents" or "a trait changed by the environment." Level 2 has eight cards. Level 3 adds "Both bean plants grew from the same kind of seed, but ___. This shows that the environment can change ___."
note.watch: From the parents: a kitten born with long, fluffy fur; Max's long, floppy ears; a puppy born with spotted fur; the color of a bean plant's flowers. Changed by the environment: a bean plant that stayed short with too little water; Max getting heavy from too much food and little exercise; a plant with pale leaves after a week in a dark closet; a tree that grew bent by strong winds. Level 3: the one watered once a week grew shorter, with fewer leaves; "traits such as height." No answer key.

3:traits-environment.routine: Plan ahead: about four weeks before, plant beans from one packet in two cups of the same soil in the same sunny window. Water one every day and the other once a week. On the day, children measure both plants in inches and count their leaves. Then read about Max the beagle together. Keep the talk on Max and the plants, never on anyone's body or weight.

3:animals-in-groups.title: Animals in Groups
3:animals-in-groups.objective: Children read about wolves, honeybees, Canada geese, and schools of fish, list how living in a group helps members find food, stay safe, or save energy, and write an argument with evidence for one animal.

note.mistake: Children think animals live in groups because they are friends, without a survival reason. They think every animal in a group does the same job.
note.words: Say: "Living in a group can help animals find food, stay safe, or save energy." Say: "Circle only what the text says." Level 1 has wolves and Canada geese: children write how each group works, circle how it helps, and finish "The ___ live in a group because ___." Level 2 has four groups. Level 3 adds "Claim: living in a group helps ___ survive. Evidence 1: ___. Evidence 2: ___."
note.watch: Right: wolves, "find food" (they hunt big animals together); Canada geese, "save energy" (each flies just behind and beside another goose, where the air is pushed up); a school of fish, "stay safe" (a hunting fish has trouble picking out one fish); honeybees, "find food" and "stay safe" (some gather food, others guard the door). Evidence comes from the texts, in the child's own words. No answer key.

3:animals-in-groups.routine: Read short texts or watch short videos about a wolf pack, a honeybee hive, a V of Canada geese, and a school of fish. Then try two models. Children walk in a V behind a leader, like geese. In a quick game, a "hunter" tries to tag one child gently, first while the class stands spread out, then while it moves together as a tight school. Talk about which was harder for the hunter, and why.

3:camouflage.title: Hide and Survive: Camouflage
3:camouflage.objective: Children act as birds picking up colored paper moths from a newspaper and a green lawn in 30 seconds, count which colors were found least, and explain why moths that match their background are more likely to survive.

note.mistake: Children think the moths choose a matching color or change color to hide. They think the bright moths were found because they were slow.
note.words: Say: "Moths that match their background are harder for a bird to find, so more of them survive and have young." Ask: "Which color was found least on the lawn? On the newspaper?" Level 1 has green and red moths on the green lawn. Level 2 has four colors on two backgrounds. Level 3 adds a bar graph and "Moths of one kind can be different colors. This matters because ___."
note.watch: The class's tallies decide. Usually green moths survive best on the lawn and gray moths on the newspaper; red and yellow are found fastest. Remember: the moths that were not found survived. Level 3: if the background changes, some moths will still match it and survive. No answer key.

3:camouflage.routine: Day 1: cut moth shapes from green, gray, red, and yellow paper, ten of each color for each background, and predict which will be found least. Day 2: scatter the moths on a green lawn (or green paper), then on sheets of newspaper; a "bird" picks up as many as possible in 30 seconds, one at a time, and the class tallies the colors found. Run several birds on each background. Day 3: color the graph, compare, and explain which moths survived.

3:survive-well-or-not.title: Survive Well, Less Well, or Not at All
3:survive-well-or-not.objective: Children read about a pond or a desert habitat, sort its plants and animals into those that survive well, less well, or not at all there, and support each choice with evidence.

note.mistake: Children think animals can move or learn to live anywhere, or that "less well" means it dies at once. They sort by which animal they like instead of by what it needs.
note.words: Say: "A living thing survives well where it can get what it needs." Ask: "What does it need? Can it get that here?" Read the desert card together: "The only water is one small water hole. In the summer it gets very small and shallow. Plants that need water often can grow only right next to the water hole." Level 1: children cut out five cards and glue each in its column. Level 2 has eight cards, and children write why. Level 3 adds a sentence about one that survives well and one that cannot.
note.watch: Right: the camel, the cactus, and the desert tortoise survive well; the horse and the sunflower survive less well, only near the small water hole, because they need water every day or often; the goldfish and the water lily need deep water and the polar bear needs ice and snow, so they cannot survive. Each "because" uses what the card says the living thing needs. No answer key.

3:survive-well-or-not.routine: Show photos of a desert with one small water hole. Label three spots in the room: survives well, survives less well, cannot survive. Read a living thing and what it needs, such as "a polar bear needs cold, ice, and snow," and children walk to a spot and say why. Then imagine a pond instead: which of the same living things would survive well there?

3:fossils.title: Fossils Tell About Long Ago
3:fossils.objective: Children press a shell or a leaf into clay to make a model fossil, then study fossil photos (a fish fossil found high on a mountain, a fern fossil found in Antarctica) and explain what each tells about the living things and environments of long ago.

note.mistake: Children think a fossil is the living thing itself, and that places have always looked the way they do now. They think fossils form in a few days, like the clay model.
note.words: Say: "A fossil is what is left of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock. Real fossils take a very long time to form." Say: "A fish fossil on a mountain means water once covered that place. A fern fossil in Antarctica means it was once warm." Level 1: two fossils; children circle what lived there and what the place was like then. Level 2 has four fossils, and children write what lived there, what the place was like then, and what it is like now. Level 3 adds "Fossils show that places change. For example, ___."
note.watch: Right: the fern in Antarctica, a land plant, a warm forest on land, now cold and icy; the fish high on a mountain, a water animal, under water, now a high, dry mountain; the seashell in a desert, a water animal, under water, now a hot, dry desert; the palm leaf in a snowy place, a land plant, a warm forest on land, now cold and snowy in winter. No answer key.

3:fossils.routine: Collect shells and sturdy leaves ahead of time. Day 1: each child flattens a ball of modeling clay, presses a shell or leaf into it, lifts it out, and studies the print. Day 2: look at photos of real fossils: a fish fossil found high on a mountain, a fern fossil found in Antarctica, seashells found in a desert. Day 3: children trade model fossils and tell what living thing made each print and where it might have lived.

3:habitat-change.title: When a Habitat Changes
3:habitat-change.objective: Children read about a change to a habitat (a new highway through a forest, a river dammed for a town) and judge the merit of solutions such as wildlife crossings and fish ladders, making a claim with evidence.

note.mistake: Children think a habitat change matters only if animals die right away, or that a solution with no cost exists. They think one solution works for every animal.
note.words: Say: "When a habitat changes, people can design solutions. Each one has good points and limits." Ask: "How does it help the animals? What does it cost?" Level 1: one solution, a wildlife bridge; children circle yes or no for four questions and finish "I think the bridge is a good solution because ___." Level 2 adds a tunnel and a chart of how each helps and what it costs, then a choice. Level 3 adds a claim, evidence, and "A limit of my choice."
note.watch: Right on Level 1: "Can the animals cross without meeting cars?" yes; "Do the animals still have to walk on the road?" no; "Can the animals on one side reach the pond?" yes; "Does building it cost money?" yes. On Levels 2 and 3, both solutions help and both cost money, and some animals may not walk into a dark tunnel. Either choice is right with evidence. No answer key.

3:habitat-change.routine: Lay a long strip of paper across the floor as a highway, with a "pond" on one side. Some children are deer, foxes, and turtles who need the pond; a few walk along the road as cars. Try crossing with no help, then over a "bridge" (a path of paper over the road) and through a "tunnel" (under a table). Talk about what each solution changed and what it would cost to build. Then look at photos of real wildlife crossings and fish ladders.

K:class-rules.title: Our Class Rules
K:class-rules.objective: Children help make three or four class rules with picture signs, act out each rule, and tell how a rule keeps everyone safe or helps us learn.

note.mistake: Children think rules are only "no" rules, or that rules are there to get children in trouble. They think a child who breaks a rule is a bad child. Some circle the picture that looks like more fun.
note.words: Say: "A rule keeps everyone safe or helps us learn." Ask about each rule: "Does it keep us safe, or help us learn?" Day 2, the page: each row shows the same child at the same moment twice; read "or" between the pictures and say the rule: "We walk in the hall." "We raise a hand to talk." "We clean up our blocks." "We look and listen at story time." Children circle the picture that follows the rule and cross out the other. Level 1 has two rows, Level 2 all four, and Level 3 four rows and a box to draw one more class rule being followed.
note.watch: Right: walking in the hall, raising a hand, cleaning up the blocks, listening at story time. Crossed out: running, shouting out, walking away from the blocks on the floor, playing with a toy car at story time. Talk about the action, never the child: "Running in the hall is not safe." On Level 3, any rule being followed is right, also a rule of your own class; ask the child to tell you the rule. No answer key.

K:class-rules.routine: On the rug, ask: "What helps us stay safe and learn?" Agree on three or four rules and write each on chart paper with a quick picture sign: walking feet, a raised hand, hands cleaning up, eyes on the book. Children act out each rule: walk to the door, raise a hand and wait, put the blocks back in the bin. Everyone signs the chart with a name or a handprint, and it stays on the wall.

K:take-turns-share.title: Taking Turns and Sharing
K:take-turns-share.objective: Children practice taking turns with the fair name jar and sharing materials at a table, then circle pictures of friends who take turns, share, or help.

note.mistake: Children think sharing means giving it away for good, and taking turns means waiting forever. They think "sorry" alone fixes it. Some think the child doing the unkind act is a bad child.
note.words: Say: "Kind friends take turns, share, and help." Ask: "Was that kind? How does the friend feel? What could you do instead?" Day 2, the page: name each picture first. Kind: two friends take turns on the slide; a friend shares the crayons; a friend helps up a friend who fell; a friend shares cookies at a picnic. Not kind: a child grabs a teddy bear from a friend; a child pushes in line; a child knocks down a friend's tower; a child tears a friend's drawing. Children circle the kind pictures and cross out the others. Level 1 has four pictures; Levels 2 and 3 have six, and Level 3 a box to draw "me helping a friend." Some pages have more kind pictures, some fewer, so children look at each one.
note.watch: Right: circle the slide, the crayons, the joined hands, and the cookies; cross out the grabbing, the pushing, the knocked-down tower, and the torn drawing. Talk about the act, not the child: "Grabbing is not kind. What could he say instead?" A child who says the friend can say sorry and help build the tower again is thinking well. On Level 3, any drawing of the child helping is right. No answer key.

K:take-turns-share.routine: Write each child's name on a craft stick and put the sticks in a jar: the fair name jar. Pull a name for who goes first, and for every turn of the day. Give each table one box of crayons to share, and use a sand timer for turns with a favorite toy. Role-play asking, "May I have a turn when you are done?" and a tower knocked down by accident: the friend says sorry and helps build it again.

K:school-helpers.title: Who Helps at Our School?
K:school-helpers.objective: Children walk the school with the teacher to meet the principal, the school nurse, the office staff, and the custodian, learn what each one is in charge of, and point to the person to ask for each kind of help.

note.mistake: Children think the teacher does every job, or that the principal is there only when someone is in trouble. They do not know who the custodian is, and think the nurse is only for big hurts.
note.words: Say: "Many grown-ups help at our school. Each one is in charge of something." Ask: "Who takes care of the books? Who helps when you get hurt?" Day 2, the page: name each problem and helper first. Problems: a hurt knee; a child who wants a book about dinosaurs; a big spill on the classroom floor; a child who needs a hot lunch; a well child in a coat, with a grown-up holding car keys, going home early. Children draw a line from each problem to its helper. Level 1 has three problems, Level 2 five, and Level 3 five and a box to draw a helper met on the walk.
note.watch: Right: the knee to the nurse, the dinosaur book to the librarian, the spill to the custodian, the lunch to the cafeteria cook, the early pickup to the office: "Your grown-up signs you out at the office." Watch for children who can say who is in charge where and whom to ask. The principal, in charge of the whole school, has no picture; name the principal on the walk. No answer key.

K:school-helpers.routine: This lesson is the walk. A day ahead, ask each grown-up for two minutes of their time. Visit the office, the nurse's room, the library, and the cafeteria, and meet the principal and the custodian on the way. Each adult says in one sentence what they are in charge of and how a child asks them for help ("If you get hurt, tell your teacher, and your teacher sends you to me."). Take a photo of each. Back in class, show the photos, name a problem (a hurt knee, a spill, a book you want to find), and children point to the right person.

K:birds-eye-view.title: The Room from Above
K:birds-eye-view.objective: Children look at classroom things from the side and from above, match each thing to its view from above, and lay paper shapes on a big plan of our room to make a first map.

note.mistake: Children think a map is a picture taken from the side, so they look for legs, wheels, or a lamp's pole. Round things mix them up: a lamp, a round table, and a cone are all circles from above.
note.words: Say: "From above, like a bird looking down, we see only the top." Ask: "What would a bird on the ceiling see?" Day 2, the first page: an eye with a sideways arrow marks the side views; an eye with a down arrow, the views from above. Level 1 has four things, Level 2 five, Level 3 five with some top views turned. The second page shows a room from above, its furniture in letter tags: four things on Level 1, six on Levels 2 and 3, turned on Level 3.
note.watch: A right line goes to what you really see from the top: the car is a long box with its roof; the bed shows its pillow; a lamp is a circle in a circle, a round table one plain circle; a cone is circles on a square base. If a child hesitates, look down at the real thing together. No answer key.

K:birds-eye-view.routine: Hold a cup, a block, and a book at eye level: that is the side. Set each on the floor; children look straight down: that is from above. Trace around the bottom of each on paper. On butcher paper, draw the room's walls; children glue cut-paper shapes for the tables, rug, bookshelf, and door where they really are: our first map.

K:family.title: Who Is in My Family?
K:family.objective: Children find each person on a picture family tree as the teacher reads the family words aloud, give each the right number, and tell one job someone at home does to help.

note.mistake: Children answer from their own family instead of the starred child's: the star child's sister is "sister" even for a child who has none. They mix up mom and sister, or dad and uncle.
note.words: Say: "This is one family. The star shows the child, and each word tells who the person is to that child." Read each word aloud and follow the lines with your finger: Mom and Dad are joined by a line, their children hang below, the grandparents (white hair) sit above, and an aunt or uncle hangs from their line beside Mom or Dad. Level 1 has Mom, Dad, and one or two brothers or sisters (maybe a baby); Level 2 adds the grandparents; Level 3, an aunt or uncle, or a baby.
note.watch: The first page has an answer key. On Level 3 of the trace page, where words have no numbers, read each word aloud with the class before they trace it, then ask, "Who is the grandpa on the tree? What is his number?" Shaky writing is fine. The tree is a made-up family, not the child's.

K:family.routine: Put the family words, each with a drawing, on the Picture Word Wall: mom, dad, sister, brother, baby, grandma, grandpa, aunt, uncle. Name each person of a puppet or picture book family. Each child tells one job someone at home does to help. "Someone at home" is always enough; no child has to name who lives there.

K:many-kinds-of-families.title: Families Come in Many Shapes
K:many-kinds-of-families.objective: Children look at pictures of many kinds of families (one parent, two parents, a grandparent raising grandchildren, a foster family, big and small families), hear that every one of them is a family, and draw the people who care for them at home.

note.mistake: Children think there is one right kind of family, with a mom and a dad, and that a grandparent raising grandchildren or a foster family is not a real family. They think people in one family must look alike.
note.words: Say: "A family is the people who love you and take care of you. Families come in many shapes." Point and name: a mom and her child; two dads and their twins; a grandmother and the two grandchildren she takes care of; a foster family, two parents and the children they care for; a big family with a grandpa and a baby; a dad and his teenager. After each: "That is a family." Level 1 has three families and a box to draw one person who cares for you. Level 2 has all six and a box to draw everyone at home. Level 3 adds a box for one thing your family does together. Say: "If you have two homes, draw one or both. You can draw anyone who takes care of you."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every drawing is the child's own family. Write the names the child says on the "names" line (Mom, Nana, Uncle Ray), and never ask for more than the child offers. A child who draws one grown-up, a foster parent, or a parent who lives away is right. If a child says a picture is "not a family," answer: "Every one is a family." No answer key.

K:many-kinds-of-families.routine: Read aloud a picture book that shows many kinds of families. Then make a class chart: as children name families they know from books and shows, draw each with stick figures (a mom and a baby, two dads, a grandma and three kids, a big family with cousins). After each one, the class says together: "That is a family." Children tell about their own family only if they want to.

K:family-traditions.title: Family Traditions
K:family-traditions.objective: Children look at pictures of traditions some families keep (a birthday, a Thanksgiving meal, Diwali lamps, a Lunar New Year visit), match each tradition to the thing that goes with it, and draw a tradition their own family keeps.

note.mistake: Children think every family keeps the same holidays, or that a tradition must be a big holiday. They think a tradition new to them is strange. Some think the red envelope is a birthday card.
note.words: Say: "Some families keep these traditions. Your family may keep others." Name each picture: a birthday party with a cake and candles; a Thanksgiving meal with a turkey and a pumpkin pie; Diwali, when families light small clay lamps called diyas; Lunar New Year, when families hang red lanterns and share oranges, and a grandparent gives a child a red envelope with a little money inside for good luck. Day 2, the page: each thing also appears in its family picture. Level 1 has two things and two pictures; Level 2 has four of each ("Each family picture gets one line"); Level 3 adds a box to draw a tradition your family keeps.
note.watch: Right: the party hat to the birthday, the pie to Thanksgiving, the diya to Diwali, the red envelope to Lunar New Year. On Level 3 there is no wrong answer: a family dinner, a visit to Grandma, or game night is a tradition. Never ask a child to explain a family's religion. A family that does not celebrate birthdays or holidays still has traditions (a Sunday walk, a story at bedtime): "Every family has its own." If a child says, "We don't do anything special," ask, "What is something you like to do with someone at home?" No answer key.

K:family-traditions.routine: Show things or pictures: a party hat, a pie tin, a small clay lamp, and a red envelope. Say: "A tradition is something a family does again and again, like a special meal or a celebration." Each child tells something the family does every year or week (a birthday cake, Sunday pancakes, a holiday visit, a bedtime story), and you write it on a chart with the child's name. A child may pass. Every family's tradition goes on the chart; none is the usual one.

K:long-ago-today.title: Long Ago and Today
K:long-ago-today.objective: Children compare pictures of things from long ago and today that do the same job, draw a line from each old thing to its new one, and ask a grown-up at home about a toy they played with when they were small.

note.mistake: Children think "long ago" means the time of the dinosaurs, or that their parents grew up with horses and buggies. They think people long ago could not wash clothes, see at night, or talk far away, or that old things are bad.
note.words: Say: "Long ago, people had the same jobs to do: wash clothes, see at night, get around, talk to someone far away. They used different things." Name each picture: a washboard and tub, a candle in a holder, a horse and buggy, a telephone on the wall with a cord; a washing machine, a lamp, a car, a cell phone. Ask: "Which one does the same job today?" Day 2, the page: read the headings "long ago" and "today." Level 1 has two pairs, Level 2 four, and Level 3 four and a box for a toy a grown-up at home played with long ago. That box is take-home: send it home after the lines are done.
note.watch: Right: the washboard and tub to the washing machine, the candle to the lamp, the horse and buggy to the car, the wall telephone to the cell phone. A child who says we still use candles is right: "Long ago, candles were how people saw at night." On Level 3 there is no wrong answer; a child who cannot ask at home can ask you or another grown-up at school. No answer key.

K:long-ago-today.routine: Lay two hoops on the floor: long ago and today. Show things or pictures: a candle and a flashlight, a horse and buggy and a toy car, a corded phone and a cell phone. Children place each in a hoop, then pair the two that do the same job. Ask: "How did people see at night before electric lights?" Send home the question: "What toy did you play with when you were little?"

K:community-helpers.title: Community Helpers and Their Tools
K:community-helpers.objective: Children match community helpers to the tools they use (a firefighter's ladder, a doctor's thermometer, a farmer's tractor), act out one job, and tell how that helper's work helps everyone in the community.

note.mistake: Children think a helper uses only one tool, or that a helper helps only one person. They think some jobs are only for men or only for women.
note.words: Say: "A community helper does a job that helps everyone, and each one uses tools." Ask: "Who uses this? How does it help?" Day 2, the page: name every picture first; the helpers change from copy to copy (a firefighter, a doctor, a nurse, a farmer, a chef, a teacher, a carpenter, a gardener). Say: "A man or a woman can do any of these jobs." Children draw a line from each helper to the tool he or she uses. Level 1 has four helpers and five pictures on the right: one is the tool of a helper who is not on the page, so it is left over. Level 2 has five of each, Level 3 six of each.
note.watch: Right: firefighter, ladder; doctor, thermometer; nurse, a needle for shots; farmer, tractor; chef, whisk; teacher, book; carpenter, hammer; gardener, rake. On Level 1 the left-over picture stays without a line, and that is correct. A child who says the teacher could use the hammer too is thinking: ask, "Which helper uses it for the job?" No answer key.

K:community-helpers.routine: Fill a prop box with cheap things: a toy stethoscope, a paper firefighter hat, a whisk, a toy hammer, a book, a garden trowel. A child picks one, acts out the job without words, and the class guesses the helper. Ask: "How does this helper help everyone in our town?" Name helpers the children may know: the firefighters at the station near school, the doctor, the school nurse.

K:wants-needs.title: Needs and Wants
K:wants-needs.objective: Children sort pictures into needs (food, water, clothes, a home) and wants (toys, candy, a TV), and tell why a family buys what it needs first when there is not enough money for everything.

note.mistake: Children call everything they like a need ("I need candy"), and think a want is bad. They think a TV is a need because their family has one.
note.words: Say: "A need is something we must have to live: food, water, clothes, and a home. A want is something nice to have." Ask: "Can we live without it?" Day 2, the page: read the group names, Needs and Wants, and name each picture. Children draw a line from each picture to its group. Level 1 has four pictures, Level 2 six, Level 3 eight. Ask the family question again with the page: "Which of these would a family buy first?"
note.watch: Right: water, an apple, bread, a shirt, and a house are needs; a ball, a doll, candy, a TV, a balloon, and a bicycle are wants. A child who says a bike is a need to get to school is thinking: ask, "Could you walk or ride the bus?" Wants are not bad: everyone has some. Never comment on what a family has or buys. No answer key.

K:wants-needs.routine: Lay two hoops on the floor: needs, marked with a drawing of a house and an apple, and wants, marked with a toy. Pass out picture cards or clean, empty packages (a cereal box, a water bottle, a page from a toy catalog). Each child puts one in a hoop and tells why. Ask: "If a family has money for only some things, what does it buy first?" Use the Sorting Hoops tool to sort again. Never ask what children have at home.

K:choosing-one-thing.title: Choosing One Thing
K:choosing-one-thing.objective: Children choose between two things they cannot both have, circle their choice, put an X on the one they do not pick (the one they give up), and tell one good thing their choice brings and one thing it costs them.

note.mistake: Children want to circle both, or think there is one right choice. They think a friend who chose the other thing chose wrong.
note.words: Say: "You can have only one. The one you do not pick is the one you give up." Day 2, the page: read each row aloud; the rows change from copy to copy. One pretend coin buys a ball or a kite, or an ice cream or a lemonade; at recess you can play outside or paint; you can take home one library book, about trucks or about dinosaurs. Each row starts with a small "1" and an arrow, with a hand holding one coin or one book: it shows what you have only one of, and it is not a choice. The recess row shows only the "1": say, "Recess has time for one thing." Level 1 has two rows, Level 2 three, and Level 3 three rows and a box to draw yourself with the thing you picked in the last row.
note.watch: There is no wrong answer. Check only that every row has one circle and one X. Ask: "What is one good thing about your choice? What did you give up?" Two children who choose differently are both right. On Level 3, the drawing shows the child with the thing circled in the last row. No answer key.

K:choosing-one-thing.routine: Set up a pretend class store with two things, such as a ball and a kite (pictures are fine). Give each child one pretend coin, a paper circle: it buys only one thing. Each child chooses, tells why, and says what he or she gave up. Then say: "Recess has time for one thing: play outside or paint." Children stand by the picture they choose.

K:goods-and-services.title: Who Makes It? Who Does It?
K:goods-and-services.objective: Children match workers to the goods they make or the services they give (a baker and bread, a builder and a house, a barber and a haircut, a mail carrier and a letter), and tell one thing each worker had to learn to do the job.

note.mistake: Children think goods just come from the store and nobody makes them. They think a service is not real work because you cannot hold it, and that the mail carrier writes the letters.
note.words: Say: "Goods are things people make. Services are things people do for us." Ask: "Does this worker make something or do something? What did the worker have to learn?" Day 2, the page: name the workers by what they wear and hold (the baker's tall hat and rolling pin, the builder's hard hat and hammer, the barber's pole, comb, and scissors, the mail carrier's bag of letters) and the results (bread, a house, a child with a new haircut, a letter in a mailbox). Children draw a line from each worker to what he or she makes or does. Level 1 has two workers, Level 2 four, Level 3 four and two boxes: a job I want to learn, and what it makes or does.
note.watch: Right: baker, bread; builder, house; barber, haircut; mail carrier, the letter in the mailbox. Bread and a house are goods; a haircut and bringing the mail are services. On Level 3 there is no wrong answer; ask, "Does your job make something or do something?" No answer key.

K:goods-and-services.routine: Set up a pretend Main Street: a bakery with play dough bread, a barbershop with a comb and a mirror (no scissors), and a post office with paper letters for class mailboxes. Children take turns as workers and customers. Then sort on the board: things a worker made, that you can hold (bread, a house), are goods; things a worker did for you (a haircut, bringing the mail) are services.

K:our-flag.title: Our Country and Its Flag
K:our-flag.objective: Children learn that our country is the United States of America, that its leaders (the president for the whole country, the mayor for a town) help make and carry out rules for everyone, and color the flag with its red and white stripes and its blue box of stars.

note.mistake: Children count only the red stripes, or think there is one stripe for each star. They think the president makes every rule alone, or that the flag belongs to one person.
note.words: Say: "Leaders help make rules and help everyone follow them." Ask: "Who leads our whole country? Who leads our town?" Name your mayor, or your town's leader. Day 2, the page: show the small colored flag and the red, white, and blue crayon chips. Level 1: children color the stripes with the red dots red, leave the other stripes white, color the box blue around the stars, and leave the stars white. Level 2 has no dots: red and white stripes, red at the top and the bottom. Level 3 adds "How many stripes?": children count and circle the number.
note.watch: Right: 7 red and 6 white stripes, red at the top and the bottom, and a blue box with white stars in the top left corner. Kindergarten coloring is rough; check the order of the colors, not the edges. On Level 3, 13 is right; a child who circles 12 may have counted the lines between the stripes: count again together, touching each stripe. The leaders are not on the page; the talk carries them. No answer key.

K:our-flag.routine: Look closely at the classroom flag. Count the stripes together and find the red stripes at the top and the bottom. Say: "Our country is the United States of America. The 13 stripes stand for the first 13 colonies, and the 50 stars for the 50 states." Then talk about leaders: the line leader helps our class, the mayor leads our town or city, the president leads the whole country. Children name a rule that leaders help everyone follow.

K:martin-luther-king.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
K:martin-luther-king.objective: Children hear the true story of Martin Luther King Jr., who worked peacefully with many others to change unfair laws that kept Black people and white people apart, and draw one way they can be fair and kind to everyone.

note.mistake: Children think Dr. King changed the laws all by himself, or mix him up with Abraham Lincoln. The building in the picture is the Lincoln Memorial; say, "Dr. King spoke on the steps of a building that honors President Lincoln, who lived long before him." They think it is happening now, or that people with different skin colors cannot be friends.
note.words: Say: "This was long ago, in 1963, in Washington, D.C. Dr. King is speaking to a huge crowd of people of many colors who came to ask for fair laws." Ask: "How can we be fair and kind to everyone?" Day 2: find him small at the top of the steps, the crowd in front. Level 1: children draw themselves and a friend being fair; Level 2, a game where everyone gets a turn. Level 3 adds "my word": read fair, kind, and share aloud; the child circles the one that fits the drawing.
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: any drawing of children taking turns, sharing, or playing together is right; ask the child to tell you about it. Any of the three words can fit; ask, "Why that word?" Friends of any skin color are right. If a child asks more about Dr. King's life, answer simply and truthfully, as much as you judge right; the page shows no violence. No answer key.

K:martin-luther-king.routine: Tell the story simply: "Long ago, in many places in our country, there were unfair laws that kept Black people and white people apart: at school, on the bus, even at water fountains. Martin Luther King Jr. worked with many other people to change those laws. He used words and marches, never fighting." Then make a fairness chain: each child draws one way to be fair or kind on a paper strip, and the class links the strips into one chain. Teach it near Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the third Monday in January.

K:fair-for-everyone.title: Fair for Everyone
K:fair-for-everyone.objective: Children look at pairs of pictures of fair and unfair moments (one child keeping the swing, children taking turns on it), circle the fair ones, and act out how to make an unfair moment fair.

note.mistake: Children think fair means "I get what I want," or that whoever got there first keeps it. They think the child in the unfair picture is a bad child.
note.words: Say: "Fair means everyone gets a turn, a share, and a place in the game." Ask: "Is this fair to everyone? How could we make it fair?" Day 2, the page: each row shows the same children at the same moment twice; read "or" between them and name the moment: the swing, the crackers, the ball game. Children circle the picture that is fair to everyone. Level 1 has two rows, Level 2 three, and Level 3 three rows and one more picture, one child with all the crayons: children draw it made fair in the box.
note.watch: Right: children taking turns on the swing, the same number of crackers for each child, everyone in the ball game. Talk about the act, never the child: "Keeping the swing is not fair to the others." On Level 3, any fair drawing is right: the crayons shared, a box in the middle of the table, or a friend handing some over. No answer key.

K:fair-for-everyone.routine: Act out three moments: a chair is the swing, paper circles are crackers, and a ball is the game. First you (or a puppet) play the one who keeps the swing, keeps all the crackers, or is left out of the game; then the class shows how to make it fair: take turns with a sand timer, share the crackers so everyone has the same, invite the friend in. Ask the class: "How do you think the left-out friend felt?" Children act only parts they agree to.

K:class-vote.title: Our Class Vote
K:class-vote.objective: Children vote once each with a picture ballot to choose the next class read-aloud, watch the votes become a class graph, and learn that the choice with the most votes wins and the whole class goes along with it.

note.mistake: Children vote twice, or vote for the book a friend picks. They think a vote is unfair when their book does not win, or that the winner is the "best" book.
note.words: Say: "Each person gets one vote. The most votes wins, and we all go along with it." Ask: "How many votes did this book get? Which book has the most boxes colored?" Count to 20 with the class. Each book has two rows of ten boxes, numbered 1 to 20 like a twenty-frame, and a star to color by the book that won. Color from 1 across the top row to 10, then go on in the bottom row from 11. The numbers above and below the boxes show the way. Read the tie rule on the page aloud. Level 1 has two books, Level 2 three books and "Did my book win?", Level 3 also a box by each book for its votes and two boxes to draw the choices for a new vote.
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: each vote is the child's own. Watch for children who vote only once, wait their turn, and can say what happens when their book did not win: "It is still fair. We read the winner." Check that each book has as many colored boxes as the class counted. If more than 20 children pick one book, that book has won. If two books tie for the most votes, vote again on just those two; if they tie again, read both, one today and one tomorrow. No answer key.

K:class-vote.routine: Show the real book for each cover, or name it. Each child circles one book (or taps once on the Class Graph). Then call each book in turn: the children who circled it stand up (or each drops a cube in that book's cup), and the class counts them aloud together. Everyone colors one box for each vote. The most votes wins; the class reads that book. Day 2: vote on a new question.

K:land-and-water.title: Land and Water on the Globe
K:land-and-water.objective: Children look at a globe, find that blue shows water and green or brown shows land, notice that there is more water than land, and color the land and water on a picture of the Earth.

note.mistake: Children think the blue is sky, or that there is more land than water because we live on land. They think the globe shows only our country.
note.words: Say: "There is more water than land on the Earth." Ask: "Is your thumb on land or on water?" Day 2, the page: the picture shows one side of the Earth, with North and South America facing us. Read the key: water blue, land green. Level 1 has the big land shapes, with a blue dot in each ocean and a green dot in each big land shape to start from (the thin island beside Greenland has none: it is land too). Level 2 has all the land, plain, and asks, "Is there more water or more land?": children circle the wave or the tree. Level 3 asks the same question and adds a star: find the United States on the class globe first, then draw the star on it on the page.
note.watch: Right: the oceans blue and the land green; the strip at the right edge is part of Africa and Europe, and it is land. On Levels 2 and 3, the wave, more water, is right. On Level 3, the star goes in the middle of North America, below Canada and above Mexico. A star on Alaska is also in the United States. Coloring will be rough; check only that land and water are not swapped. No answer key.

K:land-and-water.routine: Toss an inflatable globe around the circle, or pass the class globe. Whoever catches it looks at one thumb: is it on water or on land? The class keeps a tally on the board. After 20 catches, count. Most of the time there are more water marks; if not, toss 20 more. Say: "A globe is a small model of the Earth. Blue is water. On many globes the land is green and brown; on some, each country has its own color, but the water is always blue."

K:neighborhood-map.title: A Map of a Neighborhood
K:neighborhood-map.objective: Children look at a picture map of a neighborhood seen from above, find the school, the park, and the fire station by their map pictures, and draw a path from a house to the school.

note.mistake: Children think a map is a picture taken from the side, or that a map picture is as big as the place. They think north means "up in the sky," and cut across blocks instead of following the streets.
note.words: Say: "The streets are drawn from above, like a bird sees them. Each little picture shows what is on that block. The key tells what each picture means, and the N arrow points north, to the top of the map." Ask: "Which picture in the key means school? Where is it on the map?" Day 2, the page: Level 1 has the school, the park, and the house with the red door, with a dotted path to trace from the red door to the school. Level 2 adds a fire station (a fire truck in its door), a store, and more houses with brown doors, and children draw the path along the streets themselves. Level 3 adds an empty lot: children draw their own house there and a path along the streets to the park. On Levels 2 and 3, ask: "Where is the fire station? Find it in the key, then on the map."
note.watch: Right: the school (bell tower and flag) circled, the park (trees and a pond) with an X. Any path is right if it starts at the red-door house, stays on the streets, and ends at the school. On Level 3, any house is right; the path to the park stays on the streets. No answer key.

K:neighborhood-map.routine: Lay masking-tape streets on the floor and set toys or block buildings between them: a school, a park with a toy tree, a fire station with a toy fire truck, houses. Children stand and look down: that is how a map shows the town. Make a key: a sticky note for each place, with the same small picture. Children take turns driving a toy car along the streets from a house to the school.

K:transport-flying.title: On Land, on Water, in the Air
K:transport-flying.objective: Children sort vehicles by where they travel (on land, on water, in the air) and things that can fly from things that cannot, and tell how people and the things we buy get from place to place.
