note.mistake: Children think anything with wings can fly, sort a vehicle by where they last saw it (a parked plane, a boat on a trailer), not where it travels, and think a submarine is not a water vehicle.
note.words: Say: "Vehicles carry people and things. Some go on land, some on water, and some in the air." Ask: "Where does it travel? What does it carry?" Day 2: read the group names and name each vehicle. Level 1 has six vehicles, Level 2 nine, Level 3 twelve. The second page sorts animals and machines into Can Fly and Cannot Fly: four on Level 1, six on Level 2, eight on Level 3.
note.watch: Right: car, bus, truck, bicycle, motorcycle, and train go on land; boat, ship, sailboat, canoe, ferry, and submarine on water; airplane, jet, helicopter, hot-air balloon, and rocket in the air. A rocket flies up through the air into space: air is right. Can fly: bird, eagle, owl, bee, butterfly, airplane, helicopter. Cannot fly: dog, cat, rabbit, horse, turtle, fish, car. No answer key.

K:transport-flying.routine: Lay out three hoops: land (brown paper), water (blue paper), and air (a white paper cloud). Children drive, sail, or fly toy vehicles or picture cards into the hoops. Ask: "How did the bananas get to our store?" Trace the trip: a ship across the ocean, a truck on the road, a car home. Sort again with the Sorting Hoops tool.

K:hot-cold-places.title: Hot Places, Cold Places
K:hot-cold-places.objective: Children compare a snowy mountain town and a hot beach town, match clothes and play to each place, and tell how the weather where we live changes what we wear and do outside.

note.mistake: Children think the weather is the same everywhere as it is here today, or that every place gets snow in winter. Some match by color instead of by use.
note.words: Say: "In a cold place, people dress to stay warm. In a hot place, people dress to stay cool." Ask: "Where would people use this? Why?" Day 2, the page: name the two places, a snowy mountain town and a hot beach town, and each small picture; they change from copy to copy. Children draw a line from each thing to the place where people would use it. Level 1 has four things, Level 2 six, and Level 3 six and a box to draw what you wear outside today.
note.watch: Right: a coat, mittens, a winter hat, snow boots, and a sled go to the snowy town; a swimsuit, sandals, flip-flops, and a beach ball go to the beach town. On Level 3 there is no wrong answer: the drawing shows today's weather where you live; ask, "Why did you pick that?" No answer key.

K:hot-cold-places.routine: Tape a picture of a snowy place on one wall and a picture of a beach on the other. Fill a bag with real things or pictures: a winter hat, mittens, a scarf, a sled, a swimsuit, flip-flops, a beach ball. Each child pulls one out and walks it to the place where people would use it, and tells why. Then look out the window: "What is the weather today? What do we wear outside?"

1:rules-in-places.title: Rules in Different Places
1:rules-in-places.objective: Children read short rules, match each rule to the place where it belongs (the classroom, the library, the pool, the street), and tell how each rule keeps people safe or makes things fair.

note.mistake: Children match by things they see instead of reading the rule: books are in a classroom too. They think a rule fits every place the same way, or that rules are there to get children in trouble.
note.words: Say: "Each place has rules that fit what people do there." Ask: "Why does the pool need this rule? What could happen?" Day 2, the page: read each rule aloud; the small picture beside it shows the action (a raised hand, a finger at the lips, bare footprints by drops of water, the walk-sign figure). The places are drawn and named: the classroom, the library, the pool, the street. Level 1 has two rules and two places (never the classroom and the library together), Level 2 all four, and Level 3 all four and a playground rule to write: "We ___ so that ___."
note.watch: Right: raise your hand to talk, the classroom; use a quiet voice with books, the library; walk, do not run (the floor is wet), the pool; wait for the walk sign, the street. A child who says you raise your hand in the library too is right: ask, "Where does it belong most?" On Level 3, any playground rule with a reason is right ("We take turns on the slide so that everyone gets a turn."). No answer key.

1:rules-in-places.routine: Tape four signs around the room: classroom, library, pool, street. Read a rule card aloud ("Wait for the walk sign."); children walk to the sign where it belongs and act out the rule: a raised hand, a whisper, a slow walk, waiting for a paper walk sign. After each, ask: "What could happen without this rule? Does it keep us safe, or make it fair?" Then the class makes up one rule for the playground and says why.

1:class-meeting.title: Our Class Meeting
1:class-meeting.objective: Children hold a class meeting with three talking rules, say back what the last speaker said before adding their own idea, and decide together how the class jobs will work.

note.mistake: Children talk over each other, or say back their own idea instead of the speaker's. Some think a meeting is for telling on a classmate, or that a vote is unfair when their idea loses.
note.words: Model: "I heard Maya say jobs should change every week. I think that is fair." Talk about jobs, never about a classmate. Every level: check each talking rule you followed. Level 1 adds a box to draw "my idea for our class jobs." Level 2 adds the "I heard" frame, a job chart to circle a job you would like (line leader, door holder, paper passer, board cleaner, supply helper, messenger), and how often jobs change. Level 3 adds "Circle one:" day, week, or month, "A job I would like," and "Our class decided ___."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every check and choice is the child's own, and the decision is the class's. Watch for children who wait, look at the speaker, and say back a classmate's idea. An empty check box is honest: ask, "What will you try next time?" Add your own class's jobs. "Our class decided" is what the vote chose. No answer key.

1:class-meeting.routine: Day 1: sit in a circle and post three picture talking rules: one voice at a time, look at the speaker, wait for your turn. Practice on an easy question ("What game should we play at recess?"). The Name Sticks tool (or craft sticks in a jar) chooses who speaks first; each next speaker starts, "I heard ___ say ___. I think ___." A child may pass. Day 2, the meeting: which class jobs do we need, and how often should they change? Vote with a show of hands: call each choice, count the hands aloud together, and write the number. The most votes wins, a tie is voted again, and everyone goes along with it. Post the job chart.

1:good-citizen.title: Being a Good Citizen
1:good-citizen.objective: Children read short stories about children at school, circle the good-citizen choice in each, and circle the word that names it: honest, kind, responsible, or fair.

note.mistake: Children call every good choice "kind." They think saying "I did it" is the wrong choice because it may bring trouble. Some think the child who made the other choice is a bad child.
note.words: Say: "Honest: you tell the truth. Kind: you help someone feel good. Responsible: you do your job. Fair: everyone gets a turn or a share." Day 2, the page: four stories, each with a picture: Maya spills the paint, and the teacher asks who did it; Sam sees a child sitting alone at recess; it is Lee's day to feed the class fish; Ana's group has one ball. Read each story and both choices aloud. Level 1 has two of the stories, each with two pictures and "or" between them. Level 2 has all four with two sentence choices, and Level 3 all four and "One more: A friend drops a box of crayons. I would ___."
note.watch: Right: "I did it," honest; he asks the child to play, kind; Lee feeds the fish, responsible; they take turns, fair. If a child says kind, ask: "What did Maya do? She told the truth. That is being honest." A child who says responsible (she owned her mistake) or fair (no one else was blamed) has a good reason too. On Level 3, any helpful act is right. No answer key.

1:good-citizen.routine: Write the four words on chart paper, each with its sign: honest (a speech bubble with a check), kind (a heart), responsible (a clipboard), fair (a balance scale). A puppet acts out school moments: it spills the water and is asked who did it; it sees a second puppet (or a stuffed animal) sitting alone; it forgets to water the class plant; it keeps the only ball. Children show the good-citizen choice and name its word. Puppets, never children, sit alone or keep the ball.

1:leaders-jobs.title: Leaders and Their Jobs
1:leaders-jobs.objective: Children match leaders by their role to what they lead (the principal a school, the mayor a town or city, the governor a state, the president the whole country) and tell one thing each leader is responsible for.

note.mistake: Children think the president is the boss of every other leader, but each leader is in charge of a different place. They mix up a state and the whole country, because both are shown as maps.
note.words: Say: "Each leader leads one place, and the places get bigger." Day 2, the page: the leaders all stand at a lectern; only the word under each tells the job, so read the words aloud. The places: a school; a town hall with houses; one state up close, Colorado in orange among its neighbors (say, "This is one example state. Our state is ___."); the whole country in green, with Alaska and Hawaii in small boxes. Level 1 has two leaders, Level 2 all four and "Who says it? Circle." (four sentences, two leaders each), and Level 3 all four and "A mayor helps a town by ___."
note.watch: Right: principal, a school; mayor, a town; governor, a state; president, our whole country. "I lead the whole country": president; "I lead a state": governor; "I lead a town or a city": mayor; "I lead a school": principal. If a child sends the governor to the whole country, point to the one orange state. On Level 3, any true town job is right: fixing roads, caring for parks, keeping the town safe. No answer key.

1:leaders-jobs.routine: Draw four circles inside each other on chart paper, the smallest in the middle: our school, our town or city, our state, our country. Beside each, write its leader: our principal, our mayor (or our town's leader), our governor, the president. Say their names plainly, without opinions. Ask: "What is each one in charge of?" Invite the principal to tell the class one part of the job.

1:family-generations.title: Family Generations
1:family-generations.objective: Children order family words from the oldest generation to the youngest, read clues to fill in a family tree, and draw a tree of people important to them.

note.mistake: Children order by age, not generation: they put a baby in a row of its own, or an aunt above Mom. On the tree they answer for themselves, not for the starred child.
note.words: Say: "This is one family. Families have many shapes. A generation is one row of the family tree: grandparents; then parents, aunts, and uncles; then children, cousins, and babies." Page 1 shows the three generations in pictures, numbered 1 to 3. Level 1 has four rows of three words to number; Levels 2 and 3 have six and seven, adding aunt, uncle, cousin, and baby brother or sister. Page 2 is a tree with some names filled in; the clues (two, four, or five by level) are about the starred child.
note.watch: Right: grandparents 1; parents, aunts, and uncles 2; children, cousins, and babies 3. On the tree, an aunt or uncle hangs from the grandparents' line and a cousin below. Both pages have an answer key; the child's own tree has no wrong answer.

1:family-generations.routine: Day 1: children holding picture cards (a grandma, a mom, a girl, then an aunt and a cousin) line up by generation, oldest first. Day 2, after the pages: each child draws a tree of people important to them (family, a neighbor, anyone who cares for them); a pretend or storybook family is fine too. Children share only by choice.

1:old-postcard-clues.title: Clues in an Old Photograph
1:old-postcard-clues.objective: Children study the front and back of an old photo postcard, find the clues that tell who took the photo, when, and where (the photo studio, the year, the town), and circle the answers to short questions.

note.mistake: For "Who took the photo?" children circle the shop on the sign or the town: the sign tells what the shop is, not who made the picture. They guess the year from how old the card looks instead of reading it, and think the world was gray long ago because old photos are black and white.
note.words: Say: "An old photo is a clue to the past. 'Photo by' tells us who made the picture; the back often tells when and where." Day 2, the page: the sample card changes from copy to copy, and its towns and shops are made up. The front shows a Main Street shop sign, people in hats and coats, and an old car; the back says "Photo by," a studio, a town, and a year, with a round date stamp. Read each question and its three choices aloud. Level 1 asks two of the three questions, with the clues circled in orange. Level 2 asks all three with no help, and Level 3 adds "In [the card's year], people ___."
note.watch: Right: "Who took the photo?" is the studio after "Photo by"; "When was the photo taken?" is the year on the back; "Where was the photo taken?" is the town after the studio. A date stamp shows when a card was mailed; on these cards it is the same year as the photo. On Level 3, anything the front shows is right: people wore hats, the cars looked different. No answer key.

1:old-postcard-clues.routine: Show an old photograph or postcard: your own, or a printout of an old postcard of your town from your library's or historical society's website. Look at the front: "What do you see? What looks different from today?" Turn it over: "Is there a name? A place? A year?" Fill in a chart: Who took it? When? Where? Write "We do not know" where there is no clue.

1:ask-someone-older.title: Ask Someone Older
1:ask-someone-older.objective: Children prepare questions, interview an older person they know (a family member, a neighbor, or someone at school) about his or her childhood, and tell the class one thing the interview taught them about the past.

note.mistake: Children think older people never played games or went to school. They ask yes-or-no questions and get one-word answers, or let the person answer about today instead of long ago.
note.words: Say: "An older person is a source: he or she remembers things we never saw." Model a follow-up: "What was your favorite game? How did you play it?" Every question, the child's own too, starts "When you were little," so the answers are about the past; read them aloud first. Level 1 has two of the three questions (lunch, getting to school, games), each with a box to draw the answer. Level 2 has all three, a line for each, and one box to draw one answer. Level 3 has two, "My own question," and "I learned that ___." On the top line, a first name or "my neighbor" is enough.
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every answer is the older person's, and every question is the child's. Any older person the child knows is right. A child who cannot ask anyone outside school does the interview with you or another adult at school, and no one asks why. Never ask a child to tell more about home than he or she wants. A strong "I learned" compares then and now: "My neighbor walked to school. I ride the bus." No answer key.

1:ask-someone-older.routine: Day 1: read the page's questions aloud and add one the class wants to ask. Practice: you are the older person; children ask, listen, and draw or write your answer. Each child chooses anyone older he or she knows. Ask a few staff members ahead (the librarian, the custodian, the principal) to be interviewed at school by any child who wants. Day 2, a few days later: children tell one thing they learned. A child may pass.

1:school-play-long-ago.title: School and Play Long Ago and Today
1:school-play-long-ago.objective: Children compare a school day and games of about 100 years ago with their own, read what a child back then might have said about school, and tell which school they would like and why.

note.mistake: Children think "long ago" means when their parents were small, or the time of the dinosaurs, and that children long ago did not play. Some circle "today" for walking to school, because they walk to school too.
note.words: Say: "About 100 years ago, many children learned in one room, big and little children together. They wrote on slates, and their pens had no ink inside, so they dipped the tip in a bottle of ink." Day 2, the page: name each picture first; they change from copy to copy (a one-room school, a pen you dip in ink, walking to school with a tin pail, a hoop and stick; a big school, a computer, a school bus, a game on a tablet). Level 1 has four pictures. Level 2 adds three things a child said ("I dip my pen in ink."). Level 3 adds "I would like to go to school (long ago / today) because ___."
note.watch: Right, long ago: the one-room school, the dip pen, the tin pail, the hoop and stick, and the sentences about ink, a slate, a tin pail, or one room. Today: the big school, the computer, the school bus, the tablet, and the sentences about the bus, typing, a tablet, or a video. A child who says children walk to school today too is right: "Look at the tin pail and the old clothes." On Level 3 there is no wrong answer. No answer key.

1:school-play-long-ago.routine: Show photos of a one-room school from long ago (the Library of Congress has many) or read a picture book about one. Pass around a small whiteboard as a slate and a cup as a tin lunch pail. Outside, children roll a hula hoop with a stick or a ruler. Make a T-chart, "Long ago" and "Today": children name things for each side (a slate, a tablet; walking with a tin pail, riding the bus).

1:map-key.title: Read the Map Key
1:map-key.objective: Children read a map key, follow step directions on a grid, and make their own map with a key.

note.mistake: Children count the key's symbol as one on the map, or count the start square as step 1.
note.words: Session 1: an island map with a count box for each key symbol. Session 2: say, "Up and north are the top of the page." Two, three, or four steps by level.
note.watch: Right: each count matches the island, never the key; a bridge is where the road crosses the river. Step off the start before counting squares. A child's own map is right when its key has every symbol.

1:map-key.routine: Session 1: draw the classroom from above with a key and count its tables. Session 2: on a 4-by-4 grid taped to the floor, with everyone facing the board, a child walks the steps the class gives. On The Rail That Waits, cards also turn the beetle; on paper you only move. Session 3: children map the classroom or a pretend island, with a key.

1:city-suburb-town.title: City, Suburb and Small Town
1:city-suburb-town.objective: Children compare pictures of a big city, a suburb, and a farm town, read short sentences about how people there live, travel, and get food, and write the letter of the community each sentence tells about.

note.mistake: Children think a suburb is the same as a city, or that farm towns have no stores. They match by one word: "tall" is in both the silo sentence and the apartment sentence.
note.words: Say: "A city has tall buildings and many people close together. A suburb has houses and shopping centers near a city. A farm town is a small town with farms and fields around it." Day 2, the page: the places are lettered, and the letters change order from copy to copy: read them first. Each sentence fits one picture by something drawn only there: the subway and the tall buildings in the city, the shopping center and the garages in the suburb, the corn and the silo in the farm town. Level 1 has two places and three sentences, Level 2 three places and six, and Level 3 six and "I live in a ___. We get food from ___."
note.watch: Right: the subway and the tall apartment building, the city; the shopping center and the garage, the suburb; the corn and the silo, the farm town. Check the letters on that copy. On Level 3 there is no wrong answer: a child on a farm or in an apartment writes what fits, and any food source is a good answer (a store, a market, a garden, a farm, school lunch). Never ask more about home than the child wants to tell. No answer key.

1:city-suburb-town.routine: Show three photos: a city street with tall buildings, a suburb with houses near a shopping center, and a farm town with fields. Make a three-column chart and ask for each: "How do people get around? Where do they live? Where do they shop?" Read sentence strips ("I ride the subway to work."); children tape each under its place. Tell the class which kind of place our school is in.

1:work-fits-land.title: Work That Fits the Land
1:work-fits-land.objective: Children match places (the ocean coast, a forest, flat farmland, snowy mountains) to the work people do there (fishing, cutting lumber, growing wheat, teaching skiing), and tell how the land makes that work possible.

note.mistake: Children think any job can be done anywhere: skiing on a farm, fishing in a forest. They match the forest and the farmland because both are full of plants, without asking what grows there.
note.words: Say: "People do work that fits the land: the ocean has fish, the forest has trees, flat farmland has rich soil, the mountains have snow." Ask: "What does this land have that the worker needs?" Day 2, the page: name the workers by what they hold: a person who fishes (a fish and a crab trap), a lumber worker (a log), a wheat farmer (a tractor), a ski teacher (on skis, with a child). Level 1 has two workers and two places, Level 2 all four, and Level 3 all four, then "Place: ___" for one place the child picks and "People can ___ there because the land has ___."
note.watch: Right: the person who fishes, the ocean coast; the lumber worker, the forest; the wheat farmer, flat farmland; the ski teacher, snowy mountains. On Level 3, any true sentence about one of the four places is right: Place: a forest. "People can cut lumber there because the land has many tall trees." No answer key.

1:work-fits-land.routine: Show four photos: an ocean coast with boats, a forest, flat farmland, snowy mountains. Ask: "What does this land have? What work could people do here?" Children act out each job without words (pulling in a fish, carrying a log, driving a tractor, skiing), and the class guesses the land. Then ask: "What work do people do near us because of our land or water?"

1:caring-for-places.title: Caring for the Places We Share
1:caring-for-places.objective: Children compare pictures of a park in the morning, after careless people in the evening, and on a clean-up day, circle what people changed and who helps, and plan one way the class can care for the schoolyard.

note.mistake: Children think the wind or animals made the mess, or that a park takes care of itself. They circle things that look the same in both pictures, and on clean-up day they circle everyone, even the person who is only walking a dog.
note.words: Say: "A park belongs to everyone, so everyone takes care of it." Day 2, the page: the same park in the morning and in the evening, and on Levels 2 and 3 on a clean-up day. The changes differ from copy to copy (a candy wrapper on the grass, a cup left on the bench, a plastic bag in the pond, a branch broken by a rope swing, flowers stepped on, the trash can knocked over), and each change is one thing to circle. Level 1 has two pictures and three changes; Levels 2 and 3 three pictures and five changes, and children circle each person who helps. Level 3 adds "Our schoolyard: Our class can ___."
note.watch: Right: one circle for each change, as many as the page asks (3 on Level 1, 5 on Levels 2 and 3). Every change was made by people: a shoe print is in the flower bed, and the branch broke when someone swung too hard on the rope swing. On clean-up day, circle each helper, each fixing one change; the person walking a dog is visiting, not helping. On Level 3, any real way to help is right. No answer key.

1:caring-for-places.routine: Walk the schoolyard. Children point to signs of care (a trash can, a garden, a path) and things that need care (litter, stepped-on plants). Back in class, list ideas: pick up litter wearing gloves with a grown-up, put trash in the can, water a plant, stay on the path. The class picks one plan and does it this week. Children never pick up glass or anything sharp.

1:us-symbols.title: Symbols of the United States
1:us-symbols.objective: Children match American symbols (the flag, the bald eagle, the Statue of Liberty, the Liberty Bell) to their names, read short sentences about them, and tell why freedom and fairness for all matter in a class too.

note.mistake: Children think the Statue of Liberty is a real person, or that the Statue and the Liberty Bell are in the same city. They think a symbol is only a picture of a thing, not an idea. Some count the stripes as states.
note.words: Say: "The flag has 13 stripes for the 13 colonies and 50 stars for the 50 states. The bald eagle is our national bird. The Statue of Liberty, in New York Harbor, stands for freedom. The Liberty Bell, in Philadelphia, has a big crack." Day 2, the page: read each sentence aloud; it says "It," never the name. Level 1 has two of the symbols, and children trace each name three times. Level 2 has all four and a word box: children write each name. Level 3 adds a box to draw a symbol for our class and "It stands for ___."
note.watch: Right: "It has 50 stars, one for each state": flag; "It is our national bird": bald eagle; "It stands for freedom": Statue of Liberty; "It has a crack. It is in Philadelphia": Liberty Bell. Accept a name copied with small slips when it names the right symbol. On Level 3 there is no wrong answer: a heart for kindness, a book for learning; ask, "What does it stand for?" No answer key.

1:us-symbols.routine: Look at the class flag and pictures of the bald eagle, the Statue of Liberty, and the Liberty Bell. Say: "A symbol stands for something bigger, the way a stop sign means stop." Ask: "Freedom means we can make choices. Fair for all means everyone gets a turn. Where do we see freedom and fairness in our class?" Children share ideas for a class symbol, and you sketch a few on the board.

1:washington-lincoln.title: George Washington and Abraham Lincoln
1:washington-lincoln.objective: Children learn that George Washington was the first president and that Abraham Lincoln, the 16th, led the country through the Civil War and worked to end slavery, and sort the sources that tell us about them.

note.mistake: Children circle Lincoln for the coin because Lincoln is on the penny, and Washington for the Lincoln Memorial because it is in Washington, D.C. They think the two lived at the same time; Washington died before Lincoln was born.
note.words: Say: "A source tells us about the past. A painting shows how a person looked; a letter, words the person wrote; a coin and a building were made later to remember the person." Day 2, the page: children write the kind of source from the word box, then circle the president. The painting has a name plate; the letter is signed "A. Lincoln"; the quarter is shown front and back at real size, the back an eagle and QUARTER DOLLAR (a newer quarter's back may differ); the memorial has a small statue inside. Level 1 has two sources (the quarter adds a ring: "Put a real quarter here."). Level 2 has all four, Level 3 all four and "I would most like to see the ___ because ___."
note.watch: Right: painting, George Washington; coin, George Washington; letter, Abraham Lincoln; building, Abraham Lincoln. "Quarter" or "memorial" is right too. If children ask about the war or slavery, answer simply and truthfully, as much as you judge right. No answer key.

1:washington-lincoln.routine: Show a real quarter and a penny: "George Washington, our first president, is on the quarter. Abraham Lincoln, our 16th president, is on the penny." Tell each story simply: Washington led the army in the war for independence and became our first president. Lincoln led the country through the Civil War, when the North and the South were divided, and worked to end slavery, when people were enslaved: made to work without pay and not allowed to leave.

1:fourth-of-july.title: Why We Have the Fourth of July
1:fourth-of-july.objective: Children hear how the 13 colonies declared independence from Great Britain on July 4, 1776, circle the sentences that are real reasons the colonists gave (they wanted to make their own laws; they did not want taxes they had no say in), and tell a reason in their own words.

note.mistake: Children think the Fourth of July is about fireworks, or is the flag's birthday. They think the colonists wanted a new king or more taxes. They skip the "not" in "They did not want to pay taxes they had no say in."
note.words: Say: "Taxes are money people pay to run the country. The colonists did not want taxes they had no say in. They wanted to make their own laws and choose their own leaders." Day 2, the page: read the caption and each sentence aloud, stressing "not." The small picture by each sentence helps children find it; it does not show which are true. Level 1 has two sentences, one real. Level 2 has four, and Level 3 four and "The colonists wanted ___." The number of real reasons changes from copy to copy.
note.watch: Right: "They wanted to make their own laws," "They did not want to pay taxes they had no say in," "They wanted to choose their own leaders." Not reasons: a new king, moving to Great Britain, more taxes to the king. On Level 3, any true reason in the child's words is right: "to make their own rules," "to rule themselves." No answer key.

1:fourth-of-july.routine: Put on a paper crown and play the king: "From now on, I choose every recess game, and you each pay me two crayons a week." Ask: "Is that fair? Did you have a say?" Tell the story: long ago, the king of Great Britain, far across the ocean, ruled the 13 colonies, and laws and taxes were made for them without their say. On July 4, 1776, their leaders approved the Declaration of Independence: the colonies would make their own laws. Then the class makes one rule together, with everyone's say.

1:people-made-fairer.title: People Who Made Life Fairer
1:people-made-fairer.objective: Children hear short true stories of people who worked to make life fairer (Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Ruby Bridges, Helen Keller), read one fact about each, and write a question they would like to ask one of them.

note.mistake: Children hear "would not give up her seat" as not sharing: say plainly that the law was unfair. They think each person changed things alone, or that Rosa Parks was only tired; she said she was tired of giving in. They think Helen Keller could not learn.
note.words: Say: "Each of these people saw something unfair and worked with many others to make it fairer." Model a question: "Why did you say no?" Day 2, the page: each card names the person and prints one true sentence; read them aloud. Level 1 has two of the four people and "Why did you ___?" Level 2 has all four, "Circle Why or How," and one question. Level 3 has two questions and "___ matters because ___."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every question and reason is the child's own. A good question is about the person's story ("How did you learn to read?"). If a child asks more, answer simply and truthfully, as much as you judge right. Ruby Bridges has written books for children about her school. No answer key.

1:people-made-fairer.routine: Tell two stories a day. Rosa Parks: in 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, an unfair law made Black riders give up their bus seats to white riders; she calmly said no, and people worked together until the law changed. Ruby Bridges: some schools would not let Black children in; in 1960 in New Orleans, at six, she started first grade at a school that had been for white children only. Helen Keller could not see or hear; her teacher spelled words into her hand, and she learned to read, wrote books, and worked for people with disabilities. Dr. King led peaceful marches for fair laws in many places in our country.

1:goods-services-near-far.title: Goods and Services Near and Far
1:goods-services-near-far.objective: Children sort pictures into goods (things people make or grow) and services (work someone does for you), and read short labels to tell which goods in a sample town are made there and which come from far away.

note.mistake: Children think a service is a thing: the bus is a thing, but a bus ride is the driver's work. They think goods just come from the store, and that our bananas grow nearby; most are grown far away, in warm countries.
note.words: Say: "Goods are things people make or grow. Services are work someone does for you." Day 2, the page: name each picture first; they change from copy to copy (bread, milk, bananas, apples, a T-shirt, a kite; a haircut, a checkup at the doctor, a bus ride, story time at the library, mail brought to your home, a tooth cleaning). Read the key: color the box under each picture yellow for goods, green for services. Level 1 has four pictures, Level 2 eight, and Level 3 eight and a map of a sample town (a bakery, a dairy farm, an apple orchard, homes) with labels: read them aloud, and children circle each label about a good from our town.
note.watch: Right: bread, milk, bananas, apples, the T-shirt, and the kite are goods (yellow); the haircut, checkup, bus ride, story time, mail, and tooth cleaning are services (green). On Level 3, the three labels about bread, milk, and apples from our town are circled; the one or two about goods grown far away (bananas, pineapple) are not. For the bus ride, ask, "Who does the work?" No answer key.

1:goods-services-near-far.routine: Lay two hoops on the floor: Goods and Services. Put real goods in one (a banana, an apple, a T-shirt) and act out services for the other: brush a doll's hair, read a story, deliver a paper letter. Ask: "Is it a thing people made or grew, or work someone does for you?" Read the sticker on the banana if it names a country, find that country on the globe, then find our town.

1:jobs-earning-money.title: Jobs and Earning Money
1:jobs-earning-money.objective: Children read short sentences about workers who earn money (a baker, a bus driver, a dentist, a farmer), match each worker to what he or she is paid for, and tell what families use the money they earn for.

note.mistake: Children think money comes from a bank machine or a card, not from work. They think money can buy anything, even a hug. Some do not know what rent is.
note.words: Say: "A job is work people are paid for. Pay buys what a family needs: food, clothes, a home. Rent is money paid to live in a home." Ask: "What does this worker do to earn money?" Day 2, the page: read each sentence aloud ("I am paid to bake bread."). The workers have no names: find the baker by the tall white hat and the rolling pin, the bus driver in the bus, the dentist by the big tooth, the farmer by the basket of food. Level 1 has two workers and four pictures to circle or leave, Level 2 four workers and five pictures, and Level 3 the same and "I would like to be a ___. I would be paid to ___."
note.watch: Right: bake bread, the baker; drive people, the bus driver; check teeth, the dentist; the food I grow and sell, the farmer. Circled: food, rent for a home, clothes, shoes. Not circled: the sun, a hug, a rainbow: "Some of the best things cannot be bought." On Level 3, any job with a true pay sentence is right ("a vet, paid to help sick animals"). Caring for a home and family is work too, even when no one is paid. No answer key.

1:jobs-earning-money.routine: Play "What is my job?": a child acts out a job without words (a baker, a bus driver, a dentist, a farmer, a teacher), and the class guesses. Ask: "What is this worker paid for?" Then sort picture cards into two piles: what money can buy (food, clothes, shoes) and what money cannot buy (the sun, a hug, a rainbow). Never ask about the jobs or money of a child's family.

1:prices-market.title: Prices at the Market
1:prices-market.objective: Children read price tags at a pretend market, find the pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters that pay each price exactly, and tell which of two things costs more.

note.mistake: Children count coins, not cents: they call 4 coins 4 cents. They think a bigger coin is worth more, but the dime, the smallest, is worth more than the penny and the nickel. Some circle every coin on the tray.
note.words: Start with the biggest coin and count on: "25; 35 for the dime; 40 for the nickel; then 41, 42 for each penny." Day 2, the page: the coin key at the top shows each coin of the level at its real size, with its name and value. The tray coins have no numbers: children match each to the key. The nickel looks like nickels made since 2006; older ones show Jefferson's side. New pennies are not made anymore (since 2025), but pennies still count as money. Each thing at the stall has a price tag and a tray: circle the coins that pay its price exactly. Then: "Which costs more? Circle it." Level 1: two things, 3 to 9 cents, pennies and one nickel. Level 2: three things, up to 25 cents, dimes too. Level 3: three things, up to 50 cents, all four coins, a quarter on every tray.
note.watch: On this page, only one set of coins on each tray pays the price; the pennies are alike, so any of them will do. Some coins are left over. Say: "At a real store, any coins that make the price exactly would work." In "Which costs more?", the bigger price is right. No answer key.

1:prices-market.routine: Pass around a real penny, nickel, dime, and quarter; say each name and value, and how to tell them apart. Set up a class market: small things with sticky-note price tags under 50 cents. Partners take turns as shopper and seller with real or play coins: the shopper pays the exact price, and the seller counts it. Hold up two things: "Which costs more? How do you know?" Then practice on the Money Mat.

1:saving-goal.title: Saving for a Goal
1:saving-goal.objective: Children follow a child who saves one dollar a week for a goal, color the savings jar week by week, and tell why people save money for something they want later.

note.mistake: Children color the whole jar at once, or stop at the number in the "After ___ weeks" question. They think saving means you never get the thing. Some do not see that at one dollar a week the weeks and the dollars are the same number.
note.words: Say: "To save is to keep money now to buy something later." Ask: "After 2 weeks, how much is in the jar?" Day 2, the page: read the story aloud; the name and the goal change from copy to copy (Kim, Leo, Nia, or Ben saving for a kite, a ball, or a book). Children color one part of the jar for each week, from the bottom, until it is full. Level 1 has a $3 goal and a jar of 3 parts. Level 2 has a $5 goal, 5 parts, and a question like "After 4 weeks, Nia has $___." Level 3 adds a box, "my goal ($20 or less)": children draw a goal of their own and write its price and the weeks they need.
note.watch: Right: every part colored by the end; the weeks are the price (3 or 5); after 2, 3, or 4 weeks, the jar holds that many dollars; and "to buy it later." On Level 3, any goal of $20 or less is right when the weeks match the price ($8, 8 weeks); a pretend goal is fine. No answer key.

1:saving-goal.routine: Draw a jar of five parts on the board for a pretend class goal: a $5 kite. Pretend each day is one week: each day, a child drops a paper dollar into a clear cup, and the class colors one part from the bottom up and says, "Week 1, one dollar." Ask: "How many weeks until we have 5 dollars? Why not spend each dollar right away?" Never ask about a child's money at home.

2:class-agreement.title: Our Class Agreement
2:class-agreement.objective: Children each write the class rule they think matters most and why, read a partner's rule and reason, show how the two views are alike and different, and help write a class agreement everyone signs.

note.mistake: Children write their partner's rule as their own, or write the reason where the rule goes. They leave "Both of us" empty when the two rules differ, or think a different view is a wrong one.
note.words: Say: "Two people can see one thing in different ways. A view is what you think, and why." Day 2, the page. Level 1 shows four of six numbered rules (walk in the hallway, be kind to others, take turns, keep your hands to yourself, listen when others talk, clean up after yourself; they change from copy to copy): the child writes a rule's number and a word from the box (learn, feel safe, play, be friends, get along) for "It helps us ___," the same for the partner, and a word in each part of the circles; partners share one copy, since the numbers change. Level 2: both views written out, rule and "because." Level 3 adds "Our class agreement: We will ___ and we will ___."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every rule, reason, and circle is the child's own. Look for the partner's view as said, and something in "Both of us": the same rule or a shared reason. On Level 3, a strong sentence holds both ideas: "We will listen when others talk and we will take turns." No answer key.

2:class-agreement.routine: Day 1: ask, "Which class rule matters most to you, and why?" Model it: "I think listening matters most because it helps us learn." Partners take turns ("I think ___ because ___."), then each says back the other's view; with an odd number, make one group of three. Fill two overlapping circles on chart paper with one pair's ideas. Day 2, after the page: pairs read their sentences, the class picks four or five, writes them as "We will ___," and everyone signs with a name or a mark.

2:community-laws.title: Laws in Our Community
2:community-laws.objective: Children read community laws (stop at a red light, keep dogs on a leash in the park, do not litter, wear a helmet on a bike), match each law to the problem it stops, and tell in a sentence why a community needs that law.

note.mistake: Children think laws are only for grown-ups, or only for punishing people.
note.words: Say: "A law stops a problem before it happens." Ask: "What could happen if no one stopped at red lights?" Day 2, the page: the lettered problems are at the top, and the letters change order from copy to copy: read them first. Each law has a picture of people keeping it: a car stopped at a red light, a dog on a leash, a child dropping a wrapper into a trash can, a child with a helmet by a bike. Read each law aloud; children write a letter after "It stops problem." Level 1 has two laws and two problems. Level 2 has four of each and "Use each letter one time." Level 3 adds "The law: ___ Our community needs this law because ___."
note.watch: Right: red light, crashes at corners; leash, a pet chasing children; litter, trash on the ground; helmet, a hurt head. Check the letters on that copy. A child who says the red light also stops a hurt head thinks well: ask, "Which problem does it stop most?" With each letter used one time, the helmet takes the hurt head. Say: "In many towns and states children must wear a helmet by law. Is it a law where we live?" Ask the same about the leash. On Level 3, any true reason is right ("so cars do not crash"). No answer key.

2:community-laws.routine: Show photos of signs near school (or pictures of signs): a stop sign, a traffic light, a "no littering" sign, a dogs-on-leash sign. Say: "A rule is for one place, like our class. A law is for everyone in a community, and the government makes it." Use toy cars at a paper corner, a stuffed dog, and scrap paper on the floor: show a problem, and the class names the law that would stop it.

2:levels-of-government.title: Local, State and National Government
2:levels-of-government.objective: Children learn that a government is the people who make laws and run services for a place, sort leaders into local (the mayor, the city council), state (the governor), and national (the president, Congress), and write one job of each level.

note.mistake: Children think the president is in charge of everything, even our town's parks. "Congress" and "city council" are new words, so children guess where they go. Some mix up our state and our country, because both are maps.
note.words: Say: "Each level takes care of a bigger place: our town or city, our state, our whole country." Day 2, the page: read the definition at the top aloud. Only the words on the leader cards tell who is who; no card is a real person. The boxes nest: our town (a town hall) inside our state inside our country. The state picture, "one state," is Colorado; children write ours on "Our state is ___." Write each leader in the smallest box it fits: the mayor goes in the town box. Level 1 has three leaders, Level 2 all five, and Level 3 all five and "One job of each level: Local: ___ State: ___ National: ___"
note.watch: Right: the mayor and the city council, local; the governor, state; the president and Congress, national. On Level 3, any true job is right: "The mayor leads our city." "Congress makes laws for our country." A town council or another town leader counts as local. No answer key.

2:levels-of-government.routine: Draw three boxes inside each other on chart paper, the biggest outside: our country, our state, our town or city. Write the leaders in each: the president and Congress; our governor; our mayor (or our town's leader) and our city or town council. Say their names plainly, without opinions. Say: "Congress and the city council are groups chosen by voters. They make laws." Ask: "Who makes laws for the whole country?" Children hold up a card: local, state, or national.

2:government-services.title: Services Our Government Provides
2:government-services.objective: Children find the services a government provides in a picture of a town (a library, a park, a fire station, road repair, a public school, a mail carrier), tell them apart from businesses (a toy store, a pizza shop), and write who each service helps and why it helps everyone.

note.mistake: Children circle every building, even the stores and the homes, or think a service is something you buy. They miss the mail carrier, who has no sign, and think the school is not a service because they go there every day.
note.words: Say: "A government service is work the town, the state, or the country does for everyone." It is printed at the top. Day 2, the page: one town with signs (SCHOOL, PARK, LIBRARY, FIRE STATION, ROAD WORK, TOY STORE, PIZZA). A mail carrier at a mailbox has no sign; the yellow house is a home: no circle. Level 1 has four of the six services and one store, circle only. Level 2 has all six and both stores, then "The ___ helps ___." twice. Level 3 adds "This service: ___ It helps everyone because ___."
note.watch: Right: circle the school, park, library, fire station, road work, and mail carrier (each one the page shows), not the toy store or the pizza shop. "The library helps kids who want books" is right, as is any true answer. On Level 3: "The fire station helps everyone because firefighters come to any home." A public school is run by the local school district; mail carriers work for the U.S. Postal Service, part of our national government. No answer key.

2:government-services.routine: Show photos of our town: a library, a park, a fire station, a mail carrier, a road being fixed, and a few stores. For each, ask: "Is it for everyone? Who pays for it?" Say: "Everyone helps pay for government services with taxes. A business sells things to make money." Make a T-chart, "Government service" and "Business," and add places children know. Ask: "Who uses the library?"

2:cardinal-directions.title: North, South, East and West
2:cardinal-directions.objective: Children label the four directions on compass roses, use them to find places on a map, and give a partner directions across the classroom.

note.mistake: Children mix up east and west. They think north always means up, at the top of the page, so they write N at the top of every rose, even a turned one.
note.words: Say: "The orange tip points north. Start there and go clockwise: N, E, S, W." Page 1: Level 1 has four upright roses, one letter given, the four words below; Level 2 six roses, three of them turned; Level 3 six, all turned. Page 2: an island map with a key. In each row, start at the first picture, look the way the word says, and circle the picture that lies that way (two choices on Level 1, three on Levels 2-3; Level 3 has only a north arrow).
note.watch: Right on Page 1: when the orange tip points right, east is at the bottom, south on the left, west on top. On Page 2, the right picture lies straight that way; the others lie off to the side. No answer key.

2:cardinal-directions.routine: Find north with a compass app and tape N, E, S, W signs on the four walls. Children face north and point as you call each direction. Teach the order clockwise from north: "Never Eat Soggy Waffles." Partners give each other directions across the room ("Walk 4 steps north, then 3 steps east."), and the class checks the walk.

2:continents.title: The Seven Continents
2:continents.objective: Children find and label the seven continents on a world map, find them again on the class globe with the oceans between them, and point to North America, the continent where the United States is.

note.mistake: Children think a country is a continent, so they call the United States one, or think every island is its own continent. They mix up North and South America, and look for a sea between Europe and Asia.
note.words: Say: "Europe and Asia are one big piece of land. The dashed line on the map shows where people divide them." The page says Oceania: Australia and the islands near it. Many US books call this continent Australia; tell the class both names. Each continent has a number, and the numbers change from copy to copy: children write each name on the line with that number. Level 1 has the word box and two names already written, Level 2 the word box and all seven to write, and Level 3 no word box.
note.watch: Right: each line names the continent that carries its number on that copy: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania, Antarctica. "Australia" for Oceania is right too. Antarctica runs along the bottom of the map. Accept a name copied with small slips when it names the right land. No answer key.

2:continents.routine: Turn the class globe slowly. Say: "A continent is a very big piece of land. There are seven." Children find each one on the globe and touch the oceans between them: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Arctic, and the Southern Ocean. Chant the seven names together. Then everyone puts a finger on North America and finds the United States in it: "This is where we live."

2:places-change.title: How Places Change
2:places-change.objective: Children compare before-and-after pictures of places that change (a hill whose trees grow new leaves in spring, a desert after a rare rain, a fishing village that became a city), circle whether nature or people changed each place, and write why it changed.

note.mistake: Children think a garden or a neighborhood grew by itself, because plants grow, or that the city was always there. Some think time made the change, because "long ago and today" comes with both kinds.
note.words: Say: "Sometimes nature changes the land: sun, rain, ice, and waves. Sometimes the way people live changes it: they build and plant." Day 2, the page: read each sentence aloud; it tells when and what changed, and only the garden's says who (the neighbors). The pairs change from copy to copy: a hill whose trees grow new leaves in spring, a desert in bloom, a pond whose ice melts, a beach where the waves washed sand away; a fishing village that became a city, a field that became a neighborhood, an empty lot where neighbors planted a garden. Level 1 has two pairs, circle only. Level 2 has three and "It changed because ___." Level 3 adds a box to draw a place near our school that has changed, with "It changed: ___ It changed because ___."
note.watch: Right, nature: the hill, the desert, the pond, the beach. People: the village, the field, the garden. A good "because" names the cause: "spring came," "neighbors planted it." On Level 3, any real change near school is right: a new playground. No answer key.

2:places-change.routine: Show two pictures of one place near school, then and now (from the library or historical society, or the schoolyard in two seasons). Ask: "What changed? Who or what changed it?" Make a chart, "Nature changed it" and "People changed it," and sort what children name: snow melting, leaves falling, a new building, a garden. Then look outside for one change of each kind.

2:disaster-ready.title: When Disaster Strikes
2:disaster-ready.objective: Children learn how a flood, a hurricane, or an earthquake can affect a place (roads, homes, power, schools), find on a U.S. map the Atlantic and Gulf coasts where hurricanes most often come ashore, and list ways families get ready and neighbors help.

note.mistake: Children think floods happen only by the ocean. On the page, they circle the sandbags or the neighbors, but those are in both pictures: they were put out before the rain.
note.words: Say: "We can't stop a storm, but we can get ready, and neighbors help each other." Day 2, the page: one town, not ours, before the flood (rain is coming; sandbags line the houses) and after; every copy shows the same town and the same changes. Level 1 is the two pictures: circle the 3 things the flood changed. Level 2 adds the family emergency kit: seven things in pictures and words (a radio and medicine among them); children draw or write any 4 in the boxes. Level 3 has the kit as words, a U.S. map with three coasts to color, and "Neighbors can help by ___."
note.watch: Right: three circles on the after picture: the water over the road, the CLOSED sign, the boat with two helpers in life vests. Any 4 kit things are right. Color the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, not the Pacific; the page says "Gulf coast," so name the gulf the way your class map does. "Neighbors can help by" any kind act: "checking on each other." No answer key.

2:disaster-ready.routine: Keep it calm and about getting ready. Ask: "What kinds of big storms happen where we live?" Pull from a backpack what a family might keep in an emergency kit: water, a flashlight, canned food, a first-aid kit. Practice your school's drill for your area (for an earthquake: drop, cover, and hold on). Ask: "How can neighbors help?" (check on an older neighbor, share food, fill sandbags). Some children may have lived through a flood, a fire, or a storm: they share only if they want.

2:winter-traditions.title: Winter Traditions Families May Keep
2:winter-traditions.objective: Children read about winter traditions families may keep (Hanukkah, Christmas, Kwanzaa, Las Posadas, Lunar New Year), match each to its symbol, find on a world map the country where it began, and share a tradition from their own family if they wish.

note.mistake: Children mix up the menorah and the kinara, because both hold candles: count them (nine and seven). They think everyone keeps Christmas, or that a tradition must be a holiday.
note.words: Say: "A tradition is something a family or a group does again and again, often every year." Facts: a Hanukkah menorah holds eight candles and a helper candle, set higher or apart (in the middle on the page); a kinara has seven candles, three red, one black, three green; Las Posadas, from Mexico, is nine nights, December 16 to 24; at Lunar New Year, families give red envelopes with a little money for good luck. Day 2: read each sentence aloud. Level 1 has three traditions and a box to draw one "if you want to." Level 2 has all five and "If you want to share: a tradition I know is ___." Level 3 has all five and a world map: a line from three names to the country where each began.
note.watch: Right: Hanukkah, the menorah; Christmas, the tree; Kwanzaa, the kinara; Las Posadas, the piñata; Lunar New Year, the red envelope. On the map: Lunar New Year, China; Kwanzaa, the United States; Las Posadas, Mexico (not Brazil or India). Lunar New Year is also kept in Vietnam, Korea, and many US cities. The drawing box and the sharing line are choices: an empty box is fine. No answer key.

2:winter-traditions.routine: Day 1: introduce all five, each with its symbol, and find Mexico, the United States, and China on the globe. Day 2: the page. Invite, never ask: "If you want to, tell us about a tradition you know." Every family's tradition counts, many keep none of these, and a child may pass. Never ask a child to explain a family's religion.

2:where-it-comes-from.title: Where Does It Come From?
2:where-it-comes-from.objective: Children read sample labels on everyday things (bananas grown in Ecuador, avocados grown in Mexico, a T-shirt made in Vietnam, coffee beans grown in Colombia), find each country on a world map, and draw a line from it to our country to see how buying things connects us to faraway people.

note.mistake: Children think things are made at the store. On the map they circle the country's name box instead of the land the name points to.
note.words: Say: "A label tells where a thing was grown or made. When we buy it, we are connected to the people who grew it or made it." Day 2, the page: name each picture and read its label ("Label: grown in Ecuador"). The map names ten countries; each name sits in a box near its land, often with a short line to it. Circle the land, then draw a line from it to the star, the United States. Level 1 has two of the four things (never bananas with coffee), and their countries are outlined in orange. Level 2 has all four, found by name. Level 3 adds "One thing in our classroom: ___ Its label says it came from ___."
note.watch: Right: bananas, Ecuador; avocados, Mexico; the T-shirt, Vietnam; coffee beans, Colombia; each country circled, with a line to the star. These are sample labels: a real banana may say Guatemala or Costa Rica. On Level 3, any real label in the room is right ("crayons, made in the USA"). No answer key.

2:where-it-comes-from.routine: Bring a few things with labels: a banana with its sticker, a T-shirt tag, a box of crayons, a pencil. Read each label aloud: "Grown in ___" or "Made in ___." Find the country on a world map and stretch a piece of yarn from it to a star on our state. Ask: "Who grew or made this? How did it get here?" (by ship, truck, or plane). Before the page, find one or two things in the room whose label names a country (a crayon box, a tissue box) for everyone to use; at home only if a child wants to.

2:made-here-sold-there.title: Made Here, Sold There
2:made-here-sold-there.objective: Children sort products into those made in other countries and sold in the United States (bananas, cocoa beans, coffee) and those made in the United States and sold in other countries (airplanes, soybeans, corn), and give one example of each.

note.mistake: Children think "made here" means made in our town. They put corn in the "sold here" arrow because they buy corn at the store, or think everything we eat grows in our country.
note.words: Say: "Some things come into our country from far away. Some things made here go out to other countries." Day 2, the page: each card has a picture, the thing's name, and one fact that tells where it grows or is made: read the facts aloud. Children write each thing's name on a line in the right arrow. The U.S. map is in the middle; the small globe stands for other countries. Level 1 has four of the six cards (the mix changes from copy to copy), Level 2 all six, and Level 3 all six and "The United States sells ___ to other countries." and "The United States buys ___ from other countries."
note.watch: Right, made in other countries, sold here: bananas, cocoa beans, coffee. Made here, sold in other countries: airplanes, soybeans, corn. On Level 3, any of those three in each sentence is right. A child who says some coffee grows in Hawaii is right: "Most of ours comes from other countries." The United States buys and sells many other things too. No answer key.

2:made-here-sold-there.routine: Draw a U.S. map on the board with two big arrows: one pointing in ("Made in other countries, sold here") and one pointing out ("Made here, sold in other countries"). Hold up real things or pictures: a banana, a bag of coffee, an ear of corn, cocoa beans, a toy airplane. Ask: "Where was it grown or made? Which way does it travel?" Tape each in its arrow. Say: "Chocolate is made from cocoa beans. We sell a lot of corn, soybeans, and airplanes to other countries."

2:why-countries-trade.title: Why Countries Trade
2:why-countries-trade.objective: Children study three islands that each make something another island needs (fruit, fish, wool), draw the trades that let every island have food and warm clothes, and write why countries trade goods with each other.

note.mistake: Children draw an arrow from the island that needs a thing instead of from the island that has it. On Levels 2 and 3 they look for two islands that swap, but these trades go around in a circle.
note.words: Say: "Each island gives one thing and gets one thing. Trading lets everyone have what they need." Day 2, the page: read each island's line ("Sunny Island has fruit and needs fish."); the person on each island thinks of what it needs. The instruction says it: draw each arrow from the island that has the thing to the island that needs it. The islands' places change from copy to copy. Level 1 has two islands that trade fruit and fish, Level 2 three islands, and Level 3 three islands and "If Cold Island could not trade, ___."
note.watch: Right on Levels 2 and 3: fish from Cold Island to Sunny Island, fruit from Sunny Island to Hilly Island, wool from Hilly Island to Cold Island. On Level 1: fish from Cold Island to Sunny Island, fruit from Sunny Island to Cold Island. "Countries trade because" any true reason: "they need things other countries have." On Level 3, "it would have no wool for warm clothes" is right. No answer key.

2:why-countries-trade.routine: Make three island groups: Sunny Island gets paper fruit cards, Cold Island fish cards, and Hilly Island wool cards (yarn taped on paper). Tell each group what it needs: Sunny needs fish, Cold needs wool for warm clothes, Hilly needs fruit. Each group gives its cards to the island that needs them. Ask: "Could each island get what it needs alone? What did trading do?" Then: "Countries trade for the same reason."

2:family-relationships.title: Aunts, Cousins and Grandparents
2:family-relationships.objective: Children solve riddles about family relationships (my mom's sister is my aunt), place each relative in the right generation of a family tree, and remember that families come in many shapes.

note.mistake: Children read only the last word: "mom's brother" becomes "brother." They mix up grandpa and uncle (Mom's dad and Mom's brother), or call a cousin a brother or sister.
note.words: Say: "Read a riddle in two steps: first find Mom, then find her brother." Day 2, the page has riddles only; the tree is the class chart. It names one starred child (the name changes from copy to copy). Every riddle asks about that child ("Eli's mom's mom is Eli's ___."), and a word can answer two riddles. Level 1 has six riddles about grandparents, aunts, and uncles, with a word box. Level 2 has eight with a word box; most copies include cousins. Level 3 has eight with cousins ("an aunt's son") and no word box.
note.watch: Right: Mom's or Dad's mom, grandma; Mom's or Dad's dad, grandpa; Mom's or Dad's sister, aunt; Mom's or Dad's brother, uncle; an aunt's or an uncle's son or daughter, cousin. "Grandmother" or "grandfather" is right too. On the tree, aunts and uncles are in the parents' row and cousins in the children's row. The page has an answer key.

2:family-relationships.routine: On chart paper, draw a three-row tree for a storybook family: grandparents; Mom, her sister, Dad, his brother; a child and a cousin. Read a riddle ("My mom's sister is my ___."); a child finds Mom, then her sister, and tapes on the card: aunt. Ask: "Which row is she in?" Say: "This is one family. Families come in many shapes." Never ask children to tell about their own family.

2:two-accounts.title: Two Stories of the Same Day
2:two-accounts.objective: Children read two short accounts of the same event (the day a new library opened, told by a child and by the librarian), mark what both say and what only one says, and explain why two people can tell one event differently.

note.mistake: Children think that when two stories differ, one person is wrong. They underline in blue only the exact same words, and miss one fact said two ways (on the library day: "Lots of people came." and "Many people came.").
note.words: Say: "Two people can tell about the same day. Each tells what they saw, so the stories can differ, and both can be true." Day 2, the page: each story has its teller's picture and name. The day changes from copy to copy: a new library opens (Ava and Ms. Lin, the librarian), a town parade (Leo and Mr. Diaz, a drummer), a new playground opens (Sam and Ms. Cole, a park worker). Children need a blue and an orange crayon. Level 1 has four sentences a story: find one thing both say and one thing only one says. Level 2 has five a story: underline every sentence. Level 3 adds "They noticed different things because ___."
note.watch: Right, blue: what both tell, in their own words: the day it happened, that many people or kids came, the puppet show, the band, the fire truck, the sunny day. Orange: what only one tells (going with Grandpa, a heavy drum, checking every bolt). Underlining a shared fact in both stories is right. On Level 3, a strong reason names what each was doing: "Sam was playing, and Ms. Cole was working." No answer key.

2:two-accounts.routine: After something the class shared (recess, an assembly, a class walk), tell it in four short sentences, and have a child (or a puppet that "watched") tell the same event in four; write the two side by side on chart paper. Children underline in blue what both told and in orange what only one told. Ask: "What was each of us doing?" Say: "Neither story is wrong."

2:old-photo-questions.title: Questions About an Old Photograph
2:old-photo-questions.objective: Children look closely at an old photograph of a main street with a horse and wagon, early cars, a streetcar, and shop signs, list what they see, and write questions the photograph makes them ask about how the town has changed.

note.mistake: Children write what they think under "I see" ("People were poor."), or ask a question the photo already answers. Some think the world was gray long ago because old photos are black and white.
note.words: Say: "Historians look closely first, then think, then wonder." Day 2, the page: every copy shows the same drawn street, "Main Street, about 1910": a hardware store, a bank with columns, a streetcar on rails under its wire, a horse pulling a wagon, an early car, and people in long coats and hats. Say: "This is a drawing made to look like an old photo." Level 1: circle the five things in the list (a streetcar, an old car, a horse and wagon, the bank, a man in a hat) and finish "I wonder why ___?" Level 2: I see (two things), I think, and I wonder (two questions). Level 3: three questions and "How could we find out? We could ___."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer when the child writes what the photo shows and asks real questions. On Level 1, one circle on each of the five things (any man in a hat). A strong "I think" uses a clue: "People rode in wagons, so there were not many cars." A strong question asks about change: "Why is there no streetcar now?" On Level 3: ask a librarian or an older person, look in a book. No answer key.

2:old-photo-questions.routine: Show a printout of an old photo of our own town's main street from your library's or historical society's website (or, if none is found, the page's drawing). Make a three-column chart: I see, I think, I wonder. Children first name only what is in the photo, then what it tells about life then, then questions ("Where did people leave their horses?"). Ask: "How could we find out?"

2:why-town-changed.title: Why Did the Town Change?
2:why-town-changed.objective: Children read a short history of a sample town (a railroad station opened, then new stores and houses were built), choose which reason most likely explains why the town grew, and give the clue from the text that supports their choice.

note.mistake: Children pick the reason they like best (such as "People liked the weather.") instead of the one the story tells. They copy the first sentence, or one that names the railroad or the bridge but not the growth.
note.words: Say: "A historian picks the reason the clues show." Day 2, the page: the town and its story change from copy to copy (Oak Bend and a railroad, Mill River and a bridge, Pine Hill and a shoe factory, Sandy Creek and a highway), with pictures of the town at first and later; the towns are made up. Read the story aloud, then each reason. Children circle one reason and copy "the sentence that says the town grew and tells why." Level 1 has two reasons, Level 2 three, and Level 3 three and "___ is less likely because ___."
note.watch: Right: the reason the story names (the railroad came, a bridge was built, a factory opened, a highway was built), and the sentence to copy is the one that starts "Because of." If a child copies a sentence that only names the railroad, the bridge, the factory, or the highway, ask: "Does it tell that the town grew?" On Level 3, any reason that uses the story is right: "It snowed a lot is less likely because the story never says it snowed." No answer key.

2:why-town-changed.routine: Write two sentences on the board: "Our class got a new reading corner. Because of the reading corner, more children read at recess." Ask: "Why did more children read? Which sentence tells us?" Underline "Because of." Then ask: "What could make a town grow?" (a new road, a bridge, a railroad, jobs). If you can, show when a road, a railroad, or a factory came to our own town.

2:tools-and-skills.title: Tools and Skills for the Job
2:tools-and-skills.objective: Children sort what producers need into tools and machines (an oven, a tractor, a drill) and skills learned through school and practice (the steps to make bread, a good time to plant seeds), and explain how both help a worker make more and better goods.

note.mistake: Children think a skill is something you can buy or hold, and color a card blue because its bubble shows a thing (a cow, a loaf, bricks): the bubble is what the worker knows.
note.words: Say: "A tool or machine is a thing a worker holds or uses. A skill is something a worker knows, learned at school and by practice." Day 2, the page: children need a blue and an orange crayon. The worker is on every card: holding a tool in hand, or thinking, with a thought bubble, for a skill. Read each card aloud, then color its box. Level 1 has one worker (a baker, a farmer, or a builder; it changes from copy to copy) and four big cards. Level 2 has all three workers, twelve cards. Level 3 adds, with an oven or a mixer always in the baker's row: "The baker uses ___ to make more bread because ___."
note.watch: Right, blue: the oven, mixer, rolling pin, whisk, tractor, watering can, shovel, wheelbarrow, drill, hammer, saw, and ladder. Orange: every card with a thought bubble. On Level 3: "The baker uses a mixer to make more bread because it mixes dough faster than hands." Ask: "How does practice help a baker make better bread?" No answer key.

2:tools-and-skills.routine: Give two teams three minutes to make strips for a paper chain: one tears paper by hand, the other uses scissors and a ruler. Compare: "Which team made more? Which strips are better? Why?" Then ask: "Would the scissors help if you had never learned to cut on a line?" Lay two hoops on the floor, "Tools and machines" and "Skills," and sort cards: a mixer, a tractor, a hammer; the steps to make bread, a good time to plant seeds, a good way to measure wood.

2:cost-to-make.title: What Does It Cost to Make?
2:cost-to-make.objective: Children plan a lemonade stand, list what they must pay for before they can sell anything (lemons, sugar, cups, a sign), add the costs, and find the lowest price per cup that brings in more than the costs.

note.mistake: Children circle the kite or the ball, or add every price on the list. They think all the money that comes in is left over. At 50 cents a cup they write $500 (or $50) for 10 cups: 500 cents is $5.
note.words: Say: "Before you sell, you pay for what you need. That is the cost." Day 2, the page: read the story aloud. The price list also shows things they do not need (a kite, a ball). Children circle what they must buy, write its prices, and add. Then they find what 10 cups bring in at each price: at 50 cents, 2 cups make a dollar; at 20 cents, count by 20s (20, 40 ... 200 cents is $2). Level 1: three costs and two of the three prices, with a hint. Level 2: four costs, three prices. Level 3 adds "Choose a price that brings in more than they must pay. At ___ a cup, they have $___ left over. I chose it because ___."
note.watch: Right: lemons, sugar, and 10 cups (and poster paper for a sign on Levels 2 and 3), never the kite or the ball; the sum of their prices on that copy; 10 cups bring in $10 at $1 a cup, $5 at 50 cents, $2 at 20 cents; the lowest price that brings in more than the sum. On Level 3, left over is what comes in minus the costs; any price that brings in more, with a reason, is right (costs of $4: "At 50¢ a cup, they have $1 left over."). No answer key.

2:cost-to-make.routine: Plan a pretend class lemonade stand. Ask: "What must we buy before we can sell anything?" List the things on the board with sticky-note prices in whole dollars and add them. Then count with play dollars: "If we sell 10 cups at $1 a cup, how much comes in? At 50 cents a cup?" (two cups make a dollar). Ask: "Which price brings in more than we paid? What is left over?"

2:what-banks-do.title: What Banks Do
2:what-banks-do.objective: Children learn that a bank keeps people's money safe, pays savers a little extra called interest, and lends money to people who need it, then match each sentence to the picture that shows it.

note.mistake: Children think the bank keeps each person's own bills in a box with their name, or that borrowed money is a gift. Some think interest is money you pay the bank for saving, the other way around.
note.words: Say: "A bank keeps money safe, pays savers interest, and lends money." Day 2, the page: name each picture first: a child gives money to the teller, with the round vault door behind; a savings paper (I saved $100; The bank added $1; Now I have $101), the word "interest" not printed; a banker holding money out to a parent, who thinks of their roof being fixed. Read the sentences aloud; children copy the right one next to each picture. Level 1 has two of the three pictures and their two sentences, Level 2 all three, and Level 3 all three and "A family might borrow money because ___. They must pay it back because ___."
note.watch: Right: the vault, "The bank keeps money safe."; the savings paper, "The bank pays savers interest."; the roof, "The bank lends money." The sentences are never in the pictures' order. On Level 3: "to fix their roof" or any real need; "it is not their money" or "the bank lends money other people saved." Accept small copying slips. No answer key.

2:what-banks-do.routine: Set up a pretend bank: a desk, a shoebox vault, and play dollars. A child saves 100 dollars; the banker writes it down and puts it in the vault. Say: "After a year, the bank pays a little extra for saving: that is interest." Add 1 dollar. Then a pretend family borrows money from the same vault to fix a roof: "The bank lends some of the money people saved. That is why the family must pay it back, and the saver can still take money out." Never ask about a child's family money.

2:class-market.title: Class Market Day
2:class-market.objective: Children run a class market: each group makes a good or offers a service, sets and writes its price, everyone buys with the same play coins, and the class talks about which prices sold.

note.mistake: Children count coins, not cents: 3 coins become 3 cents. They think a bigger coin is worth more, but the dime is the smallest.
note.words: Say: "A seller picks a price people will pay." Count on from the biggest coin: "25, 35, 40, 41." After the graph, ask: "Did lower prices sell more? Why?" Level 1: what you bought and paid, and two practice trays (10 to 50 cents; dimes, nickels, pennies). Level 2: two records and two trays with quarters, up to a dollar. Level 3: one record, two trays, change from a dollar, and "At our market, ___ sold the most. I think it sold well because ___." Coins are at real size, with no numbers on the trays. Pennies are no longer made but still count as money.
note.watch: The record has no wrong answer; "My coins make" matches "It cost" when the child paid exactly. On a tray, one set of coin kinds pays the price exactly (with extra coins of a kind, any of them count). Change: count up from the price to 100 (35; 40, 50, 75, 100: 65 cents). Never ask what children have at home. No answer key.

2:class-market.routine: Session 1: groups make a good (bookmarks, paper flowers, cards) or offer a service (a drawing made to order). Session 2: groups write price tags from 10 cents to 1 dollar. On the Money Mat, the site's coin tool, pay the prices together, then pay each another way. Every child gets the same bag of play coins (2 quarters, 3 dimes, 3 nickels, 5 pennies: one dollar). Session 3: half the class sells while half shops, then they swap; sellers count the coins. Graph what sold; then each child fills in the page.

3:civic-virtues.title: Civic Virtues at School
3:civic-virtues.objective: Children read short school situations, name the civic virtue each one calls for (honesty, respect, responsibility, fairness, courage), and write what a good citizen would do.

note.mistake: Children think courage means not feeling afraid, so they miss it where the page says a stomach gets tight or a heart beats fast. They pick a virtue from one word, or use a word twice.
note.words: Say: "A virtue is a way of acting that helps a group live and work together." The situations change from copy to copy (fifteen, three for each virtue). Level 1 has three situations and only their three virtues; Levels 2 and 3 have five and all five. On every level each word is used one time. Say: "In real life one moment can need two virtues (keeping a promise is honest too). On this page each virtue goes with one situation." Level 3 adds "My own situation for a partner:". Partners swap pages and name its virtue.
note.watch: Right: a scared feeling (a tight stomach, a fast heart, shaking hands), courage; owning up (who spilled, a start too soon, whose poster), honesty; a job you said you would do (the plant, the markers, the fish), responsibility; sharing a turn or a thing (the computer, the crackers, the ball), fairness; someone new or different (new words, a new lunch, an idea unlike your own), respect.
