Any kind, true act finishes "A good citizen would": "tell the coach the truth." No answer key.

3:civic-virtues.routine: Day 1: write the five virtues and what each means on chart paper, in the page's words: honesty, telling the truth; respect, treating people well when their ways are different from yours; responsibility, doing a job you agreed to do; fairness, giving everyone the same chance; courage, doing what is right even when you feel afraid. Read short school moments aloud, never about a real classmate; the class names the virtue and what a good citizen would do. Day 2: the page.

3:constitution.title: The Constitution and Our Class Constitution
3:constitution.objective: Children learn that the U.S. Constitution, signed on September 17, 1787, is the plan for our national government and that the Bill of Rights protects freedoms such as speech and religion, then write a class constitution beginning "We the students."

note.mistake: Children mix up the Constitution with the Declaration of Independence (1776), or think it is a list of rules for kids. On Level 3 they pick a rule that protects no freedom ("Walk in the hall").
note.words: Say: "A constitution is a plan for how a group will work together." Every level prints the Constitution's first words and the three freedoms. Level 1: a line from each freedom to its picture (the pictures change order from copy to copy), then two rules with "because." Level 2: four rules. Level 3 adds "Rule number ___ protects freedom of ___ in our class." Before Level 3, be sure one class rule protects a freedom: "We listen when someone shares an idea." Never ask a child about their religion.
note.watch: Right on Level 1: speech, the speaker; religion, the church, synagogue, and mosque; the press, the reporter. The rules are the class's own: there is no wrong rule. "In order to" takes a goal: "in order to learn and be kind." On Level 3: "Rule number 2 protects freedom of speech in our class. It does this by letting everyone share ideas." No answer key.

3:constitution.routine: Day 1, near Constitution Day (September 17): show the first words, "We the People of the United States." Say: "In 1787 leaders wrote this plan for our national government. In 1791 the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, was added. It protects freedoms like speech, religion, and the press." List rules that would help our class, each with a reason, on chart paper. Day 2, after the page: the class picks four or five rules by a show of hands, writes them under "We the students of Room ___," and everyone signs.

3:deciding-together.title: Deciding Together
3:deciding-together.objective: Children deliberate on a real class question (how to use indoor recess, where to put a reading corner): they list the choices, give reasons with evidence, listen to every side, and reach a decision the whole group can accept.

note.mistake: Children argue for their favorite without a reason, or think the loudest side or the first vote wins. They hear a reason against their choice as an attack on them, or stop listening once they have spoken.
note.words: Say: "We are looking for a choice most of us can accept, not for a winner." Model: "I agree with ___ because ___." "I see it differently because ___." "So you think ___?" (say back a view before you answer it). The page is each child's record. Every level has our question, three choices with a reason for each, the choice the class reached, and "I can accept it because ___." Level 2 adds a reason against each choice and "The question I asked another group." Level 3 adds "Did my mind change?" yes or no, and what changed it or kept it.
note.watch: There is no wrong answer: every reason, question, and choice on the page is the child's own. Look for a reason backed by a fact ("The spot by the window has the most light"), a view said back fairly, and a child who changes their mind when they hear a better reason, or can say why it stayed. A child may pass when the class shares aloud. No answer key.

3:deciding-together.routine: Day 1: pose one real class question with three choices, one whose answer you will really carry out (how to use indoor recess, where to put a reading corner), and write it on the board. Small groups list a reason for and a reason against each choice on chart paper. Day 2: each group reports while the others listen and ask one question. Then the class looks for a choice, or a mix, most people can accept, and only then votes. Each child fills in the page as the class goes, on both days.

3:changing-laws.title: How People Change Laws
3:changing-laws.objective: Children read two true stories of people changing national laws (the 19th Amendment, 1920; the Americans with Disabilities Act, 1990) and a sample town's crosswalk story, and record who wanted each change, what they did, and what changed.

note.mistake: Children think one person or one day changed the law, or that a law changes as soon as people ask. They write who wanted the change under "What did they do?"
note.words: Say: "People change laws peacefully, and it can take many years." Each story has a picture; the 1915 march shows women and a man. Level 1 has one of the three stories (it changes from copy to copy), with its first answer given. Levels 2 and 3 have all three and a chart with three lines a row. Level 3 adds "One change I would ask for at school:" and "How I would ask:".
note.watch: Right: women and men gave speeches, wrote letters, and marched, and women won the right to vote ("women" alone is right too); people with disabilities spoke out, wrote to Congress, and marched, and a law requires ramps, wide doors, and fair hiring; neighbors gathered signatures and spoke at a city council meeting, and a crosswalk was painted ("the council voted yes" is right too). Even after 1920, unfair rules kept many Black, Native American, and Asian American women from voting for years. On Level 3, any peaceful way to ask is right. No answer key.

3:changing-laws.routine: Day 1: ask, "If a law seems unfair, what can people do?" List peaceful ways: speak out, write letters, gather signatures, march, vote. Tell the true stories: in 1848 at Seneca Falls, New York, women and men met to ask for women's rights, among them the right to vote, and many people carried on the work for more than 70 years, until the 19th Amendment (1920); people with disabilities spoke out, wrote to Congress, and marched until the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990). Day 2: the page.

3:continents-oceans.title: Continents and Oceans
3:continents-oceans.objective: Children locate the seven continents and five oceans on a world map and number them, then name the oceans that touch North America and the continent that lies south of Europe.

note.mistake: Children think the Pacific is two oceans because the flat map shows it on both edges. They mix up the Arctic Ocean (at the top) and the Southern Ocean (around Antarctica), and North and South America.
note.words: Say: "A globe shows the whole Earth. A flat map cuts it open, so the Pacific shows on both sides." The numbers change from copy to copy, and the Pacific carries the same number twice. Three numbers point with a short line: the Arctic Ocean at the top, the Southern Ocean and Antarctica at the bottom. A dashed line divides Europe from Asia. Levels 1 and 2 say Oceania: Australia and the islands near it; many US books call it Australia. Level 1: write each number in the box next to its name; two are already written. Level 2: the same, none written. Level 3 has no names: write each name on the line with its number.
note.watch: Right: each box or line matches the number at that place on that copy: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania, Antarctica; the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern Oceans. "Australia" for Oceania is right too. On Level 3, accept small spelling slips when the name is clear. No answer key.

3:continents-oceans.routine: Day 1: turn the class globe slowly. Children find the seven continents and the five oceans, touch each, and say its name. Ask: "Which oceans touch North America?" (the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Arctic) and "Which continent lies south of Europe?" (Africa). Then lay a flat world map beside the globe and find the Pacific on both of its edges. Day 2: the page.

3:map-scale.title: How Far Is It? Using a Map Scale
3:map-scale.objective: Children measure distances on a town map with a ruler and the map scale (1 inch stands for 1 mile), compare a town map with a state map, and tell which map shows more detail and which shows more land.

note.mistake: Children start at the end of the ruler or at 1 instead of 0, or measure from the edge of a picture instead of its dot. They think the bigger map on the page shows more land.
note.words: Say: "On this town map, 1 inch stands for 1 mile, so the inches and the miles are the same number." The sample town's five places (school, park, library, fire station, lake) are the same on every copy; where they sit and the pairs asked change. Every dot sits on a street; every asked pair lies along one. Each row has boxes under "inches" and "miles." Level 1: three distances to the nearest inch. Levels 2 and 3: to the nearest half inch. On the state map, 1 inch stands for 100 miles and the whole town is the red dot. Level 3 adds the shortest trip to two places on one street, the school between them.
note.watch: Measure the child's own copy: every distance is a whole inch on Level 1 and a whole or half inch on Levels 2 and 3. The town map shows the streets and the library; the state map shows more land and more cities. On Level 3, go to the nearer place first, back past the school, then on: the near distance twice plus the far one (for example, 1 + 1 + 1 1/2 = 3 1/2 miles). No answer key.

3:map-scale.routine: Print the page at actual size (100%), never "fit to page," and give each child a real inch ruler. Day 1: show a printed road map of our state (a printout from the state's website works). Children copy the length of its scale bar onto a paper strip and measure from city to city: "Each strip is ___ miles." Compare it with a town map: which shows the streets, which more land? Day 2, the page: practice putting the ruler's 0 on the first dot.

3:grid-map.title: Make a Grid Map of Our Community
3:grid-map.objective: Children draw a map of the school neighborhood on a lettered and numbered grid with a title, a key, a compass rose with north at the top, and a scale, then write grid locations (B3, D1) for a partner to find.

note.mistake: Children write the number before the letter (4C) or count from the wrong corner. They turn the map so north is not at the top.
note.words: Say: "Name a square by its letter across the top, then its number down the side: C4." Level 1: the school is drawn in C4 with two crossing streets whose name plates are blank: pick two real streets that cross near the school. The compass rose has N, the scale says "1 square = 1 block," and the key has five symbols to copy (school, house, park, store, a place to eat). Levels 2 and 3: a blank grid, a box to draw the compass rose, "1 square = ___ block(s)," and five key rows. Level 3 adds two "From the ___, go ___ block(s) ___ to the ___." "A house" on the checklist is any house near school, never the child's own.
note.watch: There is no wrong map: it is the child's own drawing, and a place the neighborhood does not have stays unchecked. Look for a title, a compass rose with N at the top, the scale, a key whose symbols match the map, and squares a partner can find, the letter first. On Level 3: "From the school, go 2 block(s) north to the park." No answer key.

3:grid-map.routine: Session 1: walk around the school's block if your school allows it, or look at a printed street map of the blocks around school; list on chart paper what is near and which way it is from the school. Say: "On our map, north is at the top and each square is one block." Session 2: children draw their maps on the page. Session 3: partners swap pages, find each other's squares ("The park is in square B2."), and give and follow directions ("From the school, go 2 blocks north to the park.").

3:where-people-live.title: Where People Live and Why
3:where-people-live.objective: Children compare a U.S. population dot map with a land and water map, find that more people live along the coasts, big rivers, and the Great Lakes and fewer in deserts and high mountains, and write reasons why.

note.mistake: Children decide many or few from the land map instead of the dots. They give a reason that does not fit the place ("ports" or "water" for a desert, "flat land" for the mountains).
note.words: Say: "Each dot is 100,000 people." The dots come from the 2020 Census and show the 48 states that touch each other. The letters and places change from copy to copy and are never named: each is one of eight real places, by the Atlantic (Miami, Jacksonville), on a Great Lake (Chicago, Cleveland), in a desert (Nevada's Great Basin, the Chihuahuan Desert in west Texas), or in the Rocky Mountains (Idaho, Wyoming). Circle from the dots; give the reason from the land map. The cream land is "other land": hills and valleys. Level 1: two places and the reason words (water, flat land, ports, cold, dry). Level 2: four places, one of each kind. Level 3 adds "In our state, many people live ___ because ___."
note.watch: Right: by the Atlantic or a Great Lake, many people, "because there is water, a port, and flat land" ("warm" is right too for Florida); in a desert, few, because it is dry ("cold" fits Nevada too); in the mountains, few, because it is cold and steep ("mountains" is right too). On Level 3, any true place and reason: "near the river because it brings water and trade." No answer key.

3:where-people-live.routine: Day 1: show a U.S. map and ask: "If you started a town long ago, what would you need?" (water, food, flat land, a way to ship things). Mark where the water is (the coasts, the Great Lakes, big rivers) and where living is hard (dry deserts, cold mountains). Then show a census map of where people live: did we guess right? Day 2: the page.

3:towns-near-resources.title: Towns Grow Near Resources
3:towns-near-resources.objective: Children study a map of a sample state with a river, a harbor, a forest, farmland, and a mine, choose good and poor places to start a town, and explain how water, soil, trees, or minerals helped real towns grow.

note.mistake: Children think open, empty land is best because there is room to build. On Level 1 they circle "minerals from the mine," though no site is by the mine.
note.words: Say: "A town needs water first, and a way to get food and to trade." The sites' letters change from copy to copy, half the maps are flipped, and the mine sits by the forest, far from every site. Level 1: two sites, one in the dry, rocky land: circle the better site, then what it has, then "A town there could grow because ___." Levels 2 and 3: three sites, by the river and the farmland, by the harbor, and in the dry, rocky land. For each, "Site A has ___" and, on the next line, "so a town there could ___."; then the worst place. Model the dry site: "has dry, rocky land" and "so a town there could not grow food." Level 3 adds "A resource that helped our town begin: ___."
note.watch: Right: the river site has river water and rich soil for farms; the harbor site has a harbor for ships ("the sea" is right too); the dry, rocky site has no water and is the worst place for a town. Both good sites are good. On Level 1, the better site is the one out of the dry land, with the resource it has. On Level 3, our town's real resource, found with your help. No answer key.

3:towns-near-resources.routine: Day 1: draw an island on chart paper with a river, a forest, farmland, a mine, a harbor, and a dry, rocky corner. Ask groups: "Where would you start a town? What would people need?" Groups mark a spot and say why. Name the resources: water to drink and travel on, soil for farms, trees for wood, minerals from a mine, a harbor for ships. If you can, tell what helped our own town begin. Day 2: the page.

3:levels-of-government.title: Three Levels of Government
3:levels-of-government.objective: Children sort leaders and services into local (the mayor and the city council: parks, the fire department, trash pickup), state (the governor and the state legislature: state highways, driver's licenses), and national (the president and Congress: the mail, national parks, coins and paper money), and tell which level to ask about a problem.

note.mistake: Children think the president runs everything, so they put a park, the fire department, or a state highway under national. They mix up Congress and the state legislature, which both make laws.
note.words: Say: "Each level of government has leaders and services for its own place." Every card names its level or its job: "a city park," "a state highway," "a national park." Level 1: the six leaders. Levels 2 and 3: the six leaders and two services of each level (the services change from copy to copy). Level 3 adds "The swing in a city park is broken. The level to ask: ___ Why: ___." Many places have a town board or a county instead of a city council: that is local too.
note.watch: Right, local: the mayor, the city council, a city park, the fire department, trash pickup. State: the governor, the state legislature, a state highway, a driver's license. National: the president, Congress, the mail, a national park, coins and paper money. On Level 3: local, "because the city takes care of its parks." No answer key.

3:levels-of-government.routine: Day 1: draw three boxes inside each other on chart paper: our town or city inside our state inside our country. Write each level's leaders by role, and by name if you wish, plainly and without opinions: our mayor (or town leader) and council; our governor and state legislature; the president and Congress. Ask: "Who fixes the swings in our park? Who gives a driver's license? Who makes our coins?" Children hold up a card: local, state, or national. Day 2: the page.

3:three-branches.title: Three Branches
3:three-branches.objective: Children learn that the U.S. Constitution splits the national government into three branches (Congress makes the laws, the president carries them out, the courts decide what laws mean) that check each other, and that our state government has the same three parts.

note.mistake: Children think the president makes the laws, or that a court decides who is in trouble at school. They put "decides what laws mean" under executive, because the president decides things.
note.words: Say: "Legislative makes the laws, executive carries them out, judicial decides what they mean." Every level prints what "check" means (to stop or limit), with the veto as its example. Level 1 has six cards for our national government. Levels 2 and 3 add the three state cards under "Our state government has the same three branches" and put the job cards in the national chart. Level 3 adds "Another way one branch can check another: The ___ can ___."
note.watch: Right: legislative, Congress, makes the laws, the state legislature; executive, the president, carries out laws, the governor; judicial, the Supreme Court, decides what laws mean, the state courts. On Level 3 the veto is printed, so look for another check: "Congress can pass a bill again over a veto, with two-thirds of each house." "The courts can decide a law goes against the Constitution." "The Senate can say yes or no to the judges the president chooses." No answer key.

3:three-branches.routine: Day 1: say, "The Constitution splits our national government into three branches so no one part has all the power." Three groups act it out: the lawmakers write a pretend class bill ("Recess is 5 minutes longer."; it does not change our real recess), the president signs it or vetoes it, and the judges decide whether it fits our class constitution. Then name our state's: the state legislature, the governor, the state courts. Day 2: the page.

3:taxes-services.title: Taxes Pay for Services
3:taxes-services.objective: Children trace how the taxes people and businesses pay become a fire truck, a library book, or a repaired road, and write which level of government provides each service and how it pays for it.

note.mistake: Children think a government's money comes from nowhere, or that the president pays for everything. They put highway patrol cars under local because towns have police cars too.
note.words: Say: "People and businesses pay taxes. Each level of government collects its own and uses it for its services." Follow the arrows from the payers' dollar box to the buildings marked "local: our town," "state: our state," and "national: our country." Level 1: three drawn services, one of each level (the local and national ones change from copy to copy); their names never say the level, so ask, "Who pays for this: our town, our state, or our country?" Levels 2 and 3: children draw or write three services, each with its level. Level 3 adds "Our town should spend more on ___ because ___."
note.watch: Right on Level 1, local: a fire truck, new books for the library, trash pickup; state: highway patrol cars; national: soldiers who keep us safe, astronauts exploring space. On Levels 2 and 3, any real service with its level: a fire station, local; a state park, state; the army, national. "Without taxes, the town would not have money for fire trucks." Level 3 is the child's opinion: every honest answer stands. No answer key.

3:taxes-services.routine: Day 1: label three boxes "town," "state," and "nation." Each child drops one paper token, "tax money," into each box. Read service cards (a town pool, a state park, a national park ranger, highway patrol cars); a child carries each card to the box whose money pays for it. Say: "Towns collect mostly property taxes; states collect sales taxes, income taxes, or both; the nation collects mostly income taxes." Day 2: the page.

3:ways-to-decide.title: Ways to Decide
3:ways-to-decide.objective: Children compare how decisions are made in a class vote, a town council meeting, and an election, where citizens 18 and older vote for leaders, and write one way each process gives people a say.

note.mistake: Children think everyone in the room votes at a council meeting, or that children vote in elections. In the chart they write who decides in the "How do people have a say?" row.
note.words: Say: "There is more than one fair way to decide. Ask: Who decides? What is the rule? What does one person do to have a say?" The three texts come in a new order on each copy, and the chart's columns follow them. Level 1 has the first row, "Who decides?", done. Level 2 is a blank chart. Level 3 adds "To choose a field trip, our class should use ___ because ___." Say it is a pretend choice, so no trip is promised.
note.watch: Right, a class vote: the students; the choice with the most votes wins; a student votes one time. A town council meeting: the council members; the council members vote; a person speaks at the meeting. An election: citizens 18 and older; the person with the most votes wins; a voter votes one time. (The page's election is for a mayor or a governor; voting for president works differently and comes later.) Where the two lower rows overlap, accept either sentence, in the child's own words. On Level 3, any way with a reason: "a class vote because everyone gets a say." No answer key.

3:ways-to-decide.routine: Day 1: hold a quick class vote on a small real choice (the next read-aloud book): each student votes one time, and the most votes wins. Then act out a town council meeting: five children are the council at a table, two or three others speak for a minute about a park problem, then only the council votes. Ask: "Who decided each time? How did the others have a say?" Say: "In an election, citizens 18 and older vote for leaders, like a mayor or a governor." Day 2: the page.

3:community-problem.title: Solving a Community Problem
3:community-problem.objective: Children study a sample community problem (no safe place to cross a busy street near a park), list possible solutions, choose one by weighing its costs and benefits, and write a letter to the city council proposing it.

note.mistake: Children choose the solution that costs the most because it "works best," without weighing the cost, or think the city council builds the crosswalk itself. They write the solution after "We noticed."
note.words: Say: "Every solution has a cost and a benefit. A good choice weighs both." Level 1 gives the three solutions, each with a cost and a benefit (their order changes from copy to copy): circle one, then write "We noticed ___." and "We suggest ___ because ___." Level 2: the child writes three solutions with a cost and a benefit each, and the letter with "Thank you for ___." Level 3 adds "Who would carry out the plan the city council agrees to? Circle one." Model: "We noticed there is no crosswalk by the park. We suggest a crossing guard because children cross before and after school."
note.watch: There is no wrong choice: any solution is right when its reason weighs a cost or a benefit. A strong letter names the problem, the solution, and why. On Level 3: city workers; the city council decides, and city workers paint crosswalks and put up signs (not the Supreme Court or the governor). No answer key.

3:community-problem.routine: Day 1: read the problem aloud: in a sample town, a busy street runs between the homes and the park, with no crosswalk. Groups list ways to fix it and, for each, what it costs and how it helps: a sign that says SLOW, a crossing guard, a crosswalk with a light. Say: "A guard is paid every day and helps only before and after school. A light costs the most to build, but it stops cars all day and night." Day 2: the page, then read a few letters aloud. Sending a real letter is your choice.

3:primary-secondary.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
3:primary-secondary.objective: Children sort sources into primary (a diary, an old photograph, a letter, a map made at the time) and secondary (a textbook page, an encyclopedia article written later), and explain what each kind can tell a historian about the past.

note.mistake: Children think anything old is primary, so they put the 1955 encyclopedia article there. They think a museum sign is primary because a museum keeps old things.
note.words: Say: "Ask two questions: When was it made? Was the maker there?" Level 1 prints the two definitions and four sources, both kinds, that change from copy to copy. Levels 2 and 3 have all eight sources and no definitions: keep the chart in view. Read each source and its line aloud. Level 3 adds "The source that best tells what school was like in 1900: ___ because ___."
note.watch: Right, primary: the diary (a girl wrote about her school in 1900), the photograph (taken the day the new school opened in 1871), the letter (a soldier wrote to his family during a war), the map (drawn in 1870), the newspaper (printed the day the town's bridge opened). Secondary: the textbook page (2019), the encyclopedia article (written in 1955 about the town's history), the museum sign (2021). On Level 3: the diary, "because the girl was there in 1900." No answer key.

3:primary-secondary.routine: Day 1: hold up things made at the time (a class photo, today's morning message) and things made later (our social studies book, a library book about long ago). Ask: "When was it made? Was the maker there?" Sort them on chart paper under "Primary: made at the time by someone who was there" and "Secondary: made later by someone who studied the past." Keep the chart up. Day 2: the page.

3:double-timeline.title: A Double Timeline
3:double-timeline.objective: Children place events from a sample town's history and from U.S. history on two parallel timelines (the first transcontinental railroad in 1869, the town's first school in 1870, the Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903, women winning the vote in 1920), and tell which events happened at about the same time.

note.mistake: Children place events in the order of the list, not by year, or put 1869 on the 1860 mark. They draw a line between two events on the same timeline.
note.words: Say: "Find the year first, then write the letter above it." The big marks are ten years apart and the small marks five; 1869 sits just before 1870, and 1903 just after 1900. The event letters change from copy to copy. Level 1: four events (the town's first school, 1870, and library, 1920; the railroad, 1869; the vote, 1920). Levels 2 and 3: all seven, adding the train station (1885), the paved road (1930), and the flight (1903). Level 3 adds "Two events from our town (find them with your teacher): In ___, ___."
note.watch: Right: each letter above its year on its own line, and two joining lines: the railroad (1869) and the town's first school (1870); women win the vote (1920) and the town library (1920). No other pair is within five years. On Level 3, any two real dates of our town, even ones after 1940. No answer key.

3:double-timeline.routine: Before Day 1, find two dates of our town's history (the town or library website). Day 1: tape two long paper strips on the wall, one above the other, marked 1860 to 1940 every ten years: "Our town" and "The United States." Place the U.S. events together: the first railroad across the country was finished in 1869; the Wright brothers made the first powered airplane flight in 1903; women won the right to vote in 1920. Add our town's dates (lengthen a strip if they fall outside 1860-1940) and ask: "What happened at about the same time?" Day 2: the page.

3:then-and-now.title: Life Then and Now
3:then-and-now.objective: Children compare life in a U.S. town around 1900 with life today (getting around, lighting homes, sending messages, going to school), using pictures and short texts, and write how one part of life changed and one stayed the same.

note.mistake: Children think people around 1900 lived in the dark or had no schools, and that everything changed. Some write what their own home has instead of what is true in most places today.
note.words: Say: "These are drawn sample photos, not real people." The lighting photo shows an oil lamp (a glass chimney over a flame) beside a candle. Each row has a short true text about 1900; children write what it is like today in most places, never about their own home. Level 1 has two of the four rows (they change from copy to copy). Levels 2 and 3 have all four: getting around, lighting at home, sending messages, and school. Every level has "What changed most:" and "Something that stayed the same:". Level 3 adds "The change that mattered most: ___ because ___." Ask: "What do we still do? We walk, write letters, and learn with a teacher."
note.watch: There is no wrong answer when the child writes what is true today: cars and buses, electric lights, phones and email, schools with a class for each grade. A strong "stayed the same" names something both times share: "Children still learn to read at school." On Level 3, every honest reason stands. No answer key.

3:then-and-now.routine: Day 1: set out pairs of things: a candle (unlit) and a flashlight, a letter in an envelope and a phone, a picture of a horse and wagon and a toy car. Ask: "Which did people use around 1900? Which do we use today?" Say: "The telegraph sent urgent news along wires, in clicks of code." Make a T-chart, "About 1900" and "Today." Day 2: the page.

3:economic-resources.title: Resources and Jobs in Our Community
3:economic-resources.objective: Children sort the resources a local business uses into natural resources (wheat, water), human resources (a baker's skill), and capital resources (an oven, a delivery van), and do the same for a business in their own town.

note.mistake: Children put the oven, the van, or the building under human because people made them, and wheat under human because a farmer grew it. They put the water under capital because it comes from a tap: the tap is capital, the water is natural.
note.words: Say: "Natural resources come from nature. Human resources are people and their work. Capital resources are tools, machines, and buildings people made to help make goods." The picture shows a wheat field by the van and a salt shaker on the counter. Level 1: six cards, two of each kind, that change from copy to copy, and what each kind means under its column. Levels 2 and 3: all nine cards and no meanings: keep the class chart in view. Level 3 adds a chart for "A business in our town:" with a line under each kind. Any business in town works (a pizza shop, a gas station); never ask about a family's business.
note.watch: Right, natural: wheat grown on a farm, the water for the dough, salt. Human: the skill of the baker, a cashier's work. Capital: an oven, the mixer, a van that delivers bread, the bakery building. On Level 3, a pizza shop: natural, tomatoes; human, the cook; capital, the oven. No answer key.

3:economic-resources.routine: Day 1: hold up a loaf of bread (or a picture of one) and ask: "What did it take to make this?" Write each answer on a sticky note: wheat, water, salt, the baker, an oven, a truck. Sort them on chart paper into three columns: Natural, things found in nature; Human, people and what they do on the job; Capital, things people made that help make goods. Keep the chart up. Day 2: the page.

3:cause-effect-history.title: Causes and Effects in a Town's History
3:cause-effect-history.objective: Children read a short history of a sample town, link each cause to its effect (a railroad came, so farmers could ship their crops; a factory closed, so families moved away), and write the most likely cause of one change in their own community.

note.mistake: Children join a cause to the effect beside it, or to the one that comes next in the story. They mix up the factory opening and closing, because both are about families moving.
note.words: Say: "A cause is why something happened. The effect is what happened because of it." The story is one of three sample towns (Maple Falls, Cedar Creek, Willow Bend); only the name and the years change. Level 1 has two causes and two effects; Levels 2 and 3 have all four. On every level each effect is used one time. Read the story aloud, then each cause, and ask: "What happened because of it?" Level 3 adds "In our town, ___. It happened because ___. My source: ___." Model: "In our town, many new houses were built. It happened because a factory opened."
note.watch: Right: the railroad came, farmers shipped crops to cities; the river flooded, houses were built on the hill; a factory opened, many families moved in; the factory closed, many families moved away. On Level 3, any real change whose cause the source tells, with the source named: "My source: the town's history page." No answer key.

3:cause-effect-history.routine: Day 1: chain causes and effects from class life on the board: "It rained, so recess was inside." "Recess was inside, so we played board games." Underline "so" and "because." Then read the class one change in our town and its cause from a source children can see (the town's or library's history page, a local history book). Day 2: the page.

K:word-picture-match#p-school.title: Back to School: Classroom Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-school.objective: Children name four things they use at school (student, scissors, cabinet, pen) and match each picture card to the real thing.

note.mistake: Many children call every writing tool a crayon or a marker and every cupboard a closet, so "pen" and "cabinet" get lost; others think "student" is one child's name, not a word for all of them.
note.words: Say, "This is a pen. It writes like a crayon, but it is thin." Ask, "Who is a student here?" and answer together, "We are all students!" Ask, "What do we keep in the cabinet?"
note.watch: The easy card page shows four big cards: a student holding a book, blue scissors, a red cabinet and a pen. Watch who points to the right card when you say a word, and who can say the word when you point.

K:word-picture-match#p-school.routine: Take a word walk around the room: hold up a real pen, child-safe scissors and a class name tag, stop at the cabinet, and let each child touch the thing while the class says its name. Read aloud a picture book about the first days of school and point to things we have in our room too. Teach the scissors walk: blades closed, pointing down.
week: Word walk around the room: touch and name the cabinet, a pen, the scissors and a classmate, a student.
Scissors walk at circle: blades closed and pointing down; children pass the scissors and say their name.
Classroom Word Cards: children cut on the dotted lines with help and name each picture.
Card hunt: hide the four cards around the room; finders say the word and lay the card by the real thing.
Clap each card word: pen (1), scis-sors (2), cab-i-net (3); each child takes one card home.
K:word-picture-match#p-school.check: Names the student, scissors, cabinet and pen on the cards and in the room

K:ordinal-position#p-school.title: Back to School: First and Last in Line
K:ordinal-position#p-school.objective: Children say who is first, next and last in a line and count from the flag to find the place a chip names.

note.mistake: Children start counting at the wrong end of the row or count the flag itself as "first"; others confuse "first" with the number one and look for a picture with a 1 on it instead of the picture next to the flag.
note.words: Put a finger on the flag and say, "We start here. The flag is not a picture." Touch each picture: "First, second, third." Ask, "Which one is first in line? Which one is last?"
note.watch: The page has three rows of five school things (a backpack, a ruler, a chair, a desk, books, a crayon, a globe, a pencil) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, one with a circle and one with an X. Read each chip aloud; young 3s do first and last.

K:ordinal-position#p-school.routine: Line up for real: five children stand at the door, with a paper flag taped to the door frame. The class counts places from the flag: "first, second, third." Change who stands where and ask, "Who is first now? Who is last?" Then line up five school things on the table (a backpack, a chair, a crayon, a book, a pencil) and count their places from a paper flag the same way.
week: Line leader game at the door: count from the flag who is first, second, third and last.
Five school things in a row on the table; children touch each one and say first, next and last.
Who moved? Swap two school things and say which place each one is in now.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip aloud; children count from the flag and mark.
Lining up to go outside: each child says their place in line before we walk.
K:ordinal-position#p-school.check: Says who is first and who is last in a line of five, counting from the front

K:class-rules#p-school.title: Back to School: Our Class Rules
K:class-rules#p-school.objective: Children tell a picture that follows a class rule (walking inside, cleaning up) from one that does not, and say how the rule keeps us safe.

note.mistake: Young children often circle the picture that looks most fun (the boy running past the lockers) instead of the one that follows the rule, and some think a rule only counts while the teacher is watching.
note.words: Ask, "Is this child using walking feet or running feet?" Say, "We walk inside so nobody gets hurt." Ask, "What happens if the blocks stay on the floor?" Praise with, "You cleaned up, so our room is safe."
note.watch: The page shows two pairs of pictures: a boy walking by the lockers and a boy running past them, and a child in a pink shirt walking away from spilled blocks and the same child putting the blocks into a bin. Watch that the circle and the X go on different pictures in each pair.

K:class-rules#p-school.routine: Act the rules out in the room. Walk the hallway with walking feet; then the teacher shows one quick step and asks if running inside is safe. Tip out a basket of blocks, sing a clean-up song and put every block back together, then talk about what happens when toys stay on the floor. Take photos of children following each rule for a class rule chart.
week: Practice walking feet in the hallway and talk about why we walk inside.
Clean-up song: tip out the blocks basket and put every block back together.
Our Class Rules page: circle the child who walks and the one who cleans up; cross out the others.
Take photos of children walking and cleaning up for the class rule chart.
Read the rule chart at circle; each child shows one rule with their body.
K:class-rules#p-school.check: Walks inside and helps clean up when asked, and says why the rule helps

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-school.title: Back to School: Pencil Paths and Our Classroom
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-school.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy lines to school things, then trace and color a picture of a classroom.

note.mistake: Children lift the crayon at every point of the zigzag and start each new piece anywhere, or trace from the picture back toward the dot; on the classroom picture they color first and hide the dashed lines.
note.words: Say, "Put your crayon on the orange dot. Go all the way to the stapler without lifting." On the zigzag: "Up the hill, down the hill." On the picture: "Trace every dashed line first, then color."
note.watch: The pencil path page has four lines ending at a stapler, scissors, a whiteboard and a desk; the classroom page has dashed lines for a board, a clock, a globe on a cabinet, a chair, books and a backpack. Look at the grip, the start on the dot and staying on the dashes.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-school.routine: Make the lines big first: tape a straight line, a zigzag and a wavy line on the floor and walk them heel to toe. At the table, draw the same lines with a finger in a tray of sand, then with a chunky crayon on big paper. Show the "pinch and hold" grip: the crayon rests between the thumb and two fingers, and the line starts at the dot on the left.
week: Walk the tape lines on the floor: straight, zigzag, bumps and waves.
Finger lines in a sand tray, then chunky crayons on big paper, always left to right.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the stapler, the scissors, the whiteboard and the desk.
Grip practice: pinch clothespins, roll play-dough snakes and hold the crayon three ways.
In the Classroom page: trace the board, clock, globe, chair, books and backpack, then color.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-school.check: Traces a straight line and a zigzag from the dot to the picture without lifting

K:all-about-me-personal#p-all-about-me.title: All About Me: My Favorite Things and What I Can Do
K:all-about-me-personal#p-all-about-me.objective: Children tell about themselves (name, age, favorite things, things they can do) in a sentence and mark their choices on the pages.

note.mistake: Children circle every picture in a row because they like them all, or copy a friend's choice; others check "I can swim" because they want to, not because they can, and feel hurt if they are corrected in front of friends.
note.words: Say, "Pick just one. Which fruit do you like the most?" Ask, "Can you do it now, or is it something you want to learn?" Say, "That goes on the 'I want to learn' line. Learning is great!" Model, "My name is ___ and I like ___."
note.watch: The favorite-things page has three rows of six pictures (fruits, pets, instruments) and a line to copy a word; the I Can page shows eight things with boxes and an "I want to learn to" line; the All About Me page has name, age, a self-portrait, a box for the family and three boxes to draw a favorite hobby, treat and vehicle. Read "hobby" as "something you like to do." The teacher writes for the 3s.

K:all-about-me-personal#p-all-about-me.routine: Each child brings one favorite thing from home, or picks one in class, for an All About Me basket. At circle the child holds it and finishes, "I like it because..." Read aloud a picture book about a child who is proud of what they can do. Then show real things from the pages (a toothbrush, a ball, a paintbrush, a book) and children stand up for each thing they can do.
week: Show and tell: each child holds a favorite thing and says, "I like it because..."
My Favorite Things page: circle a favorite fruit, pet and instrument; the teacher writes the words.
I can game: stand up if you can run, swim, sing, paint, ride a bike or kick a ball.
I Can page: the teacher reads each sentence; children check the things they can do.
All About Me page: draw yourself, your family and your favorites; the teacher writes name and age.
K:all-about-me-personal#p-all-about-me.check: Says own name, age and two favorite things in a sentence

K:compare-groups#p-all-about-me.title: All About Me: Count the Letters in My Name
K:compare-groups#p-all-about-me.objective: Children count the letters in their name, one letter per box, and compare with a friend's name to see whose has more.

note.mistake: Children count by saying the letter names or their whole name, or skip a letter and start over in the middle; when they compare, many say the name written bigger or wider has more letters.
note.words: Say, "Touch each letter and count: one, two, three, four." Ask, "How many letters are in your name?" Then, "Let's put our names letter under letter. Whose name has letters left over? That name has more."
note.watch: The page asks for the name one letter per box, how many letters, the first letter, a friend's name, and who has more letters (two bubbles: me, my friend). Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s trace what the teacher writes. Watch one touch per letter.

K:compare-groups#p-all-about-me.routine: Give each child a name strip and a cup of magnetic letters or letter tiles (an adult sits at the table: the pieces are small). Children build their name by matching the strip, then count the letters, touching each one. Lay two names side by side, letter under letter, and see which name has letters left over: that name has more.
week: Find your name card at arrival; at circle, point to each letter of a friend's name as we count.
Build your name with letter tiles (an adult at the table) and count the letters, touching each.
Name partners: lay two names letter under letter and find the one with letters left over.
My Name page: the teacher writes the name; children trace one letter per box and count them.
Name graph: stick name strips in rows by how many letters and count each row.
K:compare-groups#p-all-about-me.check: Counts the letters in own name and says whose name has more

K:five-senses#p-all-about-me.title: All About Me: My Five Senses
K:five-senses#p-all-about-me.objective: Children explore real things and match each one to the body part they use to sense it (hand, ear, tongue, nose).

note.mistake: Children draw every line to the hand because they touch everything, or to the eye because they see it. The lemon has two right answers: you can smell it (nose) or taste it (tongue). Accept both; only the one-line-to-each-part rule makes it the tongue.
note.words: Ask, "Which part of you tells you the drum is loud?" Say, "We hear with our ears." For the lemon: "You can smell it and you can taste it. Both are right!" Ask, "What else could tell you about the sand?"
note.watch: The first page matches a flower, sand, a saxophone and a lemon to a hand, an ear, a tongue and a nose; the second a drum, a rock, a lemon and a flower to the same four. Accept a lemon line to the nose or the tongue and ask the child to say why.

K:five-senses#p-all-about-me.routine: Set up sense stations with the real things from the pages: a flower to smell, a drum to hear, a rock and a tray of sand to touch, and lemon slices to smell and, after you check for allergies first, to taste. At each station the child points to the body part they use. Add a feely bag for touch, with only large, safe objects chosen by the teacher.
week: Sense walk: point to eyes, ears, nose, tongue and hands; sing "Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes."
Sense stations: smell a flower, touch sand and a rock, listen to a drum, smell a lemon.
Five Senses page: draw lines from the flower, sand, saxophone and lemon to the body parts.
Taste and touch (check for allergies first): a lemon slice to taste; guess things in the feely bag.
Second Five Senses page: the drum, rock, lemon and flower; say which sense each one uses.
K:five-senses#p-all-about-me.check: Names which body part hears, smells, tastes and touches

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-all-about-me.title: All About Me: Shapes Around My Body
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-all-about-me.objective: Children trace rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds, starting at the orange dot and following the arrow.

note.mistake: Children trace a circle in pieces, stopping and starting again, or go the other way round from the arrow; on squares and triangles they round off the corners instead of stopping and turning.
note.words: Say, "Start at the orange dot and go round like the arrow, all the way back home." On a square: "Stop at the corner. Turn. Keep going." Ask, "How many corners did you make?"
note.watch: The page has four rows of dashed shapes (circles, squares, triangles and diamonds), each row with an orange starting dot and an arrow, and a small body picture at the end: a leg, a foot, a face and an arm. Watch for one smooth circle and sharp square corners.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-all-about-me.routine: Make shapes with our bodies: hold hands in a big class circle, stand inside a square of tape on the floor, and make a triangle with three friends' arms. Then trace a circle on a partner's back with a finger and let them guess the shape. Finish with play-dough snakes bent into a circle and a square, and count the corners.
week: Body shapes: a class circle, a tape square on the floor and triangles made with three friends' arms.
Back tracing: draw a circle or a square on a partner's back; the partner guesses the shape.
Circles, Squares and More Shapes: trace the circle row and the square row from the orange dot.
Play-dough snakes bent into circles, squares and triangles; count the corners of each.
Finish the triangle and diamond rows, then find the leg, foot, face and arm pictures.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-all-about-me.check: Traces a circle in one stroke and a square with four corners

K:word-picture-match#p-feelings.title: Feelings Word Cards: Angry, Tired, Excited and More
K:word-picture-match#p-feelings.objective: Children name feelings from faces (angry, tired, excited, scared, sad, surprised, shy) and pick the face card that matches how someone looks.

note.mistake: Children call every unhappy face "sad" and every smiling face "happy," so tired, angry and scared all become sad. The words "content" and "merry" are new to most: give them kid meanings first (calm and happy, very jolly).
note.words: Say, "Look at the eyebrows. They are pulled down. This face is angry." Ask, "Is this face sad or tired? Look at the eyes." Say, "Content means calm and happy, like after a hug. Merry means happy and laughing."
note.watch: The first card page shows four big faces (angry, tired, content and excited); the second has eight smaller faces (shy, merry, content, tired, scared, sad, excited and surprised). Listen for feeling words other than happy and sad.

K:word-picture-match#p-feelings.routine: Pass a hand mirror around the circle: the teacher names a feeling and each child makes that face, then shows a partner. Read aloud a picture book about big feelings and stop to ask how the character feels. Act out short moments with a puppet (its block tower falls, it gets a hug, a loud noise surprises it); children hold up the face card that matches.
week: Mirror faces: make happy, sad, angry and surprised faces and look at them in the mirror.
Feelings Word Cards (four faces): angry, tired, content and excited; the teacher cuts the cards.
Puppet moments: the puppet's tower falls; children hold up the card for how it feels.
Feelings Word Cards (eight faces): add shy, merry, scared, sad and surprised.
Feelings charades: a friend finds the card, then we clap it: sad (1), an-gry (2), ex-cit-ed (3).
K:word-picture-match#p-feelings.check: Names at least four feelings from faces: happy, sad, angry and scared

K:ordinal-position#p-feelings.title: Feelings Faces in a Row: First, Next, Last
K:ordinal-position#p-feelings.objective: Children say first, next and last for a row of faces and count from the flag to find a face's place.

note.mistake: Children look for the face that "matches" the number word instead of counting places, or start from the right side because their favorite face is there. Many 3s know first and last but guess the places in between.
note.words: Say, "Start at the flag. Count each face: first, second, third." Ask, "Which face is last in this row?" Read a chip: "This one says third, with an X. Find the third face and make an X."
note.watch: The page shows three rows of five round faces (puzzled, crying, laughing, worried, angry, surprised and more) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each chip with a circle or an X. Read every chip aloud; 3s may do first and last only.

K:ordinal-position#p-feelings.routine: Five children stand in a row at the front holding face cards, with a paper flag taped at one end. Ask, "Who is first? Who is last?" and count places together from the flag. Then a child calls out a feeling; the child holding that face steps forward and says, "I am third." Mix up the line and play again so every child gets a turn.
week: Feelings line: five children hold face cards; count first, second and third from the flag.
Who moved? Two faces swap places; the class says the new first and last.
Call a feeling: the child with that face says their place, "I am fourth."
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count faces from the flag and mark.
Lining up: each child says their place in line and one feeling they have today.
K:ordinal-position#p-feelings.check: Finds the first, third and last face in a row of five

K:feelings#p-feelings.title: Feelings: How Would You Feel?
K:feelings#p-feelings.objective: Children say how they would feel in everyday moments and sort faces into feelings that feel good and feelings that feel bad.

note.mistake: Children think there is one right face for each picture and get upset when a friend fears the spider they like. On the sort page, many read the first face (eyes squeezed shut, mouth wide open) as laughing and put it under feels good: look at the eyebrows. Any face is right if the child can say why.
note.words: Ask, "How would you feel if rain came on your picnic?" Say, "Some friends feel scared of spiders, and some feel happy. Both are okay." Ask, "Does angry feel good or bad inside your body?" Say, "When I feel bad, I can smell the flower and blow out the candle."
note.watch: The first page has six pictures (a rain cloud, a spider, a party hat with a cake, an ice cream cone, slippers and the moon, a sleeping bag), each with two faces to choose from; the second has four faces to sort into Feels good and Feels bad. Accept any face the child explains.

K:feelings#p-feelings.routine: Make a feelings corner with a soft pillow and a plastic calm-down bottle (glitter and water inside, lid glued shut). Show things that bring feelings: a party hat, a toy spider, a picture of an ice cream cone, a cozy blanket. For each, children make a face and say, "I would feel..." Teach one calm-down tool: smell the flower, blow out the candle.
week: Feelings corner tour: the calm-down bottle and "smell the flower, blow out the candle."
How would you feel? A party hat, a toy spider and a cozy blanket: make the face and say it.
How Do You Feel? page: circle a face for rain, a spider, a party, ice cream, bedtime and a sleeping bag.
Feels good or feels bad: sort feeling face cards into two baskets and say why.
Feels Good or Feels Bad page: draw a line from each face to its box; share a calm-down tool.
K:feelings#p-feelings.check: Names how they feel and uses one calm-down tool when a feeling is big

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-feelings.title: Feelings Faces Pencil Paths: Lines and Crosses
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-feelings.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy paths and draw down lines, slants and crosses toward feeling faces.

note.mistake: Children push the crayon up from the bottom on down lines, so the lines wobble, and draw crosses as two lines that miss each other; on the slants they turn the paper instead of moving their hand.
note.words: Say, "Start at the top dot and pull down, like rain falling." For a cross: "Down, then across, and make them meet in the middle." Ask, "What face is waiting at the end of this line?"
note.watch: The pencil path page has a straight line, a zigzag, bumps and waves, each ending at a feeling face; the second page has rows of down lines, crosses, slants both ways and X crosses, also ending at faces. Check top-to-bottom strokes and lines that meet.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-feelings.routine: Move the lines to music: march in a straight line to a happy song, jump a zigzag, and sway like waves to a calm song. Then paint with water on the fence or a chalkboard outside: tall down lines, slanted lines and crosses. Children show the face that matches the music: a happy march, a sleepy wave.
week: Feelings music: march straight lines to happy music, sway in waves to calm music.
Pencil Path Practice: trace each line to its feeling face and name the face at the end.
Water painting on the fence or chalkboard: tall down lines, slants and crosses.
Down Lines, Slants and Crosses: start at the top dot and pull each line down.
Draw a happy face and a sad face with lines and curves; tell a friend which is which.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-feelings.check: Draws a down line from top to bottom and a cross whose lines meet

K:word-picture-match#p-family.title: My Family and My Home: Home Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-family.objective: Children name things in a home (stairs, desk, dustpan, fan, toaster, blender, armchair, iron) and tell which room each belongs in.

note.mistake: The stairs card looks like stacked colored blocks, so many children say "blocks"; "steps" is a fine word too. Children call the dustpan a "shovel," and every kitchen machine a "mixer." Some say a thing belongs where it is in their own home (the iron "lives in the closet"), which is true for them.
note.words: Say, "This is a dustpan. We sweep the crumbs into it." Ask, "Where is the toaster in your home? In the kitchen?" Say, "In some homes the iron stays in a closet. Where is it at your house?"
note.watch: The color cards show stairs, a desk with a lamp, a dustpan and a fan; the black-and-white cards show a toaster, a blender, an armchair and an iron to color. Listen for the right word and for where each one is used at home.

K:word-picture-match#p-family.routine: Turn the house corner into a home with a real dustpan and brush, a small desk and toy kitchen things. Children play family while the teacher narrates with the words: "Grandma sweeps with the dustpan." Read aloud a picture book about a family at home and name each room. Ask families to send a photo of one room at home.
week: House corner opens: play family with a real dustpan, a desk and toy kitchen things.
Home Word Cards: stairs, desk, dustpan, fan; desk and dustpan start the same: /d/, /d/!
Which room? Put each card in a kitchen, bedroom or living room box and say why.
Home Word Cards to color: the toaster, blender, armchair and iron; color and name them.
Family photo share: point to the room in your photo and name one thing in it.
K:word-picture-match#p-family.check: Names four home things and says which room each one belongs in

K:count-how-many#p-family.title: My Family: Draw and Count Who Lives With Me
K:count-how-many#p-family.objective: Children draw their family and count the people and pets, showing each number on a ten-frame.

note.mistake: Children count themselves twice or forget to count themselves; others count everyone they love (cousins, a grandma far away) and get a very big number. Accept the child's family and help them choose who lives with them for the boxes.
note.words: Ask, "Who lives at your house? Let's put one counter for each person." Say, "Don't forget you! You count too." Ask, "No pets? Then that ten-frame stays empty."
note.watch: The page has a big box to draw the family, then four parts (people in my family, brothers, sisters and pets), each with a ten-frame to color and a box for the number. Writing the number is for the 5s; younger children fill the frame and say it.

K:count-how-many#p-family.routine: Each child brings a family photo or draws one at the easel. On a big ten-frame on the rug, the child puts one large counter for each person in the family, then one for each pet, and the class counts together, touching each counter. Families are different: count whoever the child says lives with them or takes care of them.
week: Family photos on the board: each child counts the people in their own photo.
Big ten-frame on the rug: one counter for each family member; count together.
All About My Family page: draw your family in the big box.
Fill the page's ten-frames for people, brothers, sisters and pets; the teacher helps write.
Family line-up: children stand behind the number card for the people in their family.
K:count-how-many#p-family.check: Counts the people in their family drawing, touching each one once

K:many-kinds-of-families#p-family.title: My Family: Many Kinds of Families
K:many-kinds-of-families#p-family.objective: Children see that families come in many kinds and draw a person who takes care of them.

note.mistake: Children say a family "has to have" a mom and a dad, or that a family with only a grandma is "not a real family." Some draw a pet or a friend as the one who cares for them. Accept every family the child names.
note.words: Say, "Every one of these is a family." Ask, "Who takes care of you? What does that person do for you?" Say, "Families can be big or small. They are all families."
note.watch: Both pages show three family pictures of different sizes and kinds, a big box to draw someone who cares for me, and a line where the teacher writes the names the child says. Listen for "every one is a family."

K:many-kinds-of-families#p-family.routine: Build a family board from photos families send in, or drawings made at school. Look at them at circle: big families and small ones, families with grandparents, two moms, one dad, foster families. Put family figures in the block area to build their homes. Each child tells who takes care of them and one thing that person does.
week: Family board: look at the photos and say who is in each family.
Block homes: build a home for a family of figures and tell who lives there.
Many Kinds of Families page: look at the three families and draw someone who cares for you.
Helping at home: who cooks, who reads at bedtime, who brings you to school?
Second Many Kinds of Families page: draw another person who cares for you and say their name.
K:many-kinds-of-families#p-family.check: Says that families are different and names a person who cares for them

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-family.title: My Home: Trace the House and the Path to the Door
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-family.objective: Children trace a home and garden picture, a house made of shapes and pencil paths to home things, starting at the dot.

note.mistake: On the big garden picture children trace only the house and skip the small parts (flowers, butterfly, rabbit); on the shape house they color the circles before tracing them and color the roof too.
note.words: Say, "Follow the path all the way to the door." Ask, "What shape is the roof? A triangle." Say, "Trace every shape first. Then color only the circles."
note.watch: The garden page shows a house with a path, a tree, a sun, a cloud, a butterfly, tulips and a rabbit, all dashed; the shape house page has a square house, a triangle roof, a square window, and a triangle and two circles beside it; the pencil paths end at a grill, a pan, an iron and a cushion.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-family.routine: Draw a chalk path from the playground gate to the classroom door; children walk it, then push toy cars along it. Inside, build a house from big cardboard blocks and glue a paper house: a square, a triangle roof and a small square window. Children tell what is inside their own home.
week: Chalk path outside from the gate to the door: walk it, then drive toy cars on it.
Paper shape house: glue a square, a triangle roof and a square window.
The Path to the Door page: trace the house, the path, the tree, the sun and the rabbit.
The Shape House page: trace the square, triangle and circles, then color every circle.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the grill, the pan, the iron and the cushion.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-family.check: Traces a whole house picture along the dashes and names its shapes

K:story-sequencing#p-apples-fruits.title: Apples and Fruits: First, Next, Last With an Apple
K:story-sequencing#p-apples-fruits.objective: Children put three pictures of an apple being eaten in order and tell the story with first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children glue the pictures in the order they cut them out, or put the core first because it is the smallest; some think the bitten apple and the core are two different apples.
note.words: Ask, "What happened first? The apple was all whole." Say, "Next, someone took a bite. Last, only the core is left." Ask, "Can the core come first? Why not?"
note.watch: The page shows three empty frames on a line (First, Next and Last) and a strip at the bottom with a whole apple, an apple with a bite and an apple core, each on a plate. Cutting the strip is part of the work; help 3s with the scissors.

K:story-sequencing#p-apples-fruits.routine: Check for allergies first. Show a whole apple, take one bite, and keep eating until only the core is left, taking a photo at each step (the children eat thin apple slices the teacher cuts). Children retell with the photos: "First the apple is whole, next it has a bite, last it is a core." Read aloud a picture book about apples and retell it with first, next and last.
week: Real apple story (check for allergies first): whole apple, one bite, a core; take a photo of each.
Retell with the three photos: first, next, last; mix them up and fix the order.
Story Sequencing page: cut the three apple pictures and glue them under First, Next, Last.
Play-dough apple: make it whole, take a "bite," make a core, and tell each step.
Tell the apple story to a friend with the glued page, using first, next and last.
K:story-sequencing#p-apples-fruits.check: Puts three apple pictures in order and tells it with first, next and last

K:compare-size-extremes#p-apples-fruits.title: Apples and Fruits: Find the Big Apples
K:compare-size-extremes#p-apples-fruits.objective: Children compare apples by size and circle every big one.

note.mistake: Children circle the apples they like, or every apple, or one big apple and then stop because they think there is only one answer. Small apples that sit next to big ones get circled by mistake.
note.words: Ask, "Is this apple big or small?" Say, "Put your two hands around it. Big!" Ask, "Are there more big apples? Keep looking." Say, "Leave the small ones alone."
note.watch: The page shows red apples scattered over the page, some big and some small, with no words to read; the child circles every big one. Count the big apples yourself first so you know how many circles to look for.

K:compare-size-extremes#p-apples-fruits.routine: Bring real apples of very different sizes. Children sort them into a big basket and a small basket, holding two at once to feel the difference, then line them up and find the biggest. At snack, after checking for allergies, the teacher slices one big apple and one small apple and the class counts how many slices each one makes.
week: Apple sort: real big and small apples go into a big basket and a small basket.
Hold two apples: which is bigger? Line up the apples from small to big together.
Big Ones Only page: circle every big apple and leave the small ones alone.
Big and small hunt: a big block and a small block, a big book and a small book.
Snack (check for allergies first): count the thin slices from a big apple and a small apple.
K:compare-size-extremes#p-apples-fruits.check: Circles every big apple and leaves the small ones

K:fruit-vegetable#p-apples-fruits.title: Apples and Fruits: Is It a Fruit or a Vegetable?
K:fruit-vegetable#p-apples-fruits.objective: Children sort real foods and pictures into fruits and vegetables, using seeds as a clue.

note.mistake: Children sort by color (red with red) or call everything sweet a fruit and everything green a vegetable; the strawberry's seeds are on the outside, so many say it has none.
note.words: Ask, "Does it have seeds inside? Let's look." Say, "A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside." Ask, "Where does a carrot grow? Under the ground. It is a root, a vegetable."
note.watch: The first page shows an orange, a strawberry, broccoli and lettuce above a Fruits box and a Vegetables box; the second an orange, an apple, a carrot and broccoli. The child draws a line from each dot to a box. Watch who sorts by color instead of seeds.

K:fruit-vegetable#p-apples-fruits.routine: Check for allergies first. Bring an orange, an apple, a strawberry, a carrot, broccoli and lettuce. The teacher cuts the apple and the orange open and the class finds the seeds: a fruit carries seeds. Look at the carrot (a root) and the broccoli (the flower part). Children sort the real foods onto two placemats, Fruits and Vegetables, then taste small pieces: thin apple slices, orange sections, and carrot and broccoli steamed soft.
week: Fruit and vegetable basket (check for allergies first): touch, smell and name each one.
Find the seeds: the teacher cuts an apple and an orange; seeds mean it is a fruit.
Fruits and Vegetables page: lines from the orange, strawberry, broccoli and lettuce to the boxes.
Sort the real foods onto two placemats; taste small soft pieces (carrot and broccoli steamed, not raw).
Second Fruits and Vegetables page: the orange, apple, carrot and broccoli.
K:fruit-vegetable#p-apples-fruits.check: Sorts an apple, an orange, a carrot and broccoli into fruits and vegetables

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-apples-fruits.title: Apples and Fruits: Trace Big, Middle and Small Fruit
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-apples-fruits.objective: Children trace apples and bananas from big to small and follow pencil paths to fruit.

note.mistake: Children trace the small apple first because it is quick, or trace the bananas in many short pieces; on the pencil paths they stop at each corner of the zigzag and go back over the line.
note.words: Say, "Trace the big apple first, then the middle one, then the small one." Ask, "Which apple is the biggest?" On the banana: "One long curve, like a smile lying on its side."
note.watch: The first page, titled Big, Medium, Small, has a row of three dashed apples and a row of three dashed bananas from big to small; the pencil path page has a straight line, a zigzag, bumps and waves ending at a persimmon, an apple, an orange and a peach. Watch the order big, middle, small.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-apples-fruits.routine: Make apple prints with apple-shaped sponges, a big one and a small one, dipped in red paint. Roll play-dough into a big, a middle and a small apple and line them up. Run a finger along the curve of a real banana before tracing the paper ones.
week: Apple prints: stamp big and small apple-shaped sponges in red paint.
Play-dough fruit: roll a big, a middle and a small apple and a curved banana.
Big, Medium, Small page: trace the apples, then the bananas, always the big one first.
Finger-trace the curve of a real banana, then draw the curve in the air.
Pencil Path Practice: trace each line to its fruit and name it: persimmon, apple, orange, peach.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-apples-fruits.check: Traces three apples in order from big to small

K:word-picture-match#p-community-helpers.title: Community Helpers Word Cards: People Who Help Us
K:word-picture-match#p-community-helpers.objective: Children name community helpers (teacher, gardener, cashier, doctor, veterinarian and more) and tell what each one does.

note.mistake: Children name helpers by their tool ("the hammer man") or call everyone in a uniform "police." The words pharmacist, veterinarian and tailor are new: name each picture first and give a simple meaning.
note.words: Say, "A veterinarian is an animal doctor." Ask, "Who sells us food at the store? A cashier." Say, "A tailor sews and fixes clothes." Say, "Every job helps someone. A singer and a musician help us feel happy." Ask, "Who helps us here at school?"
note.watch: The first page shows four big cards (a teacher, a musician, a gardener and a cashier); the second has eight smaller cards (athlete, pharmacist, gardener, doctor, cashier, tailor, veterinarian and singer). Watch whether the child adds what the helper does.

K:word-picture-match#p-community-helpers.routine: Invite one helper to visit (the school nurse, a cafeteria cook, or a firefighter in Fire Prevention Week) and let each child ask one question. Read aloud a picture book about people who help in a town. Open a dress-up box with hats and toy tools; a child dresses as a helper and the class guesses who it is and what that helper does.
week: Helper visit: a school helper or a firefighter answers the children's questions.
Helper Word Cards: teacher, musician, gardener and cashier; say what each one does.
Dress-up guessing game: a child dresses as a helper and friends guess who it is.
Helper Word Cards (eight): add the new jobs and clap them: tai-lor (2), phar-ma-cist (3).
Thank-you pictures: each child draws a helper and tells how that helper helps us.
K:word-picture-match#p-community-helpers.check: Names four community helpers and says what each one does

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-community-helper.title: Community Helpers: Dot-to-Dot Garbage Truck
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-community-helper.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and join the dots to finish the garbage truck.

note.mistake: Children draw to the closest dot instead of the next number, and many lose their place after 5 and start again at 1; some draw lines across the truck picture instead of from dot to dot.
note.words: Say, "Find 1. Now say the next number: 2." Ask, "Where is 6? Look carefully." Say, "When we join 9 to 10, the truck is finished."
note.watch: The page shows a garbage truck with its back, wheels and cab windows drawn; dots 1 to 10 run from 1 by the front bumper up the front of the cab and across its roof to 10, with a number strip from 1 to 10 at the bottom to help the child find the next number.

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-community-helper.routine: Watch for the garbage truck on pickup day (or look at a photo) and talk about the sanitation workers who keep our streets clean. Line up ten paper-cup trash cans numbered 1 to 10; children drive a toy truck to each can in order and pick it up, counting aloud. Mix up two cups and let the class fix the order.
week: Who cleans our street? Watch for the garbage truck or look at a photo of the workers.
Toy truck pickup: drive to paper-cup cans numbered 1 to 10, in order, counting aloud.
Fix the order: two cups swap places; children put them back in counting order.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: join the dots to finish the front of the garbage truck.
Clean-up count: pick up ten blocks and drop each in the bin, counting aloud.
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-community-helper.check: Joins dots 1 to 10 in order, saying each number

K:community-helpers#p-community-helpers.title: Community Helpers and Their Tools
K:community-helpers#p-community-helpers.objective: Children match helpers (a teacher, a doctor, a builder, a gardener, a firefighter) to the tools they use.

note.mistake: Children match by color (the red hammer with the red firefighter) or give the ladder to the builder, which can also be right. Both pages have five tools for four helpers, so one is left over, but children think every tool must get a line.
note.words: Ask, "Who uses a ladder to reach a fire?" Say, "Some tools are used by more than one helper." Say, "One tool is left over. That's okay."
note.watch: The first page has a teacher, a doctor, a builder and a gardener beside a hammer, a ladder, a rake, a needle and a book; the second a firefighter, a teacher, a doctor and a builder beside a thermometer, a ladder, a tractor, a hammer and a book. Accept a sensible match the child explains.

K:community-helpers#p-community-helpers.routine: Set up a tool table with safe real or toy tools: a toy stethoscope and thermometer, a book, a toy hammer, a garden rake (for outside), a toy ladder and a firefighter hat. A child picks a tool and acts out how it is used, and the class names the helper. Visit the nurse's office or the school garden to see real tools at work.
week: Tool table: pick a toy tool, act out how it is used, and the class names the helper.
Visit the nurse's office or the school garden to see real tools at work.
Helpers and Tools page: the teacher, doctor, builder and gardener and their tools.
Helper relay: carry a toy tool to the helper picture it goes with.
Second tools page: the firefighter, teacher, doctor and builder; find the tool nobody needs.
K:community-helpers#p-community-helpers.check: Matches four helpers to their tools and says what each tool does

K:mazes#p-community-helpers.title: Community Helpers Maze: The Firefighter and the Truck
K:mazes#p-community-helpers.objective: Children follow a winding road with a crayon to help the firefighter reach the fire truck.

note.mistake: Children cut across the grass to the truck because it is close in a straight line, or stop where two roads meet and take the one that points at the truck, then reach a dead end and give up.
note.words: Say, "Firefighters stay on the road. Keep your crayon between the edges." Ask, "Where do the roads split? Which way goes to the truck?" Say, "Dead end? Go back to the split and try again."
note.watch: The maze shows a wide gray road winding through the grass, with town buildings in the background, the firefighter at the bottom left and the fire truck at the right, and a house, a fence and a bike beside the road. Watch the crayon at each split.

K:mazes#p-community-helpers.routine: Practice the fire drill route: walk the exit path from the classroom to the meeting spot outside, then talk about firefighters who come in their truck. Lay a blue tape road on the floor that bends and splits, and children walk the firefighter's way to a toy fire truck. Practice "stop, drop and roll" on the rug.
week: Fire drill walk: follow our exit path to the meeting spot outside.
Stop, drop and roll on the rug; look at pictures of a firefighter's coat and helmet.
Tape road on the floor: walk the firefighter's way to the toy fire truck.
Picture Maze: draw a line along the road from the firefighter to the fire truck.
Draw your own road for a toy car on big paper and drive along it.
K:mazes#p-community-helpers.check: Follows a winding road with a crayon to the goal and goes back at dead ends

K:word-picture-match#p-farm.title: Farm Word Cards: Animals and Farm Things
K:word-picture-match#p-farm.objective: Children name farm animals and farm things (hen, cow, pig, sheep, goat, tractor, wheelbarrow, farmer) and tell the sound or job of each.
