note.mistake: Children call the hen "chicken" and the sheep "lamb" (accept both and stretch them), and mix up goat and sheep because both have hooves and fur; most call every farm machine a "truck."
note.words: Say, "This is a hen. A hen is a mother chicken." Ask, "Is it a sheep or a goat? Look for the beard and the horns." Say, "A tractor pulls heavy things. A wheelbarrow carries them."
note.watch: The color cards show a hen, a cow, a pig and a sheep; the black-and-white cards show a wheelbarrow, a tractor, a goat and a farmer to color. Listen for the animal's name plus what it gives or does (eggs, milk, wool).

K:word-picture-match#p-farm.routine: Sing "Old MacDonald Had a Farm" with toy farm animals, and each child chooses the next animal. Read aloud a picture book about a farm and make each animal's sound when it appears. Build a farm in the block area with a toy barn and tractor, and push a child-size wheelbarrow outside while acting out farm jobs: feeding the hens, driving the tractor.
week: Sing "Old MacDonald Had a Farm" with toy animals; each child picks the next animal.
Farm Word Cards: hen, cow, pig and sheep; say each name and the animal's sound.
Block-area farm: build a barn and pens; put each card where its animal lives.
Color the wheelbarrow, tractor, goat and farmer; clap goat (1), trac-tor (2), wheel-bar-row (3).
Wheelbarrow work outside: push leaves or straw and tell what the farmer does.
K:word-picture-match#p-farm.check: Names four farm animals and one thing a farmer uses

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-farm.title: Farm: Connect the Dots 1 to 10 to Make a Duck
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-farm.objective: Children say the numbers 1 to 10 in order and join the dots in that order to finish a duck.

note.mistake: Children connect the dots by distance, jumping to the nearest dot instead of the next number; others skip from 6 to 9 because they cannot find 7, or start at the biggest number they know.
note.words: Say, "Put your crayon on 1. Now find 2. Say it, then draw to it." Ask, "What comes after 6?" Say, "Look for the number, not the closest dot."
note.watch: The page shows a duck with its beak, eye, chest, wing and feet drawn; dots 1 to 10 make the top of its head and its back down to the tail, with no lines between them. Watch the child say each number before drawing to it.

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-farm.routine: Count real things in order before the dots: ten toy ducks in a row, one number for each duck the child touches. Lay paper plates numbered 1 to 10 in a path on the floor and children hop from 1 to 10, saying each number. Then play "What comes next?": the teacher says a number on a plate and the class says the next one.
week: Ten toy ducks in a row: touch and count each one from 1 to 10.
Number plate path: hop from 1 to 10 on the floor, saying each number.
What comes next? The teacher says a number; the class says the next one.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: start at 1 by the beak and join the dots over the duck's head and down its back.
Count the farm toys in the block area to 10, then color the finished duck.
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-farm.check: Says the numbers 1 to 10 in order and joins the dots in that order

K:animal-groups-homes#p-farm.title: Farm: Farm Animals and Wild Animals
K:animal-groups-homes#p-farm.objective: Children sort animals into farm animals and wild animals and tell who takes care of each.

note.mistake: Children sort by size (big animals are wild) or by color, and many call the zebra a striped horse that lives on a farm; some put the goat with the wild animals because it has horns.
note.words: Ask, "Does a farmer take care of this animal?" Say, "A zebra looks like a horse, but it lives in the wild." Ask, "What does a goat give the farmer?"
note.watch: The page shows a horse, an elephant, a goat and a zebra above two boxes, Farm Animals and Wild Animals; the child draws a line from the dot under each animal to a box. Watch the zebra and the horse.

K:animal-groups-homes#p-farm.routine: Put a toy barn and a box of grass and toy trees (the wild) on the rug. Children pull toy animals from a bag (a horse, a cow, a goat, a pig, an elephant, a zebra, a lion) and decide: does a farmer take care of it, or does it live in the wild? Talk about what farm animals give us (milk, eggs, wool) and why an elephant does not live on a farm.
week: Toy animal bag: pull an animal, say its name and where it lives.
Barn or wild? Sort the toy animals and tell why each one goes there.
Farm and Wild Animals page: lines from the horse, elephant, goat and zebra to the boxes.
What farm animals give us: milk, eggs and wool; feel a ball of wool.
Build a farm and a wild place in the block area and put each toy animal home.
K:animal-groups-homes#p-farm.check: Sorts a horse, a goat, an elephant and a zebra into farm and wild

K:mazes#p-farm.title: Farm Mazes: Hen, Horse, and Babies and Mothers
K:mazes#p-farm.objective: Children draw a line along a wide maze road from the start to the goal without crossing the edges.

note.mistake: Children draw a straight line from start to goal across the grass, or follow the first road into a dead end and scribble out; on the babies and mothers maze they draw all three lines to the nearest mother.
note.words: Say, "Stay on the road, between the edges, like a tractor on the lane." Ask, "Is this road a dead end? Go back and try another way." Ask, "Who is this baby's mother? Find her road."
note.watch: The hen maze has a wide road to the corn with one short dead end, and a scarecrow, haystacks and a bird beside it; the horse maze has more branches on the way to the carrot; the babies and mothers maze has a chick, a calf and a foal at the top and a horse, a hen and a cow at the bottom.

K:mazes#p-farm.routine: Make a farm maze on the floor with masking tape and chairs: wide roads and one dead end. Children push a toy tractor through it, then walk it as a hen looking for corn. In a sand tray, children drag a finger along a road the teacher draws. Talk about dead ends: "Oops, turn around and try another way."
week: Floor maze with tape and chairs: walk from the barn to the corn and find the dead end.
My First Maze: draw a line along the wide road from the hen to the corn.
Sand tray roads: push a toy tractor along a road the teacher draws.
My First Maze: find the road from the horse to the carrot; back up at dead ends.
Babies and Mothers Maze: draw a line from each baby to its own mother.
K:mazes#p-farm.check: Draws a line through a wide maze road without crossing the edges

K:word-picture-match#p-fall-forest.title: Fall Forest Animal Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-fall-forest.objective: Children name forest creatures (deer, raccoon, grasshopper, spider) and tell one thing each one does in fall.

note.mistake: Children call the deer a "reindeer," the raccoon a "cat" or "bear," and the spider and grasshopper just "bugs"; some believe every forest animal sleeps all winter long.
note.words: Say, "This is a deer. Deer live in forests near us." Ask, "What does the raccoon have on its face? A mask!" Say, "A grasshopper jumps with its long back legs."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a grasshopper, a deer, a raccoon and a spider, each with its word under the picture. Watch who uses each animal's own name instead of "bug" or "dog."

K:word-picture-match#p-fall-forest.routine: Take a fall walk and look for signs of animals: a squirrel burying a nut, a spider web, holes in leaves. With an adult watching, collect leaves, acorns and pine cones for a science table (acorns are small, so an adult stays at that table). Read aloud a picture book about forest animals in fall and find each card's animal in it.
week: Fall walk: look and listen for animals; collect leaves and pine cones with an adult watching.
Forest Word Cards: name the grasshopper, deer, raccoon and spider; the teacher cuts.
Science table: find the toy forest animals hiding among the leaves and name them.
Hop like a grasshopper, tiptoe like a deer, then clap: deer (1), rac-coon (2), grass-hop-per (3).
Tell a friend one forest animal and what it does to get ready for winter.
K:word-picture-match#p-fall-forest.check: Names a deer, a raccoon, a grasshopper and a spider and tells one fact

K:heavy-light#p-fall-forest.title: Fall Forest Animals: Which Is Heavier?
K:heavy-light#p-fall-forest.objective: Children compare two forest animals and decide which is heavier, thinking about the real animals.

note.mistake: Children circle the animal that looks bigger in its drawing, but both pictures sit in circles of the same size; others choose the animal they like or the one closer to their hand.
note.words: Ask, "In real life, which is heavier, a wolf or a squirrel?" Say, "The pictures are the same size. Think about the real animals." Ask, "Could you carry a deer? Could you carry a mouse?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of forest animals in equal circles (a wolf and a squirrel, a beaver and a mouse, a squirrel and a deer); the child circles the heavier one. Listen for a reason about the real animals, not the drawings.

K:heavy-light#p-fall-forest.routine: Use a balance scale with fall things: a pine cone and a leaf, a big rock and a feather, a small pumpkin (the teacher lifts it) and a pine cone. Children guess first, then watch which side goes down. Then they hold two things, one in each hand, and say which feels heavier. Talk about real forest animals: is a deer heavier than a squirrel?
week: Balance scale: a pine cone and a leaf, a rock and a feather; guess, then check.
Hand scales: hold two fall things, one in each hand, and say which is heavier.
Heavy or Light? page: circle the heavier forest animal in each pair.
Act it out: stomp like a heavy deer, scamper like a light mouse.
Make a heavy and light chart with the fall things we weighed.
K:heavy-light#p-fall-forest.check: Chooses the heavier of two real things or animals and says why

K:seasons#p-fall-forest.title: Fall and the Four Seasons: Our Tree
K:seasons#p-fall-forest.objective: Children watch a tree change with the seasons and match pictures to winter, spring, summer and fall.

note.mistake: Children think a tree with no leaves is dead, and on the sort many put the lamb in winter because it is woolly; the surfboard is new to most, and some put the pumpkin in summer because it is orange like the sun.
note.words: Ask, "What happens to our tree's leaves in fall?" Say, "In winter the tree rests. It is not dead." Ask, "When are baby lambs born? In spring." Say, "A surfboard is for the ocean in summer."
note.watch: The sort page shows a child skating, a surfboard, a pumpkin and a lamb above four boxes for winter, spring, summer and fall; the tree page has four bare trees labeled winter, spring, summer and fall for the child to draw on.

K:seasons#p-fall-forest.routine: Adopt a tree on the playground. Visit it, feel the bark, look at the leaves and take a photo; come back to the same tree each season to compare. Inside, look at fall things (a pumpkin, red and yellow leaves) and talk about how the tree looks with snow on it, with new buds and with green leaves.
week: Adopt a playground tree: touch the bark, look at the leaves, take a photo.
Leaf sort: green, red, yellow and brown leaves; why do leaves change color in fall?
Four Seasons Sort page: lines from the skater, surfboard, pumpkin and lamb to the seasons.
Season dress-up: a scarf for winter, sunglasses for summer, a rain hat for spring, a sweater for fall.
Draw the Tree in Four Seasons: add leaves, snow, flowers or fruit to each tree.
K:seasons#p-fall-forest.check: Matches a picture to each season and says how a tree looks in fall

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-fall-forest.title: Fall Leaves and Forest Pencil Paths
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-fall-forest.objective: Children trace a leaf and zigzag lines, then follow pencil paths to forest creatures.

note.mistake: Children round off the zigzag tips into bumps, or race through and miss the points; on the leaf they trace only the outline and skip the veins inside.
note.words: Say, "Stop at every tip of the zigzag, then turn." Ask, "Can you find the lines inside the leaf? Trace them too." Say, "Go slowly, like a leaf floating down."
note.watch: The Autumn Leaves page has a dashed leaf with veins, a cloud, a sun, a short zigzag and a long zigzag along the bottom; the pencil path page ends its four lines at a grasshopper, a bee, a worm and an owl. Look for sharp turns at each tip.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-fall-forest.routine: Make leaf rubbings: lay a real leaf under thin paper and rub it with the side of a peeled crayon, then trace the leaf's edge with a finger. Rake leaves into a pile with child rakes and walk zigzag paths through it. Draw zigzags in the air like the edge of a leaf.
week: Leaf rubbings: rub crayons over real leaves and trace the edges with a finger.
Rake leaves with child rakes and walk zigzag paths through the pile.
Autumn Leaves page: trace the leaf, the cloud, the sun and the zigzags.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the grasshopper, the bee, the worm and the owl.
Glue real leaves on paper and draw zigzag grass under them.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-fall-forest.check: Traces a zigzag with sharp points and the outline of a leaf

K:word-picture-match#p-construction.title: Construction and Tools Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-construction.objective: Children name building tools (hammer, pliers, nail, plunger, wheelbarrow, saw, pickaxe, work gloves) and show what each one does.

note.mistake: Children call every tool a hammer, and the plunger is new to most ("a stick with a cup"); some think a nail is a toy because it is small. Name each picture first, and keep real nails and saws out of children's reach.
note.words: Say, "Pliers pinch and hold." Ask, "What do we use a plunger for? To fix a stuck sink." Say, "Nails and saws are sharp. Only grown-ups use real ones."
note.watch: The color cards show pliers, a hammer, a nail and a plunger; the black-and-white cards show a wheelbarrow, a handsaw, a pickaxe and work gloves to color. Watch for the tool's name and a gesture that shows how it is used.

K:word-picture-match#p-construction.routine: Open a construction zone with toy tools, hard hats, safety goggles and big cardboard boxes; children name each toy tool as they use it. Read aloud a picture book about building a house and point to each tool. Outside, children pull on real work gloves and carry blocks in a child-size wheelbarrow. Real saws and nails are for grown-ups only.
week: Construction zone opens: hard hats, goggles, toy tools and big boxes to build with.
Tool Word Cards: pliers, hammer, nail and plunger; act out how each one is used.
Work gloves and a child wheelbarrow outside: carry blocks to the building site.
Color the wheelbarrow, handsaw, pickaxe and gloves; clap gloves (1), pick-axe (2), wheel-bar-row (3).
Tool sort: tools for building, a tool for fixing a sink, and tools only grown-ups touch.
K:word-picture-match#p-construction.check: Names four tools and shows how each one is used

K:conservation#p-construction.title: Construction and Tools: Same Number?
K:conservation#p-construction.objective: Children count two groups of tools, even when one is spread out, and say whether they have the same number.

note.mistake: Children say the spread-out row has more because it is longer, without counting; after the spread-out game, others circle the check every time because they expect "the same." Writing the number is a challenge for the 5s; 3s can say it.
note.words: Ask, "This row looks longer. Does it have more? Let's count." Say, "Touch each tool once." Ask, "Five and five: is that the same number?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of rows of tools, one row neat and one spread out, with a box for each number and a check and an X to circle: six saws and six saws (the same), four plungers and three plungers, four hammers and five hammers. Watch one touch per tool.

K:conservation#p-construction.routine: Use toy tools or big building blocks. Put four toy hammers in a tight row and four spread far apart, and ask which row has more. Children count both rows, touching each tool, and find they are the same. Then they line the rows up one under one to check. Repeat with five and six blocks so children see that spreading things out does not change how many there are.
week: Tool count: line up toy hammers and count them, touching each one.
Spread them out: does the number change? Count again to find out.
One under one: line up two rows of blocks to see if one has more or they are the same.
Same Number? page: count each group of tools and circle the check if they match.
Partner game: one child builds a tight row, one a spread-out row; count and compare.
K:conservation#p-construction.check: Counts two rows of up to six things and says if they are the same number

K:goods-and-services#p-construction.title: Construction: Who Builds the House?
K:goods-and-services#p-construction.objective: Children match workers to what they make: the builder builds a house and the cook makes bread.

note.mistake: Children think a house was "always there" or came from a store, and some match the cook to the house because both workers wear hats; others say the cook "does" the bread instead of making it.
note.words: Ask, "Who builds a house?" Say, "A builder builds houses. A cook or a baker makes bread." Ask, "What did our class build today?"
note.watch: The page shows two workers on the left (a builder holding a tool and a cook with a rolling pin) and two things on the right (a loaf of bread and a house); the child draws a line from each worker to what that worker makes.

K:goods-and-services#p-construction.routine: Build a house as a class with big cardboard bricks and a paper roof; every child has a job (carrier, builder, painter). Talk about the builder's work. Then, after you check for allergies first, knead a little bread dough together and the adult bakes it in the school kitchen. Children say which worker made each thing: the house, the bread.
week: Class house: build with cardboard bricks; each child has a builder's job.
Who made it? Look at photos of a house, a loaf of bread, a sweater and a chair.
Who Makes It? page: draw lines from the builder and the cook to what they make.
Bread dough (check for allergies first): knead it, wash hands, no tasting; the adult bakes it.
School walk: find things builders made (walls, doors, windows, shelves).
K:goods-and-services#p-construction.check: Says who builds a house and who makes bread

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-construction.title: Construction Tools: Pencil Paths and Tool Shapes
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-construction.objective: Children trace pencil paths to tools and trace rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds.

note.mistake: Children press so hard at the corners of the squares and triangles that the paper tears, and on the pencil paths they slow down only at the end and run past the tool picture.
note.words: Say, "Builders measure and go slowly. Go slowly at the corners." Ask, "How many sides does the triangle have?" Say, "Stop when you reach the tool."
note.watch: The color pencil path page ends its lines at a flashlight, a hammer, a nail and a plunger; the black-and-white shape page has rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds with a wrench, a hammer, a screwdriver and a saw at the row ends.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-construction.routine: Tap golf tees into a block of craft foam with a wooden toy hammer while an adult sits at the table. Then lay painter's tape lines on the floor as a "building plan" and build block walls on them: a square wall, a triangle roof. Children run a finger along each tape line before they build.
week: Tool work: tap golf tees into foam with a wooden toy hammer (an adult at the table).
Building plan: lay painter's tape lines on the floor and build block walls on them.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the flashlight, the hammer, the nail and the plunger.
Shape walls: build a square, a triangle and a diamond with long blocks.
Circles, Squares and More Shapes: trace each row of shapes from the dot.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-construction.check: Traces a square and a triangle with corners, from the starting dot

K:word-picture-match#p-pets.title: Pets Word Cards: Cat, Chinchilla, Parrot, Frog
K:word-picture-match#p-pets.objective: Children name pets and say what every pet needs (food, water, a home and gentle hands).

note.mistake: The chinchilla is new to almost every child (they say "mouse" or "bunny"), and some think a frog cannot be a pet; others say pets need only food and forget water, a clean home and gentle hands.
note.words: Say, "This is a chinchilla. It is a soft pet with big ears and a long tail." Ask, "What does a parrot need?" Say, "Some families keep a frog as a pet in a tank."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards (a cat, a chinchilla, a parrot and a frog), each with its word. Name the pictures first, then watch who can say what each pet needs.

K:word-picture-match#p-pets.routine: Set up a pet shop and vet in dramatic play with stuffed animals, empty food bowls, a pet bed and a toy stethoscope. If the class has a pet, children help the teacher feed it and then wash hands (no other animal handling). Read aloud a picture book about caring for a pet. Ask families to share a photo of a pet they have or would like.
week: Pet shop and vet open: care for stuffed pets with bowls, beds and brushes.
Pets Word Cards: the cat, chinchilla, parrot and frog; name the pictures first.
Class pet care, or a stuffed pet: feed it and fill the water with the teacher, then wash hands.
Pet photo share: children tell about a pet at home or one they would like.
Card game: say what each pet eats, then clap its name: cat (1), par-rot (2), chin-chil-la (3).
K:word-picture-match#p-pets.check: Names four pets and one thing every pet needs

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-pets.title: Pets: Connect the Dots 1 to 10 to Draw a Kitten
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-pets.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and connect the dots to finish a kitten.

note.mistake: Children trace over the kitten's drawn lines instead of joining the dots, or skip a dot where two sit close together under the paws; others start at 10 because it is on the left, where they start to read.
note.words: Say, "Start at the orange dot, 1, at the tip of the tail. Now find 2." Ask, "What number comes after 4?" Say, "The dots make the tail and the ground the kitten sits on."
note.watch: The page shows a sitting kitten; dots 1 to 4 run down its tail and dots 5 to 10 along the ground under its paws, starting at the orange dot, with a number strip from 1 to 10 at the bottom. Watch the child find each number before drawing to it.

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-pets.routine: Set ten paper-plate pet bowls numbered 1 to 10 in a row. Children "feed" the pets by putting one large pom-pom in each bowl while counting aloud (an adult stays close). Then the teacher says a number and a child finds that bowl. Line up ten stuffed pets for the vet and count them from 1 to 10.
week: Feed the pets: one large pom-pom in each numbered bowl, from 1 to 10.
Find the bowl: the teacher says a number and a child finds that bowl.
Vet line: count the stuffed pets from 1 to 10 as they wait for the vet.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: join the dots down the kitten's tail and along the ground under its paws.
Color the kitten and count its whiskers and paws.
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-pets.check: Connects dots 1 to 10 in order and names the picture

K:animal-groups-homes#p-pets.title: Pets and Wild Animals
K:animal-groups-homes#p-pets.objective: Children sort animals into pets and wild animals and say why a wild animal does not live in a house.

note.mistake: Children say any animal they love can be a pet ("a lion can live in my room"), or put the goldfish with the wild animals because fish live in the ocean.
note.words: Ask, "Who feeds this animal, a person or the animal itself?" Say, "A goldfish lives in a bowl at home. It is a pet." Ask, "Why can't a lion be a pet?"
note.watch: The page shows a dog, a zebra, a goldfish and a lion above a Pets box and a Wild Animals box; the child draws a line from each animal's dot to a box. Listen for the reason the child gives.

K:animal-groups-homes#p-pets.routine: Set out two places: a pet bed with bowls (home) and a box of grass, rocks and branches (the wild). Children choose toy animals (a dog, a goldfish, a cat, a lion, a zebra, a bear) and put each one in its place, telling why. Talk about how pets need people to care for them, and wild animals find their own food.
week: Home or wild? Put toy animals on the pet bed or in the wild box and say why.
Pets need us: list what our class pet, or a stuffed pet, needs every day.
Pets and Wild Animals page: lines from the dog, zebra, goldfish and lion to the boxes.
Animal charades: act like a pet or a wild animal; friends say which one it is.
Pet care chart: food, water, a clean home and gentle hands.
K:animal-groups-homes#p-pets.check: Sorts four animals into pets and wild animals and says why

K:mazes#p-pets.title: Pets Mazes: The Puppy's Ball and the Kitten's Milk
K:mazes#p-pets.objective: Children draw a line along a wide maze road to help a puppy and a kitten reach their goal.

note.mistake: Children trace along the road's edge instead of its middle, or turn into a side road toward a flower and get stuck; on the kitten maze many start at the milk and draw backward to the kitten.
note.words: Say, "Start where the puppy is, at the arrow." Ask, "Which road takes you to the ball?" Say, "Keep your line in the middle of the road."
note.watch: The puppy maze has a wide road from the puppy at the left to a soccer ball at the right, with a tree, a butterfly, a kitten, a bird and a tulip beside it; the kitten maze has a wide road through a farmyard from the kitten to a bottle of milk, with side roads that end.

K:mazes#p-pets.routine: Make a puppy path in the gym or outside with cones and hoops; children crawl through like puppies to fetch a soft ball. Then roll a ball along a bendy tape road and walk beside it. In a sand tray, children draw a road with a finger from a toy dog to a toy ball.
week: Puppy path: crawl through hoops and around cones to fetch a soft ball.
Tape road: roll a ball along a bendy tape road without leaving it.
My First Maze: help the puppy get to the ball along the wide road.
Sand tray roads: draw a finger road from a toy dog to a toy ball.
My First Maze: help the kitten get to the milk and turn back at dead ends.
K:mazes#p-pets.check: Follows a wide maze road from start to goal and turns back at a dead end

K:word-picture-match#p-thanksgiving.title: Thanksgiving Word Cards: Pie, Pumpkin, Bread, Corn
K:word-picture-match#p-thanksgiving.objective: Children name harvest foods (pie, pumpkin, bread, corn) and say one thing they are thankful for.

note.mistake: Children call the pie a "pizza" or "cake" and the corn a "banana" because of its shape; some think a pumpkin is only a decoration. "Thankful" is a new word: many say "I want..." when they mean "I am thankful for..."
note.words: Say, "Being thankful means being glad for something we have." Model, "I am thankful for my family." Ask, "What is inside the corn husk?" Say, "Pumpkins are food. We can make pie and soup from them."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a pie, a pumpkin, a loaf of bread and an ear of corn. Watch for the names and listen for a sentence that starts "I am thankful for."

K:word-picture-match#p-thanksgiving.routine: Check for allergies first. Bring a real pumpkin, an ear of corn in its husk and a loaf of bread, with a photo of a pie. Children feel, smell and describe each one and peel back the corn husk together. Read aloud a picture book about being thankful. Make a thankful chain: each child says, "I am thankful for..." and the teacher writes it on a paper strip.
week: Harvest basket: feel and describe a real pumpkin, an ear of corn and a loaf of bread.
Thanksgiving Word Cards: clap pie, bread, corn and pump-kin; which word takes two claps?
Peel the corn husk and look at the kernels; count a row of them together.
Thankful chain: each child says what they are thankful for; link the paper strips.
Taste bread or corn (check for allergies first) and describe it with the card words.
K:word-picture-match#p-thanksgiving.check: Names pie, pumpkin, bread and corn and says one thing they are thankful for

K:numeral-formation#p-thanksgiving.title: Thanksgiving: Count and Trace 1 to 5
K:numeral-formation#p-thanksgiving.objective: Children count small groups of harvest things to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.

note.mistake: Children trace the numbers without counting the pictures, or count the lone scarecrow as "one, two" because they touch it twice; many write 2 and 5 backward, which is normal at this age.
note.words: Ask, "How many pumpkins? Touch and count." Say, "The last number we say tells how many." Say, "Start the 5 at the top: down, around, and a hat on top."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one scarecrow, two hay bales, three pumpkins, four ears of corn and five pies), each with a number to look at and two to trace. Watch one touch per picture and the last number said.

K:numeral-formation#p-thanksgiving.routine: Set up a harvest counting table with real things: one small pumpkin, two ears of mini corn, three gourds, four leaves and five pine cones. Children count each group, touching each one, and put the matching number card beside it. Then put five gourds in a basket and take them out one at a time, counting down together.
week: Harvest table: one pumpkin, two corn, three gourds, four leaves and five pine cones.
Match a number card to each group; touch and count to check.
Count and Trace page: count each row of harvest pictures and trace the number.
Make 5: put five gourds in a basket, then count them out one by one.
Air numbers: trace 1 to 5 in the air and on a friend's back.
K:numeral-formation#p-thanksgiving.check: Counts up to 5 harvest things, touching each one, and says how many

K:family-traditions#p-thanksgiving.title: Thanksgiving and Family Traditions
K:family-traditions#p-thanksgiving.objective: Children learn that families keep special days in different ways and match a tradition to each family picture.

note.mistake: Children think every family keeps the same holidays theirs does, or that a special day they don't know is "not real"; some match the pie to the red-envelope picture because both families have food on the table.
note.words: Say, "Families celebrate in different ways, and all of them are special." Ask, "What does your family do on a special day?" Ask, "Which family has a pie on the table?"
note.watch: The page shows a pie and a red envelope on the left and two family pictures on the right: a family at a table with a turkey and pie, and a grandmother giving a child a red envelope under red lanterns. The child draws a line from each thing to its family.

K:family-traditions#p-thanksgiving.routine: Invite families to share a special day they keep (a birthday, Thanksgiving, Diwali, Lunar New Year, an Eid meal) with a photo, a food or an object. Set up a special day table. Children look, touch and try what is offered (check for allergies first) and tell what their own family does on a special day.
week: Family tradition share: a family brings a photo or object from a special day.
Special day table: look, touch and talk about each family's things.
Family Traditions page: lines from the pie and the red envelope to the family pictures.
Our thankful table: set a pretend table and say what we are thankful for.
Draw your family's special day and tell the class about it.
K:family-traditions#p-thanksgiving.check: Tells one way their family celebrates and listens to another family's way

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-thanksgiving.title: Thanksgiving Pencil Paths: Turkey, Leaf and Pie
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-thanksgiving.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy, wavy and loopy pencil paths to harvest pictures.

note.mistake: Children flatten the bumps into a straight line and skip the humps, and on the waves they go up and down in sharp points like a zigzag; some trace from the picture back to the dot.
note.words: Say, "Bumps go up and over, up and over, like a turkey hopping." Ask, "Are the waves pointy or round? Round." Say, "Begin at the orange dot every time."
note.watch: The first page ends its four lines at a turkey, a red leaf, a scarecrow and a pie; the review page has five lines (straight, waves, a zigzag, small bumps and big bumps) ending at a pie, a scarecrow, bread, a leaf and corn. Look for round bumps and pointy zigzags.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-thanksgiving.routine: Draw chalk lines outside (straight, bumpy and wavy) and children walk them like turkeys, then hop the bumps. At the art table, children dip a cotton swab in paint and dot a straight line across the paper, then a wavy line. Finish with finger lines in a tray of sand.
week: Chalk lines outside: walk straight, bumpy and wavy paths like a turkey.
Cotton swab dots: paint a straight line of dots, then a wavy line.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the turkey, the leaf, the scarecrow and the pie.
Finger paths in a tray of sand: straight, then bumpy, then wavy.
Pencil Path Review: trace five lines to the pie, scarecrow, bread, leaf and corn.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-thanksgiving.check: Traces bumpy and wavy lines from the dot without turning them into zigzags

K:category-sort#p-toys.title: Toys: Cut, Sort and Paste Robots, Boats and Rockets
K:category-sort#p-toys.objective: Children sort toy pictures into groups of the same kind and say why each one belongs there.

note.mistake: Children glue a picture wherever there is space or split two of a kind into different columns; cutting the strip into squares is hard, and many cut through the middle of a picture.
note.words: Ask, "What toy is at the top of this column? Find all the ones that match it." Say, "Cut on the line between the pictures." Ask, "Why does this boat go here?"
note.watch: The page has three columns topped by a robot, a boat and a rocket, with two boxes in each, and a strip of six pictures (robots, boats and rockets) to cut out at the bottom. Help 3s cut the strip apart; watch the sorting.

K:category-sort#p-toys.routine: Tip a basket of real toys onto the rug (cars, blocks, dolls, balls, toy boats). Children sort them into hoops by kind and say the rule: "All the balls go here." Sort again: toys that roll and toys that don't. Read aloud a picture book about a favorite toy. Before the page, children snip paper strips with child-safe scissors.
week: Toy sort on the rug: put real toys into hoops by kind and say the rule.
Sort again: toys that roll and toys that don't roll.
Snip practice: cut strips of paper with child-safe scissors.
Cut, Sort and Paste page: cut out the robots, boats and rockets and glue each in its column.
Tell a friend how you sorted, then build with the toys from one group.
K:category-sort#p-toys.check: Sorts toys by kind and tells the rule for the group

K:compare-size-extremes#p-toys.title: Toys: Long and Short
K:compare-size-extremes#p-toys.objective: Children compare toy vehicles and find the longest one in each row.

note.mistake: Children choose the toy that looks tallest instead of the longest, or compare real toys without lining up the ends. On the page the four toys in a row are bigger and smaller copies of one toy, so the longest is also the biggest: ask how they know.
note.words: Ask, "Which one is the longest? Put the ends together to check." Say, "Long means from one end to the other end." Ask, "Which plane is longer, this one or that one?"
note.watch: The page has three rows of four toys (yellow and red airplanes, dump trucks and green cars), bigger and smaller copies of one toy; the child circles the longest in each row. Ask the child to show "from one end to the other end" with two fingers.

K:compare-size-extremes#p-toys.routine: Line up real toy cars, trucks and trains of different lengths on a table. Children set two side by side with the back ends lined up to see which is longer. Build a long cube train and a short cube train and compare them. Then find the longest ribbon or jump rope laid on the floor and walk along it.
week: Toy cars side by side: line up the back ends and find the longest car.
Cube trains: build a long train and a short train and compare them.
Ribbons on the floor: find the longest one and walk along it.
Long and Short page: circle the longest toy in each row.
Lay block towers on their side and find which one is longest.
K:compare-size-extremes#p-toys.check: Finds the longest of four toys by lining up their ends

K:push-pull#p-toys.title: Toys: Push or Pull?
K:push-pull#p-toys.objective: Children tell a push from a pull by moving toys, and match pictures to push or pull.

note.mistake: Children say "push" for everything that moves forward and mix up where the person stands: walking in front with a rope is a pull. The toy train has the person behind it, which many still call a pull.
note.words: Ask, "Is the person in front pulling, or behind pushing?" Say, "Pull brings it toward you. Push moves it away from you." Ask, "Where is the rope?"
note.watch: The page shows four pictures with arrows: a person pulling a red sled by a rope, a person pushing a shopping cart, a person pushing a toy train, and a person pulling a toy dump truck by a rope. The child draws a line from each to push or pull.

K:push-pull#p-toys.routine: Bring toys that move: a wagon, a toy train with a string, a toy shopping cart, a ball, and a box with a rope tied to it. Children move each one and say "I push it" or "I pull it." Mark two areas with signs, push toys and pull toys. Try the wagon both ways: from behind it is a push, from the front with the handle it is a pull.
week: Moving toys: push the shopping cart, pull the wagon, and say which you did.
Rope or hands? Move a box with a rope, then without one.
Push or Pull? page: lines from the sled, the cart, the train and the truck to push or pull.
Push and pull walk: find doors, drawers and chairs that we push or pull.
Push a ball and pull a wagon outside; tell a friend which was harder.
K:push-pull#p-toys.check: Shows a push and a pull with a toy and says which is which

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-toys.title: Toys Pencil Paths in Color and Black and White
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-toys.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy pencil paths to toys.

note.mistake: Children trace with the wrist lifted off the table, so the lines wander; on the black-and-white page they start coloring the toys before the lines are done, and the waves turn into scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Drive your crayon like a car on the road. Stay on the dashes." Ask, "Which toy is at the end of the wavy road?" Say, "Lines first, coloring last."
note.watch: The color page ends its lines at a toy plane, a bike, a doll and a stack of blocks; the black-and-white page ends at a toy train, a guitar, a car and a plane to color. Look at the wrist on the table and dash-by-dash tracing.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-toys.routine: Drive toy cars along tape roads on the floor: a straight road, a zigzag road and a wavy road. Then roll play-dough snakes and bend them into the same shapes. Children draw a road for their toy car on a whiteboard with a marker and drive it.
week: Tape roads: drive toy cars along straight, zigzag and wavy roads.
Play-dough snakes: bend them into zigzags and waves.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the plane, the bike, the doll and the blocks.
Whiteboard roads: draw a road for your toy car and drive it.
Pencil Path Practice to color: trace to the train, the guitar, the car and the plane.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-toys.check: Traces four kinds of lines from the dot to the toy

K:word-picture-match#p-cooking-baking.title: Cooking and Baking Word Cards: Bakery and Kitchen
K:word-picture-match#p-cooking-baking.objective: Children name baked foods and kitchen things (pie, cookie, bagel, croissant, refrigerator, apron, blender, oven) and say what each is for.

note.mistake: Children call every baked thing "bread" or "cake," and the croissant and bagel are new words ("the curvy bread," "the donut"); on the kitchen cards the blender gets called a "mixer" and the refrigerator "the fridge," which is right too.
note.words: Say, "A bagel has a hole like a donut, but it is bread." Ask, "Where do we keep the milk cold? In the refrigerator." Say, "An apron keeps our clothes clean when we cook."
note.watch: The bakery cards show a pie, a cookie, a bagel and a croissant; the kitchen page has eight smaller cards: a bottle, a jar, a refrigerator, an apron, a teapot, a blender, a pot and an oven. Watch who uses the new words bagel, croissant and apron in play.

K:word-picture-match#p-cooking-baking.routine: Check for allergies first. Bake simple muffins together: children measure, pour and stir (no tasting raw batter), and the adult works the oven while children stand back. Read aloud a picture book about baking. Open a bakery and kitchen in dramatic play with play food, an apron, a teapot and unbreakable pots, where children sell "bagels" and "croissants."
week: Bake (check for allergies first): measure, pour and stir; no tasting raw batter; the adult runs the oven.
Bakery Word Cards: name the pie, cookie, bagel and croissant.
Pretend bakery: sell play bagels, croissants and cookies to friends.
Kitchen Word Cards: bottle, jar, refrigerator, apron, teapot, blender, pot and oven; find each one.
Bakery game: name a card and clap it: pot (1), ap-ron (2), re-frig-er-a-tor (5).
K:word-picture-match#p-cooking-baking.check: Names two baked foods and two kitchen things

K:ordinal-position#p-cooking-baking.title: Cooking and Baking: Which Treat Is Third?
K:ordinal-position#p-cooking-baking.objective: Children count places in a row of baked foods from the flag and find first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children point to the treat they would like to eat instead of counting, or count the flag; when a chip says "3rd," some look for three of something on the page.
note.words: Say, "The flag shows where we start. First, second, third." Ask, "Which treat is first? Which is last?" Read, "This chip says fifth with a circle. Count five from the flag and circle it."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five baked foods (pies, a bun, a cupcake, a muffin, cake slices, a pretzel, a bagel, toast) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row. Read each chip aloud; 3s may find first and last.

K:ordinal-position#p-cooking-baking.routine: Line up five play baked foods on a tray with a paper flag at one end: a bun, a cookie, a muffin, a slice of pie and a bagel. Children count places from the flag: first, second, third. Then five children each hold a play food and stand in a bakery line; a customer asks, "May I have the third one?" and the class counts to find it.
week: Bakery tray: count five play foods from the flag: first, second, third.
Bakery line: a customer asks for the second or the fourth treat; the class counts to find it.
Baking steps: what did we do first, next and last when we made muffins?
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up to wash hands and say your place in the bakery line.
K:ordinal-position#p-cooking-baking.check: Counts places from the front to find the third of five things

K:weather-temperature#p-cooking-baking.title: Cooking and Baking: Hot and Cold
K:weather-temperature#p-cooking-baking.objective: Children sort things into hot and cold and learn that some kitchen things are too hot to touch.

note.mistake: Children think an oven is safe to touch when they see no flame, and some put the snowman under hot because snowmen "melt." The rule is simple: never touch, ask a grown-up.
note.words: Ask, "Is an oven hot or cold when it is on?" Say, "Hot things can hurt us. We ask a grown-up." Ask, "Where does the ice go, hot or cold?"
note.watch: The page shows a snowman, an oven, a block of ice and a grill above a Hot box and a Cold box; the child draws a line from each dot to a box. Listen for "too hot to touch."

K:weather-temperature#p-cooking-baking.routine: Feel the difference safely: an ice cube in a bowl and a cup of warm (not hot) water. Walk the kitchen with the cook: the oven and stove get hot, only grown-ups use them, and we stand back. Watch ice melt on a plate near a sunny window. Then sort pictures of foods into a "fridge" box and an "oven" box.
week: Feel safely: an ice cube and a cup of warm water; which is cold, which is warm?
Kitchen safety walk: the oven and stove are hot; we stand back and grown-ups use them.
Hot and Cold page: lines from the snowman, the oven, the ice and the grill to the boxes.
Melt watch: ice on a plate in the sun and ice in the shade; which melts first?
Fridge or oven? Sort food pictures into a cold box and a hot box.
K:weather-temperature#p-cooking-baking.check: Sorts hot and cold things and says not to touch the hot ones

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-cooking-baking.title: Cooking and Baking: Swirls and Pencil Paths
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-cooking-baking.objective: Children trace spirals and loops like cinnamon rolls and steam, and follow pencil paths to bakery and kitchen pictures.

note.mistake: Children draw a spiral as circles inside circles, lifting the crayon each time, or go round the wrong way and run out of room; the steam loops are small, and many turn them into scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Start at the outside dot and curl in, round and round, like a cinnamon roll." Ask, "Did your crayon lift?" Say, "Little loops, like steam from a hot cup."
note.watch: The Bakery Swirls page has a big spiral, two steam loops over a teacup and a swirl on a cupcake; the bakery pencil paths end at a pie, a bun, a pretzel and a cake; the kitchen paths end at a mixer, an oven, a pot and a covered cake dome.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-cooking-baking.routine: Roll play-dough snakes and curl them into cinnamon-roll spirals, then twist them into pretzels. Children stir pretend batter (sand and water) in big circles with an unbreakable spatula and a whisk. Draw spirals in shaving cream on the table, starting at the outside and curling in to the middle, the way the page does.
week: Play-dough cinnamon rolls: roll a snake and curl it into a spiral.
Shaving-cream spirals: start at the outside and curl in to the middle, like the page.
Bakery Swirls page: trace the big spiral, the steam loops and the cupcake swirl.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the pie, the bun, the pretzel and the cake.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the mixer, the oven, the pot and the cake dome.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-cooking-baking.check: Traces a spiral round and round without lifting

K:word-sentence-tracing#p-space.title: Space Words: Galaxy, Planet, Rocket
K:word-sentence-tracing#p-space.objective: Children say three space words (galaxy, planet, rocket), hear their first sounds and trace them with a finger, then a crayon.

note.mistake: Children trace the dashed letters from right to left or start each letter at the bottom, and some write their own name instead of the word. For 3s and young 4s the words are a stretch: they say the word and trace its first letter.
note.words: Say, "This word says rocket. Rocket starts with /r/." Ask, "What is this picture? A planet, very far away in space." Say, "Start each letter at the top, and go from left to right."
note.watch: The page has three rows (a galaxy, a ringed planet and a rocket), each with the word to look at, the same word dashed to trace and empty lines to write it. Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s name the picture and trace the first letter.

K:word-sentence-tracing#p-space.routine: Darken the room and shine a flashlight on a small ball moon and a big ball earth. Make cardboard-tube telescopes and find planet and rocket pictures taped to the ceiling. Read aloud a picture book about space and stop at each rocket and planet. Write galaxy, planet and rocket big on chart paper; children trace each word with a finger while the class says it slowly.
week: Flashlight sky: in the dark room, shine a light on a ball moon and a big ball earth.
Space read-aloud, then trace galaxy, planet and rocket with a finger on the chart.
Tube telescopes: find the pictures on the ceiling and clap rock-et (2), plan-et (2), gal-ax-y (3).
Trace and Write the Words page: say each word, then trace it (writing it is a challenge for the 5s).
First sounds: rocket starts with /r/, planet with /p/; find a friend whose name starts the same.
K:word-sentence-tracing#p-space.check: Says galaxy, planet and rocket and names the first sound of rocket

K:before-after-back#p-space.title: Space: Count Back From 10 to Blast Off
K:before-after-back#p-space.objective: Children count back from 10 to 1 and connect the dots in that order to finish a rocket.

note.mistake: Children start the dot-to-dot at 1 out of habit, or count back "10, 9, 8, 7, 5" and skip a number; most 3s can count back only from 5, and that is fine.
note.words: Say, "We start at 10 and count down: 10, 9, 8." Ask, "What comes before 7?" Say, "When we get to 1, the rocket blasts off!"
note.watch: The page shows a rocket whose top and sides are made by dots numbered 10 down to 1, with 10 at the orange dot and a number strip from 10 to 1 at the bottom. Counting back is a challenge for the 5s: 3s join the dots as the teacher calls the numbers.

K:before-after-back#p-space.routine: Build a cardboard box rocket. Children crouch beside it, count back together from 10 to 1 and "blast off" with a jump. Lay ten number cards in a row on the floor and children step backward from 10 to 1. Build a tower of ten cubes and take one cube off for each number the class says.
week: Box rocket blast off: count back from 10 to 1 together, then jump.
Step back: walk backward on number cards from 10 down to 1.
Cube tower: start with ten and take one off for each number we say.
Dot-to-Dot Count Back: start at 10 and connect the dots down to 1 to finish the rocket.
Rocket races: count back from 5 or from 10 before each race on the playground.
K:before-after-back#p-space.check: Counts back from 10 (or from 5) without skipping a number

K:day-night#p-space.title: Space: The Day Sky and the Night Sky
K:day-night#p-space.objective: Children sort things into the day sky and the night sky (the sun, a star, a comet, a bird).

note.mistake: Children think the sun "turns off" at night and that stars are made each evening; many put the bird in the night box because birds sleep in trees, and the comet is new to almost everyone.
note.words: Ask, "When do we see the sun?" Say, "The stars are always there. We see them when it is dark." Ask, "When does a bird fly, in the day or at night?" Say, "A comet is a bright light with a long tail."
note.watch: The page shows a sun, a comet, a bird and a star above a Day box and a Night box; the child draws a line from each picture's dot to a box. Name the comet first, then listen for reasons that use light and dark.

K:day-night#p-space.routine: Go outside on a clear morning and look at the day sky for clouds, birds and sometimes the moon (never look straight at the sun). Inside, turn off the lights and cover the ceiling lights with paper stars; children lie on the rug and look at the "night sky." Each child makes a day half and a night half on paper with sun and star stickers.
week: Day sky walk: look for clouds, birds and the moon (never look at the sun).
Night sky inside: lights off, paper stars on the ceiling; lie down and look up.
Day and Night page: lines from the sun, the comet, the bird and the star to the boxes.
Day and night sort: pajamas, a pillow, sunglasses and a lunch box.
Make a day half and a night half on paper with sun and star stickers.
K:day-night#p-space.check: Sorts the sun, a star and a bird into day and night

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-space.title: Space Tracing: Rockets, Stars and Spirals
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-space.objective: Children trace a rocket, stars and planets, and spirals that go round and round.

note.mistake: Children trace the five-pointed stars as blobs and miss the points, and on the spiral they jump from ring to ring; on the big rocket some press so hard the crayon breaks.
note.words: Say, "Stars have points: up, down, up, down." Ask, "Can you go round and round without lifting?" Say, "Hold the crayon gently, like a little bird."
note.watch: The rocket page has a dashed rocket, a ringed planet, a flying saucer and four stars; the spiral page has one big spiral among stars and two loopy paths to a saucer and a star; the last page has one big rocket inside a circle with a moon and stars.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-space.routine: Press star and circle cookie cutters into play-dough and trace the shapes with a finger. Spin slowly on the rug like planets, then draw spirals in the air and on a whiteboard. Paint a tall rocket at the easel with long up-and-down strokes.
week: Play-dough stars and planets with cookie cutters; trace the edges with a finger.
Planet spins on the rug, then spirals in the air and on a whiteboard.
Rocket to the Stars page: trace the rocket, the planet, the stars and the flying saucer.
Space Spirals page: trace the big spiral round and round, then the loops.
My First Tracing: trace the big rocket in its circle, slowly, all the way round.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-space.check: Traces a star's points and a spiral without lifting the crayon

K:word-picture-match#p-winter.title: Winter Word Cards: Snow, Ice and Cold-Weather Animals
K:word-picture-match#p-winter.objective: Children name winter things and animals of the cold (cabin, sweater, igloo, snowman, walrus, penguin, seal) and use the words in a sentence.

note.mistake: Children call the walrus and the seal both "seal," the igloo a "snow house" (accept it, then name it) and the fireplace an "oven"; skating and skiing get mixed up.
note.words: Say, "A walrus has long tusks. A seal does not." Ask, "Do you skate on ice or ski on snow?" Say, "An igloo is a house made of blocks of snow."
note.watch: The first page has eight cards (a cabin, a fireplace, a sweater, a skater, an igloo, a skier, a seal and a snowman); the second has four big cards (a walrus, earmuffs, boots and a penguin). Listen for "walrus" and "seal" told apart.

K:word-picture-match#p-winter.routine: Bring winter inside: a bin of real snow or crushed ice with mittens to wear, toy penguins, seals and a walrus, and a cabin made from a box. Children build a tiny snowman in the bin and tell a friend about it. Read aloud a picture book about a snowy day. Show photos of skaters and skiers, of penguins near the South Pole and of walruses near the North Pole.
week: Snow bin: play in real snow or crushed ice wearing mittens; name what we feel.
Winter Word Cards: cabin, fireplace, sweater, skating, igloo, skiing, seal and snowman.
Paper-plate skating on the rug; pretend skiing with arms and knees.
Build a small snowman in the snow bin and tell each step to a friend.
Card hunt: find the hidden winter cards and clap each name: seal (1), ig-loo (2), snow-man (2).
Cold-animal trays: penguins on one, a walrus and seals on the other; they live far apart.
Winter Word Cards: walrus, earmuffs, boots and penguin.
Waddle like a penguin and flop like a seal, naming the animal as you move.
Sort the winter cards: animals in one pile, things we wear or use in another.
Winter word show: each child holds a card and says a sentence about it.
K:word-picture-match#p-winter.check: Names four winter things and two animals that live in the cold

K:numeral-formation#p-winter.title: Winter: Count and Trace 1 to 5
K:numeral-formation#p-winter.objective: Children count winter pictures to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.

note.mistake: Children count the small pictures too fast and touch one twice, most often the four snowflakes in a row; others trace the number before counting and just copy its shape.
note.words: Say, "Count first, then trace." Ask, "How many snowflakes? Touch each one." Say, "Four: down, across, and one long line down."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one snowboarder, two pink coats, three walruses, four snowflakes and five fireplaces), each with a number to look at and two to trace. The pictures are small; let the child touch each one with a finger before tracing.

K:numeral-formation#p-winter.routine: Count real winter things: one mitten, two scarves, three hats, four paper snowflakes and five cotton-ball snowballs. Children set each group on a mat with its number card. Play snowball toss: toss cotton balls into a bucket and count how many went in, up to five. Roll play-dough snowmen and count the balls in each.
week: Winter count: one mitten, two scarves, three hats, four snowflakes, five snowballs.
Match a number card to each winter group; touch and count to check.
Snowball toss: toss cotton balls into a bucket and count how many went in.
Play-dough snowmen: roll the balls and count them; make one with three.
Count and Trace page: count each row of winter pictures and trace the number.
Mitten match: count the pairs of mittens hanging on the line.
Snowflakes on the window: the teacher folds and cuts; children count up to five.
Number hunt: find the numbers 1 to 5 on paper snowflakes hidden in the room.
Count the penguins: line up toy penguins and count to five.
Count and Trace again with a friend, touching each picture before tracing.
K:numeral-formation#p-winter.check: Counts up to 5 winter pictures and traces the matching number

K:hot-cold-places#p-winter.title: Winter: Hot Places and Cold Places
K:hot-cold-places#p-winter.objective: Children match things people use to a snowy place or a sunny beach, and talk about how the cold changes what we wear and do.

note.mistake: Children say we wear coats "because it's winter," not because it is cold, and think the beach is never chilly; some send the wool hat to the beach because "a hat is for the sun."
note.words: Ask, "Would you wear this in the snow or at the beach?" Say, "We wear a coat to keep warm when it is cold." Ask, "Is this a sun hat or a warm hat?"
note.watch: Both pages show a snowy mountain place with a cabin and a sunny beach place; the first has a beach ball, a sled, a swimsuit and flip-flops to match, the second a pink coat, green mittens, a beach ball and a wool hat. Listen to the reasons children give.

K:hot-cold-places#p-winter.routine: Set up two corners: a cold place with blankets, mittens, hats and a sled, and a hot place with a beach towel, sunglasses and a sun hat. Children dress for one place and act out a day there. Put a cup of water outside or in the freezer overnight and look at the ice together the next morning.
week: Freeze it: put a cup of water outside or in the freezer overnight.
Check the ice; feel cold with mittens on and with mittens off.
Cold corner and hot corner: dress for each and act out a day there.
Hot Places, Cold Places page: lines from the ball, the sled, the swimsuit and the flip-flops.
Penguins and seals: why are they comfortable in the cold?
Ice blocks: freeze toy animals in ice and melt them with warm water.
Animal coats: feel wool, a feather and fleece; which keeps an animal warm?
Hot Places, Cold Places page: lines from the coat, the mittens, the beach ball and the hat.
Pack a bag: choose what to bring to the snowy place and to the beach.
Share: one thing you would do in the cold and one thing in the heat.
K:hot-cold-places#p-winter.check: Matches clothes and toys to a cold place or a hot place and says why

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-winter.title: Winter Tracing: Snowman Shapes and Penguins on Ice
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-winter.objective: Children trace a snowman made of shapes and a scene of penguins and a seal on the ice.

note.mistake: Children trace the snowman's circles as one long oval and forget the square hat and the triangle; on the penguin page they trace only the penguins and leave out the igloo and the wavy line of the water.
note.words: Say, "Three circles, one on top of another, then a square hat." Ask, "Did you trace the igloo too?" Say, "Follow the wavy line where the water meets the ice."
note.watch: The snowman page has a dashed square hat, three circles for the body, and one more circle and a triangle beside it; the penguin page shows an igloo, a seal, two penguins, a sun and a wavy line of water under the ice. Look for whole shapes that close.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-winter.routine: Build a snowman outside, or with play-dough, from three balls of different sizes, then trace circles in the snow with a stick or in a tray of salt with a finger. Draw icy lines in shaving cream ("fake snow") and waddle along a tape line like penguins, feet close together.
week: Snowman building: three balls from big to small, outside or with play-dough.
Snow drawing: circles with a stick in the snow, or with a finger in a salt tray.
The Shape Snowman page: trace the circles, the square and the triangle; color the circles.
Penguin waddle along a tape line, feet close together and arms at our sides.
Shaving-cream snow: draw circles and wavy lines with a finger.
Penguins on the Ice page: trace the igloo, the seal, the two penguins and the ice.
Cotton-ball snow: glue cotton balls onto the traced snowman.
Ice cracks: draw zigzag cracks and wavy water with chalk on dark paper.
Color the penguin page and tell a friend what the penguins are doing.
Make a winter picture with circles, triangles and wavy lines.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-winter.check: Traces circles that close and a whole winter picture along the dashes

K:word-picture-match#p-clothes.title: Clothing Word Cards: What We Wear
K:word-picture-match#p-clothes.objective: Children name pieces of clothing (coat, pants, leggings, slippers, boots, dress, shorts, mittens) and say when they wear them.

note.mistake: Children call every kind of pants "pants" (leggings and the jumpsuit too) and every top a "shirt"; the necktie and the belt are grown-up clothes many 4-year-olds have no word for, and mittens and gloves get mixed up.
note.words: Say, "Leggings are soft, stretchy pants." Ask, "Is a jumpsuit pants or a shirt? It is both in one piece!" Say, "Mittens keep all our fingers together. Gloves have a place for each finger."
note.watch: The color page has eight cards (slippers, a belt, a green jumpsuit, a red coat, yellow pants, leggings, a hat and a tie); the black-and-white page has eight to color (a necktie, a sock, boots, a dress, shorts, mittens, a hat and a jacket). Listen for a word for each piece and when the child wears it.

K:word-picture-match#p-clothes.routine: Fill a dress-up basket with real clothes in big sizes: a coat, pants, leggings, slippers, a hat, a dress, shorts and mittens. Children put each one on over their own clothes and say what it is and when they wear it. Read aloud a picture book about getting dressed for the weather. Hang a clothesline and clip a real piece of clothing beside each card.
week: Dress-up basket: put on a coat, a hat and mittens over our clothes and name them.
Clothing Word Cards: slippers, belt, jumpsuit, coat, pants, leggings, hat and tie.
Clothesline: clip real clothes on a line and say a word for each one.
Clothing Word Cards to color: necktie, sock, boots, dress, shorts, mittens, hat and jacket.
Get-dressed game: clap each piece as you put it on: hat (1), mit-tens (2), leg-gings (2).
K:word-picture-match#p-clothes.check: Names six pieces of clothing and says when to wear one of them

K:compare-groups#p-clothes.title: Clothing: Match Them Up, More or the Same
K:compare-groups#p-clothes.objective: Children match clothes one to one between two rows and say which row has more, or that they are the same.

note.mistake: Children draw two lines to one partner or say the longer-looking row has more; on the row of ten jackets and ten coats many lose track halfway and circle a row instead of coloring the star. Watches are not clothes to some children: name the pictures first.
note.words: Say, "One line to one partner, like socks in pairs." Ask, "Is anyone left without a partner? That row has more." Say, "If everyone has a partner, color the star."
note.watch: The page has five pairs of rows of small black-and-white clothes: five T-shirts and seven boots, five watches and two hats, ten jackets and ten coats (the same), three pairs of mittens and five shorts, five dresses and four caps. The rows run up to ten, so 3s do rows 2, 4 and 5.

K:compare-groups#p-clothes.routine: Tip a laundry basket of socks onto the rug and match them into pairs; any sock left over has no partner. Hang hats and mittens in two rows on a clothesline and pair each hat with a mitten to find the extras. Then share caps and scarves between two friends: "One for you, one for me."
week: Sock pairs: match the socks from a laundry basket; which sock has no partner?
Clothesline rows: pair each hat with a mitten and find the extras.
One for you, one for me: share caps and scarves between two friends.
Match Them Up page: draw a line from each picture to a partner; circle the row with more.
Two rows of clothes on the line: color the star when every one has a partner.
K:compare-groups#p-clothes.check: Matches two rows one to one and says which has more or that they are the same

K:seasons#p-clothes.title: Clothing for Summer and Winter
K:seasons#p-clothes.objective: Children sort clothes into summer clothes and winter clothes and say how clothes keep us warm or cool.

note.mistake: Children put the cap under winter because it is a hat, and many think boots are only for snow (rain boots too); some say we wear a coat because it is "big," not because it keeps us warm.
note.words: Ask, "Do you wear a swimsuit when it is hot or cold?" Say, "A coat keeps our body warm." Ask, "Could this cap go to the beach? Why?"
note.watch: The page shows a red coat, a blue cap, brown boots and a swimsuit above a Summer box and a Winter box; the child draws a line from each dot. Accept the cap in either box when the child gives a reason.

K:seasons#p-clothes.routine: Put a coat, boots, a cap and a swimsuit in a basket. Children try on the coat and boots and say how they feel (warm, heavy, puffy). Before going outside each day, look at the weather together and decide what we need to wear. Make a summer and winter clothing mural with pictures cut from catalogs.
week: Weather check at the door: what do we need to wear outside today?
Try on a coat and boots, then a sun hat: how does each one feel?
Summer and Winter Clothes page: lines from the coat, the cap, the boots and the swimsuit.
Clothing mural: summer clothes on the sun side, winter clothes on the snow side.
Pack a suitcase for a snowy trip and another for a beach trip.
K:seasons#p-clothes.check: Sorts four pieces of clothing into summer and winter and says why

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-clothes.title: Clothing Pencil Paths: Lines to Hats and Socks
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-clothes.objective: Children trace pencil paths, zigzags and a square wave to pieces of clothing, and practice the small moves of getting dressed.

note.mistake: On the square wave children slant the up and down strokes into a zigzag, and on the zigzags they lift the crayon at each point. Buttons and zippers are hard for 3s: the practice matters more than finishing.
note.words: Say, "Square wave: up, across, down, across, like the top of a castle." Ask, "Where does this line take you? To the hat." Say, "Pinch the clothespin like a crocodile's mouth."
note.watch: The color page ends its lines at a scarf, a cap, red pajamas and a green T-shirt; the black-and-white page has straight lines and zigzags to a tie, a sock and glasses, and a square-wave line to a hat. Look for straight up-and-down strokes on the square wave.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-clothes.routine: Practice the hand work of getting dressed on a dressing board: pull a zipper, push a big button through its hole, press a snap and lace a shoe card. Clip clothespins onto a line of socks and mittens. Lay long scarves on the floor in wavy and zigzag shapes and walk beside them.
week: Dressing board: zip, button, snap and lace with our fingers.
Clothespin line: clip socks and mittens onto a string with clothespins.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the scarf, the cap, the pajamas and the T-shirt.
Scarf paths: lay scarves in wavy and zigzag shapes and walk beside them.
Straight Lines and Zigzags: trace to the tie, the sock and the glasses, then the square wave.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-clothes.check: Traces zigzags and a square wave with corners, and zips or buttons with help

K:word-picture-match#p-healthy-food.title: Healthy Eating: Breakfast Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-healthy-food.objective: Children name breakfast foods (pancake, grapefruit, raspberry, porridge) and tell what they eat in the morning.

note.mistake: Children call porridge "soup" or "cereal" and the grapefruit an "orange"; some say breakfast must be cereal, so a friend's rice or tortilla breakfast sounds "wrong" to them.
note.words: Say, "Porridge is warm oatmeal. Some families call it hot cereal." Ask, "Is a grapefruit sweet or sour?" Say, "Families eat many different breakfasts, and they are all breakfast."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a pancake, half a grapefruit, a raspberry and a bowl of porridge. Listen for the names and for a describing word (sweet, sour, warm, soft).

K:word-picture-match#p-healthy-food.routine: Check for allergies first. Have a class breakfast tasting: a small piece of pancake, raspberries cut in half and warm oatmeal (porridge). Children name each food and say whether it is sweet, sour or soft. Read aloud a picture book about breakfast. Graph what everyone ate for breakfast and open a breakfast cafe in dramatic play with play food.
week: Breakfast talk: what did you eat this morning? Draw it on a paper plate.
Breakfast Word Cards: pancake, grapefruit, raspberry and porridge.
Tasting (check for allergies first): pancake, raspberries and porridge; sweet, sour or soft?
Breakfast cafe: order with the card words and clap them: pan-cake (2), rasp-ber-ry (3).
Breakfast graph: put your picture in the row of the breakfast you like best.
K:word-picture-match#p-healthy-food.check: Names four breakfast foods and describes one by its taste

K:numeral-formation#p-healthy-food.title: Healthy Eating: Count and Trace Breakfast Foods
K:numeral-formation#p-healthy-food.objective: Children count breakfast foods up to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.

note.mistake: Children guess the jam jars and muffins because they sit close together, saying "five" for any long row; others trace the 1 as a dot or a circle.
note.words: Say, "Touch each muffin and count with me." Ask, "How many blueberries? Two." Say, "One is a straight line down from the top."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one strip of bacon, two blueberries, three croissants, four jam jars and five muffins), each with a number to look at and two to trace. Watch touch counting, and that the last number said is the one traced.

K:numeral-formation#p-healthy-food.routine: Set a play breakfast table: one strip of play bacon, two blueberries, three croissants, four jam jars and five muffins. Children count each group onto a plate and put the number card next to it. At snack, after you check for allergies first, each child counts out up to five apple slices before eating.
week: Play breakfast table: count one, two, three, four and five foods onto plates.
Number card match: put the right card by each plate and count to check.
Snack count (check for allergies first): count out up to five apple slices.
Count and Trace page: count each row of breakfast foods and trace the number.
Muffin tin count: put up to five large pom-poms in the cups (an adult at the table).
K:numeral-formation#p-healthy-food.check: Counts up to 5 foods and traces the matching number

K:healthy-food#p-healthy-food.title: Healthy Eating: Everyday and Sometimes Foods
K:healthy-food#p-healthy-food.objective: Children sort foods into everyday foods that help us grow and sometimes foods.

note.mistake: Children say sweet foods are "bad" and that one cookie makes you sick, or call fruit "not healthy" because it is sweet. Keep the words everyday and sometimes, not good and bad.
note.words: Say, "Broccoli is an everyday food. It helps us grow." Ask, "When do we eat cupcakes? On special days. It is a sometimes food." Say, "No food is bad. Some we eat every day, some sometimes."
note.watch: The page shows a cookie, a tomato, a cupcake and broccoli above a Healthy box and a Not Healthy box; read the boxes as everyday food and sometimes food. Watch that no child shames a food a friend likes.

K:healthy-food#p-healthy-food.routine: Check for allergies first. Show real foods: broccoli, a tomato and an apple, with a cookie and a cupcake (or pictures of them). Talk about everyday foods that help our bodies grow strong and sometimes foods we eat at a party. Children taste soft-steamed broccoli and small tomato pieces (never whole cherry tomatoes), then build a "growing plate" with play food.
week: Food basket: broccoli, a tomato, an apple and a cookie; which help us grow every day?
Tasting (check for allergies first): soft-steamed broccoli and small tomato pieces; soft or juicy?
Healthy Foods page: lines from the cookie, the tomato, the cupcake and the broccoli to the boxes.
Growing plate: make a play-food lunch that is mostly everyday foods.
Grocery play: fill a basket with everyday foods and one sometimes food.
K:healthy-food#p-healthy-food.check: Sorts two everyday foods and two sometimes foods

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-healthy-food.title: Healthy Eating Pencil Paths to Breakfast
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-healthy-food.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy lines to breakfast foods.

note.mistake: Children trace fast and skip the middle of each line, jumping from the dot to the food, or hold the crayon in a fist like a spoon.
note.words: Say, "Hold your crayon with three fingers, not like a spoon." Ask, "Which food is at the end of the zigzag?" Say, "Go slowly, all the way to the juice."
note.watch: The page has four lines (straight, a zigzag, bumps and waves) ending at a bottle of milk, half an avocado, a bowl of cereal and a glass of juice. Look at the grip: three fingers, not a fist.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-healthy-food.routine: Pour and scoop at the sensory table: children pour sand from cup to cup with a funnel, scoop it with spoons and move play pancakes and fruit with tongs. Spread pretend butter (play-dough) on cardboard toast with a craft stick. Then draw lines with a finger in a tray of sand.
week: Pour and scoop: sand from cup to cup with a funnel and spoons.
Tongs practice: move play pancakes and fruit from plate to plate.
Finger lines in a tray of sand: straight, zigzag and wavy.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the milk, the avocado, the cereal and the juice.
Spread pretend butter on cardboard toast with a craft stick.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-healthy-food.check: Holds the crayon with three fingers and traces a line to its end

K:word-picture-match#p-post-office.title: Post Office Word Cards: Stamp, Package, Scale
K:word-picture-match#p-post-office.objective: Children name post office things (stamp, package, scale, delivery) and tell how a letter gets to a friend.

note.mistake: Children think the mail carrier writes the letters and call every box a "present"; the scale is a new picture, and many call it a clock or a phone.
note.words: Say, "A stamp pays for the letter's trip." Ask, "What do we put on the scale? A package, to see how heavy it is." Say, "The mail carrier brings the letters to our homes."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a scale with a screen, a stamp with a lighthouse, a mail carrier holding a package (delivery) and a cardboard package. Watch who can tell the order: write, stamp, mail, deliver.

K:word-picture-match#p-post-office.routine: Open a post office in dramatic play with envelopes, stickers for stamps, a kitchen scale, small boxes to wrap and a mail bag, and build a class mailbox from a shoebox. Children draw a letter, put a stamp on it and mail it. Read aloud a picture book about a letter's trip. Walk to the nearest mailbox together to mail a real letter to each family.
week: Post office opens: build the class mailbox; envelopes, sticker stamps, a scale and a mail bag.
Post Office Word Cards: scale, stamp, delivery and package.
Write a letter (draw or scribble) to someone at home and put a stamp on it.
Mailbox walk: mail our letters at the nearest mailbox.
Package play: wrap, weigh and deliver; clap stamp (1), pack-age (2), de-liv-er-y (4).
K:word-picture-match#p-post-office.check: Names a stamp, a package and the mail carrier and tells how a letter travels

K:ordinal-position#p-post-office.title: Post Office: Which Letter Is First?
K:ordinal-position#p-post-office.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of post office pictures and find first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children deliver to the house they like best instead of the one in the place named; on the page some count only the envelopes and skip the mailbox and truck pictures between them.
note.words: Say, "Count every picture from the flag, not only the letters." Ask, "Which house is third?" Read, "This chip says second with an X. Count two from the flag and make an X."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five post office pictures (envelopes, a mailbox, a mail truck, stamps, a package, a scale and a mail carrier) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each with a circle or an X.

K:ordinal-position#p-post-office.routine: Line up five envelopes on a shelf, each with a different sticker, and a paper flag at one end. A "mail carrier" picks up the letters in order, counting first, second, third. Then set up five toy houses in a row and children deliver a letter to "the third house" or "the last house."
week: Letter line: five envelopes in a row; pick them up in order from the flag.
Toy houses in a row: deliver a letter to the third house, then the fifth.
Mailbox line: children line up with their letters and say their places.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Who gets mail first, next and last at our pretend post office?
K:ordinal-position#p-post-office.check: Counts places from the front to find the third and the last

K:goods-and-services#p-post-office.title: Post Office: Who Brings the Mail?
K:goods-and-services#p-post-office.objective: Children match workers to the job they do for people: the mail carrier brings the mail and the barber cuts hair.

note.mistake: Children think the mail carrier owns the mailbox or makes the letters, and match the barber to the mailbox because he stands beside the barber pole; some call a haircut "a thing" the barber makes.
note.words: Say, "A mail carrier brings letters to our homes. That is a job that helps people." Ask, "What does a barber do?" Say, "Some workers make things, and some do things for us."
note.watch: The page shows a mail carrier with a bag and a barber with scissors beside a barber pole on the left, and a child in a barber chair and a blue mailbox on the right; the child draws a line from each worker to the job that worker does.

K:goods-and-services#p-post-office.routine: Watch for the mail carrier at school or invite one to visit, and ask what they carry and where it goes. Act out jobs: one child is the mail carrier with a bag, another is a barber with a toy comb and a mirror (no real scissors near hair). Children say what each worker does for people.
week: Mail carrier watch: see the mail arrive at school or meet a mail carrier.
Job charades: act out a mail carrier, a barber and a baker; friends guess.
