Who Makes It? Who Does It? page: lines from the mail carrier and the barber to their jobs.
Barbershop play with toy combs and mirrors (no real scissors).
Thank-you picture for our mail carrier, drawn together.
K:goods-and-services#p-post-office.check: Says what a mail carrier and a barber do for people

K:mazes#p-post-office.title: Post Office Maze: Help the Mail Carrier
K:mazes#p-post-office.objective: Children follow a winding road with a crayon to help the mail carrier reach the mailbox.

note.mistake: Children choose the road that points straight at the mailbox and hit dead ends near the top; others draw through the grass between roads because the roads sit close together.
note.words: Say, "The mail carrier stays on the road." Ask, "This road stops. What can you do?" Say, "Go back to where the roads split and try the other way."
note.watch: The maze shows a winding tan road with many branches through the grass, the mail carrier at the left start, a blue mailbox with a flag at the top right, and a frog, a duck, an umbrella and a rain boot beside the road.

K:mazes#p-post-office.routine: Set up a mail route in the room: tape roads between chairs, each chair with a child's name. Mail carriers walk the route with a bag and drop a letter at each chair. Then children post letters through slots of different sizes cut in a box (the teacher cuts the slots).
week: Mail route: walk the tape roads between chairs and drop a letter at each one.
Mail slots: push letters through slots of different sizes in a box.
Big paper map: drive a toy mail truck from the post office to a house.
Picture Maze: draw a line along the road from the mail carrier to the mailbox.
Draw a road from your house to a friend's house and deliver a letter on it.
K:mazes#p-post-office.check: Finds the road to the goal and goes back at a dead end

K:word-picture-match#p-friendship-valent.title: Friendship and Valentine's Day Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-friendship-valent.objective: Children name Valentine pictures (a heart key, candy, heart balloons, a cupcake) and say one kind thing to a friend.

note.mistake: Children think Valentine's cards are only for best friends and leave others out; the heart key and the heart balloons are new pictures, and many call the wrapped candy "a bow."
note.words: Say, "We make a card for every friend, so everyone feels loved." Ask, "What is this? It is a key with a heart." Model, "You are a good friend because you share."
note.watch: The page shows four big black-and-white cards to color: a key with a heart, a wrapped candy with hearts, heart balloons and a cupcake with a heart. Listen for a kind sentence when the child gives a card.

K:word-picture-match#p-friendship-valent.routine: Use the class mailbox from Post Office week. Each child makes one card for every child in the class (with a name list and stickers), so no one is left out. Read aloud a picture book about friendship. At circle, pass a paper heart and say one kind thing to the friend next to you. Look at the card pictures together and decorate the mailbox with them.
week: Kind words circle: pass a paper heart and say one kind thing to a friend.
Valentine Word Cards: name the key, the candy, the balloons and the cupcake, then color.
Card making: one card for every friend, with stickers and drawings.
Mailbox: deliver a card to every friend's cubby, clapping the friend's name as we say it.
Friendship talk: what does a good friend do? Each child gives one idea.
K:word-picture-match#p-friendship-valent.check: Says one kind thing to a friend and names the Valentine cards

K:ordinal-position#p-friendship-valentin.title: Friendship and Valentine's: Places in Line
K:ordinal-position#p-friendship-valentin.objective: Children find first, next and last and count places from the flag in rows of Valentine pictures.

note.mistake: Children count the flag as first, or count the small hearts inside one picture instead of the pictures; with two chips under a row, many mark only one of them.
note.words: Say, "Start next to the flag. That picture is first." Ask, "Which is fourth? Count with me." If asked about the rings, say, "Grown-ups who love each other sometimes wear rings."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five black-and-white Valentine pictures (an envelope, a heart with wings, a pair of rings, a cake, heart balloons, a key, a lock) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row. Read both chips aloud for every row.

K:ordinal-position#p-friendship-valentin.routine: Five children line up at the class mailbox to deliver cards, with a paper flag at the front. Ask, "Who is first? Who is next? Who is last?" and count places together. Then line up five Valentine things on a table (a card, a paper heart, a cupcake picture, a candy box, a flower) and play "What is in third place?"
week: Mailbox line: five children line up to deliver; who is first, next and last?
Count places from the flag: first, second, third, fourth, fifth.
Valentine line: five things in a row; find the second and the fourth.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up for a friendship walk and say your place.
K:ordinal-position#p-friendship-valentin.check: Finds first, next and last in a line and names the third

K:take-turns-share#p-friendship-valentin.title: Friendship: Taking Turns and Sharing
K:take-turns-share#p-friendship-valentin.objective: Children tell kind acts (sharing, taking turns, helping) from unkind ones and practice them.

note.mistake: Children cross out the slide because only one child is playing, but waiting for a turn is kind; some think sharing means giving a toy away forever, so they refuse. Others circle the torn drawing because the boy holding it smiles.
note.words: Ask, "Is this friend being kind? How can you tell?" Say, "Sharing means you use it now and get it back later." Ask, "How does the friend feel about the torn picture? What could he do to help?"
note.watch: The page shows four pictures: a child holding a friend's torn drawing while the friend cries, a child waiting by the slide while a friend slides, two children passing blocks across a table, and a child helping up a friend who fell. Three are kind; the torn drawing is not. Ask why each time.

K:take-turns-share#p-friendship-valentin.routine: Play turn-taking games with a sand timer and one special toy: each child holds it until the sand runs out, then passes it on. Act out a puppet show: one puppet grabs the crayons, and the children show the puppet how to ask and share. All week, catch kind acts and add them to a friendship chart.
week: Puppet show: one puppet grabs the crayons; children teach it to ask and share.
Sand-timer turns with one special toy; pass it on when the sand runs out.
Taking Turns and Sharing page: circle the friends who are kind; cross out the others.
Helping hands: practice helping a friend who falls or drops their things.
Friendship chart: name the kind acts we saw this week.
K:take-turns-share#p-friendship-valentin.check: Takes turns with a toy and names one kind act

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-friendship-valen.title: Valentine Pencil Paths: Hearts, Slants and Crosses
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-friendship-valen.objective: Children trace pencil paths and draw down lines, slants and crosses toward Valentine pictures.

note.mistake: On the slants children start at the bottom instead of the top dot, and crosses come out with one line much longer than the other; when lacing, they wrap the yarn around the edge instead of going through the holes.
note.words: Say, "Slants slide down, like a slide at the park." Ask, "Where is the top dot? Start there." Say, "Make the cross lines meet in the middle, like a hug."
note.watch: The pencil path page ends its four lines at a pair of rings, a candy, a lock and a heart with wings; the second page has rows of down lines, crosses, slants both ways and X crosses ending at a bag, glasses, a cake, a calendar and a flower.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-friendship-valen.routine: Make hearts with two hands and draw big hearts in the air. Lace yarn through holes punched around a cardboard heart. At the art table, children squeeze glue in down lines and crosses on paper and sprinkle paper hearts on top (an adult helps with the glue bottle).
week: Air hearts: draw big hearts in the air with a finger, then on a whiteboard.
Lacing hearts: lace yarn through the holes punched in a cardboard heart.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the rings, the candy, the lock and the winged heart.
Glue lines: squeeze glue in down lines and crosses, then sprinkle paper hearts.
Down Lines, Slants and Crosses: trace each row to the bag, glasses, cake, calendar and flower.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-friendship-valen.check: Draws a slant and a cross, starting each line at the top

K:word-picture-match#p-doctors-healthy-h.title: Doctors and Healthy Habits Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-doctors-healthy-h.objective: Children name doctor's office things (doctor, tissue, wheelchair, crutches) and tell how each one helps.

note.mistake: Children say the doctor "gives shots" and is scary, or think a wheelchair or crutches mean someone is sick forever; the tissue box has a red cross on it, so many call it a first-aid kit.
note.words: Say, "A doctor helps us stay healthy and get better." Ask, "What do crutches do? They help someone walk while a leg heals." Say, "A wheelchair helps people move. Many people use one every day."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a doctor with a stethoscope, a tissue box, a wheelchair and a pair of crutches. Listen for what each one helps with, and for kind words about people who use wheelchairs.

K:word-picture-match#p-doctors-healthy-h.routine: Set up a doctor's office with a toy stethoscope, bandages, a tissue box and a scale. Children take turns as doctor and patient, listen for heartbeats and wrap a "hurt" arm. Read aloud a picture book about a visit to the doctor or the dentist. Invite the school nurse to show a real stethoscope, and talk about how crutches and wheelchairs help people move.
week: Doctor's office opens: a toy stethoscope, bandages, tissues and a scale.
Doctor Word Cards: doctor, tissue, wheelchair and crutches; how does each one help?
School nurse visit: listen to a real heartbeat with the nurse's stethoscope.
Play doctor and patient with the card words; doctor and dentist start the same: /d/, /d/!
Tissue habit: catch a pretend sneeze in a tissue and throw it away.
K:word-picture-match#p-doctors-healthy-h.check: Names four doctor's office things and says how one helps

K:ordinal-position#p-doctors-healthy-hab.title: Doctors' Tools in a Row: First and Last
K:ordinal-position#p-doctors-healthy-hab.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of doctor's office pictures and mark the place each chip names.

note.mistake: Children mark the picture they know (the ambulance) instead of the one in the place on the chip, or count from the end of the row nearest their drawing hand.
note.words: Say, "First is right next to the flag." Ask, "Which picture is fourth?" Read, "This chip says fifth with an X. Find the fifth picture and cross it out."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five hospital pictures (a hospital bed, a stretcher, a chest X-ray, tissues, a nurse, a mask, a thermometer, an ambulance, gloves, crutches) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

K:ordinal-position#p-doctors-healthy-hab.routine: Line up five toy doctor things on a tray with a paper flag: a stethoscope, a box of bandages, a tissue box, a toy thermometer and a face mask. Children count places from the flag. Then patients wait in line at the pretend doctor's office and the nurse calls, "First patient, please," then the next, until the last.
week: Doctor's tray: five toy doctor things in a row; count places from the flag.
Waiting room line: the nurse calls the first patient, then the next one.
Who is last? Change the line and say the new last patient.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up for hand washing and say your place in line.
K:ordinal-position#p-doctors-healthy-hab.check: Finds first and last and counts to a place in a row of five

K:hygiene-habits#p-doctors-healthy-habit.title: Healthy Habits: Brushing, Washing and Sleeping
K:hygiene-habits#p-doctors-healthy-habit.objective: Children match healthy habits to the things we use (toothbrush, soap, bed, comb) and put the hand-washing steps in order.

note.mistake: Children rinse before using soap or skip drying, and think hands are clean if they look clean; on the steps page they number the pictures left to right instead of by what happens first.
note.words: Say, "Soap first, then scrub, scrub, scrub." Ask, "What do we do after we rinse? We dry." Ask, "What does this child need to get ready for bed?"
note.watch: The habits page shows four children (one under the moon at bedtime, one brushing at the mouth, one with messy hair, one at the sink) above a toothbrush, soap, a bed and a comb. The steps page has five sink pictures to number: wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry; wet and rinse look alike, and rinse has bubbles on the hands. Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s point.

K:hygiene-habits#p-doctors-healthy-habit.routine: Practice the habits for real. Put a little glitter on hands as pretend germs and watch soap and water wash it away. Wash hands at the sink with soap while singing the ABC song (about 20 seconds). Brush a toy's teeth up and down with a big toothbrush and comb a doll's hair. Each child takes home a toothbrushing chart.
week: Glitter germs: put glitter on hands and wash it off with soap and water.
Hand washing for real: wet, soap, scrub while singing the ABC song, rinse, dry.
Healthy Habits page: lines from each child to the toothbrush, the soap, the bed or the comb.
Big toothbrush: brush a toy's teeth up and down; talk about visiting the dentist.
Hand Washing Steps page: write or point to 1 to 5 to put the steps in order.
K:hygiene-habits#p-doctors-healthy-habit.check: Washes hands with soap in the right order and names three healthy habits

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-doctors-healthy-.title: Doctors and Healthy Habits: Pencil Paths and Bath Time
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-doctors-healthy-.objective: Children trace straight, wavy and bumpy lines to doctor's office pictures and trace a bath time picture.

note.mistake: Children trace the small bumps as one long flat line, and the wavy line flattens out halfway across; on Bath Time the bubbles are small circles that children close too early or draw on top of each other.
note.words: Say, "Little bumps, one after another, like ripples in the tub." Ask, "Did your bubble close? Come back to where you started." Say, "Trace slowly around the duck's head."
note.watch: The first page ends its four lines at blue scrubs, a thermometer, a face mask and a bandaged arm; the wavy page has curves and small bumps ending at scrubs, a stretcher, a doctor and a wheelchair; Bath Time has a tub, a rubber duck and round bubbles.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-doctors-healthy-.routine: Wrap a doll's arm with a strip of soft cloth, going round and round like a bandage. Blow soap bubbles outside and draw bubble circles in the air with a finger. At the water table, squeeze a bottle and watch the water make wavy lines.
week: Bandage wrap: wind a soft cloth strip round and round a doll's arm.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the scrubs, the thermometer, the mask and the bandage.
Bubbles outside: blow bubbles and draw bubble circles in the air.
Wavy Lines and Curves: trace to the scrubs, the stretcher, the doctor and the wheelchair.
Bath Time page: trace the tub, the rubber duck and the bubbles, then color.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-doctors-healthy-.check: Traces wavy and bumpy lines and closes a small circle

K:word-picture-match#p-weather.title: Weather Word Cards: Puddle, Stormy, Rainbow, Mittens
K:word-picture-match#p-weather.objective: Children name weather words (puddle, stormy, rainbow, mittens) and describe today's weather.

note.mistake: Children say "it's raining" on any cloudy day and call a thunderstorm just "rain"; "stormy" is a new word, and many think mittens are a kind of weather rather than something we wear in it.
note.words: Say, "Stormy means rain, wind and thunder all together." Ask, "What do we wear when it snows? Mittens!" Ask, "What do you see in the sky today?"
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a puddle, a storm cloud with rain and lightning (stormy), a rainbow and a pair of blue mittens. Watch whether children use the words to tell today's weather.

K:word-picture-match#p-weather.routine: Start each day with a weather helper who looks out the window, tells the class the weather and puts a picture on the weather chart. Read aloud a picture book about rain or snow. On a rainy day, put on rain boots and stomp in puddles; on a sunny day, spray a fine mist from a spray bottle in the sunny window and look for a rainbow. Act out a storm with drums for thunder.
week: Weather helper: look out the window and tell the class today's weather.
Weather Word Cards: puddle, stormy, rainbow and mittens; act out each one.
Puddle stomp in rain boots, or a spray-bottle rainbow in the sunny window.
Storm sounds: drums for thunder, then clap the card words: rain-bow, pud-dle, storm-y.
Weather report: each child says one sentence about today's weather, holding a card.
K:word-picture-match#p-weather.check: Names four weather words and tells today's weather

K:ordinal-position#p-weather.title: Weather: First, Next, Last on the Weather Line
K:ordinal-position#p-weather.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of weather pictures and find first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children count the raindrops or clouds inside one picture instead of counting the pictures, or start counting at the umbrella because it is bright; with two chips under a row, many do only the first.
note.words: Say, "Count the boxes from the flag, one box at a time." Ask, "What weather is in the fourth box?" Read, "This chip says second with a circle. Circle the second picture."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five weather pictures (a scarf, sunglasses, clouds, a raincoat, a storm cloud, a sun, a rainbow, a snowflake, an umbrella, mittens) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

K:ordinal-position#p-weather.routine: Keep a weather line on the wall: each day, clip that day's weather picture in the next place after the flag. At the end of the week, count back through it: "The first day was sunny, the second day was rainy." Then five children hold weather cards in a row and the class finds who is first and last.
week: Weather line: clip today's weather picture in the first place.
Clip the second day's weather; say which picture is first and which is second.
Five children hold weather cards in a row; find first, third and last.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Weather line review: what was the weather on the third day?
K:ordinal-position#p-weather.check: Finds the first, third and last picture in a row of five

K:weather-ready#p-weather.title: Weather: Ready for Rain, Snow and Sun
K:weather-ready#p-weather.objective: Children choose what to wear or bring for rain, a hot day and a snowstorm.

note.mistake: Children circle what they like (sunglasses in the rain) or what they wore that day; the sunscreen tube is new to many, and some pick mittens for a hot day "just in case."
note.words: Ask, "Will sunglasses help in the rain?" Say, "In a snowstorm we need a warm coat." Ask, "What keeps us cool on a hot day? A drink of water."
note.watch: The first page has a rain row (an umbrella, sunglasses, sunscreen) and a hot row (mittens, a water bottle, a wool hat); the second a hot row (a water bottle, a coat, mittens) and a snowstorm row (flip-flops, shorts, a pink coat). The child circles the right thing in each row.

K:weather-ready#p-weather.routine: Keep a "ready bag" by the door with an umbrella, sunglasses, a closed tube of sunscreen to look at, mittens, a water bottle and a wool hat. Each morning, look outside and pick what we need. Test a raincoat: spray water on a raincoat and on a cotton shirt and see which one stays dry.
week: Ready bag: look outside and pick what we need from the bag.
Raincoat test: spray water on a raincoat and a cotton shirt; which stays dry?
Ready for the Weather page: circle what to bring for rain and for a hot day.
Dress the bear: put the right clothes on a teddy bear for snow, rain and sun.
Second Ready for the Weather page: a hot day and a snowstorm.
K:weather-ready#p-weather.check: Chooses what to wear for rain, snow and a hot day and says why

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-weather.title: Weather Tracing: A Rainy Day and a Windy Day
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-weather.objective: Children trace raindrops, an umbrella and a cloud, then spirals and loops for a windy day.

note.mistake: Children make raindrops as dots instead of drops with a point on top, and the kite's tail loops grow bigger and bigger until they run off the page; spirals turn into circles stacked on each other.
note.words: Say, "A raindrop has a point at the top and a round bottom." Ask, "Can you make the loops the same size, like the kite's tail?" Say, "Spiral in, round and round, smaller and smaller."
note.watch: The rainy day page shows a cloud, four drops, an umbrella, a duck and a rain boot; the windy day page has a kite with a loopy tail, a spiral blown by the wind and a balloon on a string. Look for drops with a point and loops of even size.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-weather.routine: Make it rain: children tap their fingertips on the table for light rain, then harder, and paint raindrops at the easel. On a windy day, take streamers outside and watch them twirl, then twirl our arms the same way. Make a paper kite with a long tail and draw loops along the tail.
week: Rain fingers: tap the table softly, then harder; paint raindrops at the easel.
A Rainy Day page: trace the cloud, the drops, the umbrella, the duck and the boot.
Streamer walk outside: watch the wind twirl them and twirl our arms the same way.
The Windy Day page: trace the kite, its loopy tail, the spiral and the balloon string.
Make a paper kite and draw loops along its tail.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-weather.check: Traces raindrops and a kite's loops along the dashes

K:category-sort#p-transportation.title: Transportation: Sort Boats, Bikes and Motorcycles
K:category-sort#p-transportation.objective: Children cut out vehicle pictures, sort them into groups of the same kind and tell how each one moves.

note.mistake: Children glue the sailboat with the bikes because both are red, or put a ship with the motorcycles because they were next to each other on the strip; many cut right through the middle of a picture.
note.words: Ask, "What is the picture at the top of this column? Find all the ones like it." Say, "A sailboat has a sail. A ship is a big boat with no sail." Ask, "Does it have wheels? Does it float?"
note.watch: The first page has three columns topped by a ship, a sailboat and a bike, with six pictures to cut at the bottom; the second has two big groups, a ship and a motorcycle, with eight pictures in two strips to cut. Help 3s cut; watch the sorting.

K:category-sort#p-transportation.routine: Tip a bin of toy vehicles onto the rug: boats, bikes, motorcycles, cars, trains and planes. Children sort them by kind into hoops, then by where they go (road, water, sky). Read aloud a picture book about things that go. Before the pages, children practice cutting along straight lines on paper strips with child-safe scissors.
week: Vehicle bin: name each toy vehicle and how it moves.
Sort the toy vehicles by kind into hoops and say the rule for each hoop.
Snip practice: cut along straight lines on paper strips with child-safe scissors.
Cut, Sort and Paste page: cut the bikes, ships and sailboats and glue each in its column.
Vehicle parade: each child holds a toy vehicle and says its name and what it does.
Sort again: things that fly, things that float and things that roll; say the rule for each hoop.
Cut and Paste: Two Big Groups page: cut the ships and motorcycles apart.
Glue the ships in one group and the motorcycles in the other.
Tell a friend why this ship goes here: it floats on water.
Vehicle wall: put up the sorted pages and name every vehicle on them.
K:category-sort#p-transportation.check: Sorts vehicles by kind and says the rule for each group

K:compare-size-extremes#p-transportation.title: Transportation: The Tallest and the Biggest
K:compare-size-extremes#p-transportation.objective: Children compare vehicles, find the tallest in a row and circle every big one.

note.mistake: Children pick the tallest by the flag on top of the sail; on Big Ones Only they circle the three big planes in the top row and stop, missing the big plane at the bottom right.
note.words: Ask, "Which sailboat is the tallest? Line up the bottoms." Say, "Tall means from the bottom to the top." Ask, "Are there more big planes? Look in every row."
note.watch: The Tall and Short page has three rows of four (sailboats, rockets, sailboats), and the child circles the tallest in each; the Big Ones Only page has nine purple planes, four big and five small, and the child circles every big one.

K:compare-size-extremes#p-transportation.routine: Stand toy sailboats and rockets on the table and find the tallest by lining up their bottoms. Fold a big paper plane and a small one (the teacher folds) and fly them outside. Stand beside a tall cardboard rocket taped to the wall and see who is shorter and who is taller than its window.
week: Toy boats and rockets on the table: line up the bottoms and find the tallest.
Tall and short walk: find tall and short things on the playground.
Tall and Short page: circle the tallest sailboat or rocket in each row.
Paper planes: a big one and a small one (the teacher folds); fly them.
Stand beside the cardboard rocket on the wall: who reaches its window?
Big and small sort: big vehicles and small vehicles from the toy bin.
Big Ones Only page: circle every big plane and leave the small ones.
Garage game: big trucks park in the big garage, small cars in the small one.
Draw a big boat and a small boat and tell which one is bigger.
Show a friend the tallest and the biggest vehicle you can find in the room.
K:compare-size-extremes#p-transportation.check: Finds the tallest in a row and circles every big one

K:transport-flying#p-transportation.title: Transportation: Land, Water and Air
K:transport-flying#p-transportation.objective: Children sort vehicles by where they travel (land, water, air) and things that can fly and cannot fly.

note.mistake: Children put the helicopter on land because it sits on legs, and say a fish flies because it "swims up"; many think every animal can fly if it jumps high enough.
note.words: Ask, "Where does a ship go? On the water." Say, "A helicopter flies in the air." Ask, "Can a bee fly? Can a car?"
note.watch: The first page shows six vehicles (a plane, a truck, a boat, a helicopter, a train and a ship) and three boxes, Land, Water and Air; the second shows an owl, a bee, a goldfish and a car above Can Fly and Cannot Fly.

K:transport-flying#p-transportation.routine: Make three zones on the rug: a road (black paper), water (a tub of water) and air (a string across the room). Children test toy vehicles: does it float? Boats go in the tub, cars on the road, paper planes hang on the string. Then test what flies: drop a feather, a paper plane and a block from the same height.
week: Three zones: road, water tub and air string; put each toy vehicle where it travels.
Float test: which toy vehicles float in the water tub?
Land, Water and Air page: lines from the six vehicles to land, water or air.
Vehicle watch: count cars passing the school, look for a plane in the sky.
Sing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" and act out other vehicles.
Fly test: drop a feather, a paper plane and a block; which ones glide?
Things That Fly page: lines from the owl, the bee, the fish and the car to can fly or cannot.
Paper planes: fold and fly them; talk about wings.
Look outside for things that fly: birds, bugs, leaves in the wind.
Sort toy vehicles and toy animals into can fly and cannot fly.
K:transport-flying#p-transportation.check: Sorts vehicles into land, water and air and says which things can fly

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-transportation.title: Transportation Tracing: Bus, Balloon and Helicopter
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-transportation.objective: Children trace pencil paths to vehicles, a bus made of shapes, and a hot air balloon and a helicopter.

note.mistake: Children trace the bus wheels as ovals that do not close, and on the hot air balloon they trace the outside and skip the stripes; the helicopter's thin rotor lines get missed.
note.words: Say, "Circle wheels: go round and close them." Ask, "Did you trace the stripes inside the balloon?" Say, "Look at the picture first, then trace the same picture next to it."
note.watch: The pencil path page ends at a ship, a motorcycle, a digger and a plane; the shape bus has a long rectangle, square windows, circle wheels and extra shapes; Look, Then Trace shows a hot air balloon and a helicopter in frames with a dashed copy beside each.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-transportation.routine: Roll toy cars through paint on big paper to make wheel tracks. Glue a paper bus from shapes: a long rectangle, square windows and circle wheels. Outside, walk a "bus route" along chalk lines and stop at each "bus stop." Hold a paper-plate steering wheel and turn it along a tape road.
week: Car tracks: roll toy cars through paint on big paper.
Chalk bus route: walk the lines and stop at each bus stop.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the ship, the motorcycle, the digger and the plane.
Paper shape bus: glue a long rectangle, square windows and circle wheels.
The Shape Bus page: trace the rectangle, the squares and the circles, then color the circles.
Steering wheel drive: turn a paper-plate wheel along a tape road.
Look, Then Trace page: trace the hot air balloon and the helicopter next to each picture.
Paper helicopter (the teacher folds): drop it and watch it spin down.
Draw a road for a car, a sky path for a plane and a wavy path for a boat.
Trace and color a vehicle of your choice from this week's pages.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-transportation.check: Traces the shapes of a bus and a balloon and closes the circles

K:word-picture-match#p-plants-gardens.title: Plants and Gardens Word Cards: Flowers and Vegetables
K:word-picture-match#p-plants-gardens.objective: Children name flowers and vegetables (crocus, dahlia, tomato, radish, pumpkin, lettuce and more) and tell which part we look at or eat.

note.mistake: The flower names phlox, crocus, peony and dahlia are new: let children say "flower" while they learn them. On the vegetable cards the yellow squash looks like a pear and the cauliflower gets called "white broccoli"; name those pictures first.
note.words: Say, "This flower is a dahlia. Let's say it together: DAH-lee-uh." Ask, "Which vegetable grows under the ground? The radish." Say, "This yellow squash looks like a pear, but it is a vegetable."
note.watch: The flower cards show a phlox, a crocus, a peony and a dahlia; the vegetable page has eight smaller cards: lettuce, a squash, a cauliflower, a tomato, asparagus, a radish, a pumpkin and celery. Watch for "flower" and "vegetable" used correctly even before the new names stick.

K:word-picture-match#p-plants-gardens.routine: Bring a pot of real flowers and a basket of real vegetables (a tomato, a radish, lettuce, celery). Children smell the flowers and wash the vegetables in a tub. Read aloud a picture book about a garden. Plant marigold seeds in cups with an adult at the table (seeds are small). Name each card picture first: crocus, peony, dahlia and phlox are new words.
week: Garden basket: wash the real tomato, radish, lettuce and celery in a tub.
Flower Word Cards: phlox, crocus, peony and dahlia; name the pictures first.
Plant marigold seeds in cups (an adult at the table) and label each cup.
Vegetable Word Cards: where does each grow? Clap squash (1), pump-kin (2), to-ma-to (3).
Garden walk: look for flowers and vegetables at school or in a neighbor's garden.
K:word-picture-match#p-plants-gardens.check: Names two flowers and four vegetables and says where one grows

K:ordinal-position#p-plants-gardens.title: Plants and Gardens: Flowers in a Row
K:ordinal-position#p-plants-gardens.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of flowers and find first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children count the petals of one flower instead of the flowers, or count the flag; the flowers look alike, so many lose their place in the middle of the row.
note.words: Say, "Count the flowers, not the petals." Ask, "Which flower is fifth?" Say, "Keep your finger on the flower you are counting."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five flowers (red flowers, a sunflower, tulips, a blue flower, a lily, a purple spike) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each with a circle or an X. Read each chip aloud.

K:ordinal-position#p-plants-gardens.routine: Set five paper flowers in a row on the window sill with a flag at one end and name the first and the last. Children are seeds in a row on the rug: the first seed grows up, then the next, until the last. Line up the class seed cups and water the second cup, then the fourth.
week: Paper flower row on the window sill with a flag: name the first and the last.
Grow game: children are seeds in a row; the first grows up, then the next.
Watering line: water the second and the fourth seed cup in the row.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Sprout check: which cup in the row sprouted first?
K:ordinal-position#p-plants-gardens.check: Counts places from the flag to find the first, third and last flower

K:plant-needs#p-plants-gardens.title: Plants and Gardens: What Plants Need to Grow
K:plant-needs#p-plants-gardens.objective: Children find out that a plant needs water and light to grow and circle the plant that gets both.

note.mistake: Children think plants eat soil or need toys and music to grow, and on the page they circle the plant with a drum or a book because that picture is fun; many think the tallest plant is the healthiest, but the plant in the dark grows tall, pale and floppy.
note.words: Ask, "What does our plant need: water, light, or a toy?" Say, "Plants need water and light to grow green and strong." Ask, "Which plant is green? Which one is pale? Why?"
note.watch: The page has five rows, each with two potted plants and arrows from what each one gets (a sun, a water drop, blocks, a glove, a drum, a book, a guitar, a pencil); the child circles the plant that gets both water and sun.

K:plant-needs#p-plants-gardens.routine: The week before, sprout bean seeds on a wet paper towel in a zip bag. On the first day, plant two sprouted beans in cups the same way, with an adult at the table. Put one cup in a sunny window and one in a dark closet, and water both. Each day children look and draw what they see. By the end of the week the plant in the light is green and strong; the one in the dark is pale yellow and floppy, even if it grew taller.
week: Plant two beans that sprouted on a wet paper towel last week (an adult at the table).
One cup in the sunny window, one in a dark closet; water both and guess what will happen.
What Plants Need page: circle the plant that gets both water and sun.
Check the cups: look at the color of the leaves and stems and draw what we see.
Compare the cups: the plant in the light is green and strong; the one in the dark is pale and weak.
K:plant-needs#p-plants-gardens.check: Says a plant needs water and light and shows it with our seed cups

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-plants-gardens.title: Plants and Gardens: Trace the Flowerpot
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-plants-gardens.objective: Children trace a flowerpot picture and pencil paths to flowers.

note.mistake: Children trace the flower as one big circle and miss each petal's curve, and skip the lines that cross the window; on the pencil paths they stop at the flower before the line ends.
note.words: Say, "Trace each petal, one at a time." Ask, "What is in the window? What is on the table?" Say, "Go all the way to the clover."
note.watch: The Flowerpot page shows a window with four panes, a butterfly, a flower in a pot, a teacup with steam and a table line; the pencil path page ends its four lines at a clover and three flowers. Look at each petal traced.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-plants-gardens.routine: Plant a real flower in a pot together and press the soil down with our fingers. Make tissue-paper flowers: crumple the petals and twist the stems. Draw flowers in the sand tray with a stick: a circle in the middle and petals around it.
week: Plant a real flower in a pot and press the soil with our fingers.
Tissue-paper flowers: crumple the petals and twist the stems.
The Flowerpot page: trace the window, the butterfly, the flower in its pot and the teacup.
Sand-tray flowers: draw a circle and petals with a stick.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the clover and the flowers.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-plants-gardens.check: Traces a flower petal by petal and a window with its lines

K:word-picture-match#p-bugs.title: Bugs Word Cards: Ant, Slug, Centipede, Millipede
K:word-picture-match#p-bugs.objective: Children name small creatures (ant, slug, centipede, millipede) and say how each one moves.

note.mistake: Children call every small creature a "bug" or an "ant"; centipede and millipede are new words that look alike (both have many legs), and the slug gets called a snail with no shell. Name the pictures first, then the differences.
note.words: Say, "A slug is like a snail with no shell." Ask, "Does a centipede have many legs or a few?" Say, "We look at bugs with our eyes, not our hands."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards (a centipede, a millipede, a slug and an ant), each with its word. Listen for "centipede" and "millipede" after you name them, and for "look, don't touch" on the walk.

K:word-picture-match#p-bugs.routine: Go on a bug walk with plastic magnifying glasses. An adult lifts a log or a flat rock, the class looks without touching, and the adult puts it back gently. Watch how each creature moves and count legs from a distance. Read aloud a picture book about bugs. Back inside, match the bugs we saw to photos and make finger legs walk across the table.
week: Bug walk: look under a log with magnifying glasses; look, don't touch.
Bugs Word Cards: the centipede, millipede, slug and ant; name the pictures first.
Move like a bug: march like an ant, slide like a slug, wiggle many legs like a centipede.
Bug photo table: match each card to a photo; clap ant (1), slug (1), cen-ti-pede (3).
Bug report: each child tells a friend one bug they saw and how it moved.
K:word-picture-match#p-bugs.check: Names four small creatures and how one of them moves

K:numeral-formation#p-bugs.title: Bugs: Count and Trace 6 to 10
K:numeral-formation#p-bugs.objective: Children count groups of 6 to 10 bugs, with help, and trace the number that tells how many.

note.mistake: With 6 to 10 bugs in two rows, children lose count where one row ends and the next begins and count a bug twice; 6 and 9 get traced upside down.
note.words: Say, "Touch each bee and push it a little as you count." Ask, "Where did we stop? Keep going from there." Say, "This is a big number for us. Let's count slowly together."
note.watch: The page has five rows (six butterflies, seven bees, eight red worms, nine ladybugs and ten green caterpillars), each with a number to look at and two to trace. It is a challenge for the 5s: 3s and young 4s count with the teacher and trace one number only.

K:numeral-formation#p-bugs.routine: Fill a garden tray with paper bugs. Children count them onto a ten-frame, one bug in each box, so they can see how many: six butterflies, then seven bees. Count the dots on paper ladybugs. Act out a counting rhyme with fingers crawling up the arm like bugs, from one to ten.
week: Bug tray: count paper bugs onto a ten-frame, one in each box.
How many bugs? Fill the ten-frame to 6, then 7, and count the empty boxes.
Ladybug dots: count 6 to 10 dots on paper ladybugs.
Count and Trace page: count each row of bugs and trace the number (a challenge for the 5s).
Bug hunt: find paper bugs hidden in the room and count them up to ten.
K:numeral-formation#p-bugs.check: Counts 6 to 10 bugs, touching each one, with help

K:animal-groups-homes#p-bugs.title: Bugs and Their Homes
K:animal-groups-homes#p-bugs.objective: Children match animals to their homes: the ant to an anthill, the spider to a web, the bee to a hive, and more.

note.mistake: Children match the bee to a flower (where it visits) instead of the hive, and the rabbit to the anthill because both are holes in the ground; some think spiders live only in houses.
note.words: Ask, "Where does a bee live? In a hive." Say, "A spider makes its own home: a web." Ask, "Who lives in a hole under the ground?"
note.watch: The page shows six animals on the left (an ant, a rabbit, a spider, a bee, a bird and a beaver) and six homes on the right (a web, an anthill, a nest, a burrow, a hive and a dam). The bugs are the ant, the spider and the bee; the others are part of the same page.

K:animal-groups-homes#p-bugs.routine: Look for bug homes on the playground: an anthill, a spider web on a fence (look closely, don't touch) and holes chewed in leaves. Back inside, build bug homes: a yarn web across a chair, a hive from an egg carton and a sand anthill. Children put toy bugs in the homes and say who lives there.
week: Bug home hunt outside: an anthill, a spider web and chewed leaves (look, don't touch).
Build homes: a yarn web, an egg-carton hive and a sand anthill.
Animal Homes page: draw a line from each animal to its home.
Toy bugs go home: put each toy bug in the home it built.
Draw a bug in its home and tell a friend about it.
K:animal-groups-homes#p-bugs.check: Matches an ant, a spider and a bee to their homes

K:mazes#p-bugs.title: Bugs Mazes: The Ladybug and the Bee
K:mazes#p-bugs.objective: Children follow a maze road to help a ladybug reach a sunflower and a bee reach a flower, then color the garden.

note.mistake: On the coloring maze children color the garden before they find the road and lose the path, and the road's edges are thin black lines that the crayon wanders across; on the ladybug maze they go straight up the middle of the grass.
note.words: Say, "Find the road first, color later." Ask, "Where does the bee start? At the A." Say, "Stay between the black lines."
note.watch: The ladybug maze has a wide road from the ladybug at the bottom left to a sunflower at the top right, with one dead end and a bee, a caterpillar and flowers in the grass; the coloring maze is a black-and-white garden with the bee at the start (A), a winding road with dead ends to a flower at the top right, and a butterfly, a bird, a plant and a sun to color.

K:mazes#p-bugs.routine: Build a block maze on the floor and children crawl through it like ladybugs to a paper sunflower. Fly a toy bee on a stick along a ribbon path laid on the table without leaving the ribbon. Draw finger roads through a tray of soil from a toy bug to a flower.
week: Block maze: crawl like ladybugs to the paper sunflower.
Bee flight: move a toy bee along a ribbon path without leaving it.
My First Maze page: help the ladybug get to the sunflower.
Soil tray: draw finger roads from a toy bug to a flower.
Maze Coloring Page: draw the bee's way to the flower, then color the garden.
K:mazes#p-bugs.check: Finds the road through a maze and stays between its edges

K:word-picture-match#p-spring-babies-bir.title: Spring Word Cards: Baby Animals and Birds
K:word-picture-match#p-spring-babies-bir.objective: Children name spring baby animals and birds (chick, lamb, caterpillar, flamingo, toucan, penguin, hawk and more) and say one thing each does.

note.mistake: Children call every bird "birdie" and mix up the toucan and the hornbill; pelican, hornbill and macaw are new words to name first. Many think the caterpillar is a worm and that lambs hatch from eggs like chicks.
note.words: Say, "A caterpillar hatches from a tiny egg and grows into a butterfly." Ask, "Does a lamb come from an egg? No, it is born from its mother." Say, "This is a toucan. Look at its big, colorful beak."
note.watch: The spring cards show grass, a chick, a lamb and a caterpillar; the first bird cards show a pelican, a flamingo, a hornbill and a toucan; the second a macaw, a toucan, a penguin and a hawk. Only the hawk lives near most schools: on the bird walk, listen for bird words (beak, wings, feathers, nest).

K:word-picture-match#p-spring-babies-bir.routine: Bring spring in: a photo of a nest or a nest the class builds from twigs and yarn, hard-boiled eggs to look at, and photos of lambs, chicks and calves. Read aloud a picture book about baby animals. Go on a bird walk with paper-tube binoculars and hang a feeder made from an orange half and birdseed (the adult cuts). Talk about who hatches from an egg.
week: Spring table: look at a nest photo, eggs and photos of lambs, chicks and calves.
Spring Word Cards: grass, chick, lamb and caterpillar; who will each one grow into?
Peep like a chick, hop like a lamb, crawl like a caterpillar; clap chick (1), cat-er-pil-lar (4).
Hatch game: children curl up like eggs and hatch as chicks.
Who comes from an egg? Sort the spring cards into egg and not egg.
Bird walk with paper binoculars: look and listen for birds.
Bird Word Cards: pelican, flamingo, hornbill and toucan; name the pictures first.
Hang an orange-half bird feeder (the adult cuts) and watch who comes.
Bird Word Cards: macaw, toucan, penguin and hawk; which ones can fly?
Spring report: each child names a bird or a baby animal and what it does.
K:word-picture-match#p-spring-babies-bir.check: Names three baby animals and three birds

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-spring-babies-bi.title: Spring: Dot-to-Dot Chick and Ostrich, 1 to 10
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-spring-babies-bi.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and connect the dots to finish a hatching chick and an ostrich.

note.mistake: Children connect the chick's dots in a circle around its head because the numbers curve, and skip from 4 to 6; on the ostrich the dots run close together down a thin neck, and children lose the order where they bunch up.
note.words: Say, "Say the number, find it, then draw." Ask, "What comes after 5?" Say, "Start under the ostrich's beak and go down, down, down its long neck to number 10."
note.watch: The chick page shows a chick breaking out of a cracked egg, the top of its head made by dots 1 to 10 in a curve; on the ostrich page the head is drawn, and dots 1 to 10 run from under the beak down the front of the neck to the chest. Each page has a number strip at the bottom.

K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-spring-babies-bi.routine: Fill an egg carton with ten paper eggs numbered 1 to 10, each hiding a paper chick. Children open the eggs in order, counting aloud. Then mix the eggs up on the rug and children put them back in the carton from 1 to 10. Hop like chicks along a 1-to-10 number path on the floor.
week: Egg carton count: open ten paper eggs numbered 1 to 10, in order.
Fix the eggs: put the mixed-up paper eggs back in order from 1 to 10.
Chick hops along a 1-to-10 path on the floor, saying each number.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: connect the dots to finish the chick hatching from its egg.
Color the chick and count its toes and the pieces of shell.
Bird tracks: count bird footprints printed on paper, 1 to 10.
What comes next? The teacher says a number; children say the next one.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: start at 1 under the ostrich's beak and join the dots down its long neck.
Ostrich and chick: which one has the longer neck? Count the dots on each.
Count the birds at our feeder, or in a picture, up to ten.
K:dot-to-dot-sequence#p-spring-babies-bi.check: Joins dots 1 to 10 in order on two pictures

K:animal-babies#p-spring-babies-birds.title: Spring: Animal Babies and Their Parents
K:animal-babies#p-spring-babies-birds.objective: Children match grown-up animals to their babies (hen and chick, cow and calf, sheep and lamb, horse and foal, butterfly and caterpillar).

note.mistake: Children match by color or size (the white chick to the white sheep), and nearly everyone matches the caterpillar to the wrong parent because it looks nothing like a butterfly; some think a calf is a baby horse.
note.words: Ask, "Who is this baby's mother? Look at the shape, not the color." Say, "A caterpillar grows into a butterfly." Ask, "What is a baby cow called? A calf."
note.watch: The first page has a cow, a butterfly, a horse, a hen and a sheep on the left and a chick, a calf, a caterpillar, a lamb and a foal on the right; the second has the same animals in a new order. The child draws a line from each grown-up to its baby.

K:animal-babies#p-spring-babies-birds.routine: Use photos of baby animals and toy animal families, big and small. Children match each baby toy to its parent and say the baby's name: chick, calf, lamb, foal. If you can, keep caterpillars in a class habitat and watch them change (look, don't touch). Talk about how babies look like their parents and how they look different.
week: Toy animal families: match each baby to its grown-up and say the baby's name.
Baby names: chick, calf, lamb, foal and caterpillar, each with its parent.
Animal Babies page: draw a line from each grown-up animal to its baby.
Alike and different: how is a lamb like a sheep? How is it different?
Caterpillar watch: a class habitat or photos; what will it become?
Baby photos: children bring a baby photo of themselves; how have we changed?
Second Animal Babies page: the hen, horse, sheep, cow and butterfly in a new order.
Act out a mother animal and its baby; friends guess which ones.
Draw an animal and its baby side by side.
Tell a friend which baby looks most like its parent and which looks different.
K:animal-babies#p-spring-babies-birds.check: Matches five grown-up animals to their babies and names three babies

K:mazes#p-spring-babies-birds.title: Spring Mazes: Babies, Mothers and Nests
K:mazes#p-spring-babies-birds.objective: Children draw a line along maze roads to help baby animals find their mothers and birds reach their nests.

note.mistake: On the babies and mothers maze children follow one road and then send all three babies to the mother they reached first; on the swan maze they start at the nest because it is at the top of the page.
note.words: Say, "Each baby has its own road to its own mother." Ask, "Which baby is number 2? Follow its road." Say, "The swan starts at the bottom. Find the arrow."
note.watch: The meadow maze has a chick, a calf and a lamb at the top, numbered 1 to 3, with roads down to a cow, a sheep and a hen; the birdhouse maze has a wide road with dead ends from a bird to a birdhouse in the sky; the swan maze has a winding road from the swan at the bottom right to a nest at the top left.

K:mazes#p-spring-babies-birds.routine: Lay tape roads on the floor: children carry a baby animal toy along a road to its matching mother toy. Build a nest from twigs, yarn and paper strips in a bowl. Outside, follow a chalk trail from a "baby bird" to a hoop nest, and turn back at the chalk dead ends.
week: Baby finds mother: carry a baby animal toy along a tape road to its mother.
Babies and Mothers Maze: draw a line from each baby to its own mother.
Chalk trail outside: walk from the baby bird to the hoop nest.
Nest building: weave twigs, yarn and paper strips in a bowl.
Maze talk: where did you have to turn back? Show a friend.
Ribbon path on the table: fly a paper bird along it to a paper nest.
My First Maze: help the bird get to the birdhouse.
Sand tray: draw a road for a toy duck to its nest.
Picture Maze: help the swan reach the nest along the winding road.
Draw your own maze from a bird to a nest for a friend to try.
K:mazes#p-spring-babies-birds.check: Follows a maze road from a baby to its mother and from a bird to its nest

K:word-picture-match#p-pond.title: Frogs and the Pond Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-pond.objective: Children name pond and reptile animals (frog, turtle, alligator, gecko) and tell where each one lives.

note.mistake: Children call the alligator a "dinosaur" or a "crocodile" and the gecko a "lizard" (right, and gecko is its name); some think a turtle can take its shell off.
note.words: Say, "A gecko is a kind of lizard that can climb walls." Ask, "Where does a frog like to sit? On a lily pad." Say, "A turtle's shell is part of its body. It cannot take it off."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: an alligator, a frog, a gecko and a turtle. Name the gecko first, then watch who tells where each animal lives (in water, on land or both).

K:word-picture-match#p-pond.routine: Make a pond in the water table with toy frogs, turtles and an alligator, rocks and green paper lily pads. Children make each animal swim, rest on a rock or hide. Read aloud a picture book about a pond. Show a photo of a gecko climbing a wall. Sing a counting song about frogs on a log and move the toy frogs as the class sings.
week: Water-table pond: toy frogs, turtles and an alligator swim, rest on rocks and hide.
Pond Word Cards: alligator, frog, gecko and turtle; name the gecko first.
Frog jumps: one hop on a lily pad for each clap: frog (1), tur-tle (2), al-li-ga-tor (4).
Where does it live? Put each card by the water table or by the land rock.
Pond story: each child tells what one pond animal did today.
K:word-picture-match#p-pond.check: Names a frog, a turtle, an alligator and a gecko and where one lives

K:one-more-one-less#p-pond.title: Frogs and the Pond: One More
K:one-more-one-less#p-pond.objective: Children count a small group of pond animals, draw one more and say how many there are now.

note.mistake: Many children start counting again from 1 after adding, which is fine, but some draw two or three more in the box or forget to count the one they drew; writing the new number is for the 5s.
note.words: Say, "Three frogs. One more jumps on. Count them all." Ask, "Is it more or fewer now?" Say, "Draw just one more frog in the box."
note.watch: The page has four rows (three frogs, two orange lizards, four turtles and one alligator), each with a "1 more" label, an empty box to draw one more and a box for the new number. Watch that only one is drawn and that all are counted.

K:one-more-one-less#p-pond.routine: Put three toy frogs on a log and say, "One more frog jumps on. How many now?" Children count, add one frog and count again. Repeat with toy turtles and lizards, always adding just one. Then children take turns being the frog that jumps onto a mat, and the class says the new number.
week: Frogs on a log: three toy frogs; one more jumps on; count again.
One more turtle: add one turtle at a time and say the new number.
Be the frog: children jump onto a mat one at a time; the class says how many now.
One More page: count the pond animals, draw one more and say how many now.
One more block: build towers and add one block, saying the new number.
K:one-more-one-less#p-pond.check: Adds one more to a group of up to 5 and says the new number

K:animal-home#p-pond.title: Frogs and the Pond: A Home for a Frog
K:animal-home#p-pond.objective: Children find what a frog needs in its home (water, food, a place to hide) and build a frog home.

note.mistake: Children add things they like to the frog's home (a toy, a bed) and think frogs eat leaves; some glue the grasshopper in as the frog's pet rather than its food.
note.words: Ask, "What does a frog eat? Bugs, like a grasshopper." Say, "A frog needs water to keep its skin wet." Ask, "Where can the frog hide?"
note.watch: The page shows a frog in a box at the top, a big frame for the frog's home and three pictures to cut out at the bottom: a small pond, a grasshopper and tall grass. The child glues them into the home and draws the frog.

K:animal-home#p-pond.routine: Build a frog home in a clear tub: a little water, rocks, plants and a log, with a toy frog. Talk about what the frog needs: water to keep its skin wet, bugs to eat and a place to hide. Look at photos of eggs, tadpoles and frogs. Children check the home each day and add one thing a frog needs.
week: Frog home tub: water, rocks, plants and a log for a toy frog.
What does a frog need? Water, food and a place to hide.
Frog photos: egg, tadpole, frog; which comes first?
A Home for a Frog page: cut and glue the pond, the grasshopper and the grass, then draw the frog.
Tell a friend why the frog needs each thing in its home.
K:animal-home#p-pond.check: Says three things a frog needs: water, food and a place to hide

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-pond.title: Frogs and the Pond Tracing: Swan, Ducks and Fish
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-pond.objective: Children trace a pond picture, big-middle-small ducks and fish, and pencil paths to turtles and lizards.

note.mistake: Children trace the swan's long neck in small jerky pieces and skip the cattails; on the big, middle, small page they trace the fish's outline but miss the fins and the lines on its body.
note.words: Say, "The swan's neck is one long curve. Go slowly." Ask, "Which duck is the biggest? Trace it first." Say, "Don't forget the fins on the fish."
note.watch: At the Pond shows a swan, a frog on a lily pad, cattails, a sun and a cloud; Big, Middle, Small has a row of three ducks and a row of three fish; the pencil path page ends its lines at two turtles and two lizards.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-pond.routine: Float paper leaves in the water table and blow them across with straws, then run a finger over the ripples. Lay green paper lily pads on the floor and hop toy frogs across them. Paint long blue wavy water lines at the easel.
week: Water table ripples: blow paper leaves with straws and trace the ripples with a finger.
At the Pond page: trace the swan, the frog, the cattails and the pond, then color.
Blue wavy water at the easel: long wavy strokes across the paper.
Big, Medium, Small page: trace the ducks and the fish from big to small.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the turtles and the lizards.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-pond.check: Traces the swan's neck and three ducks in order from big to small

K:word-picture-match#p-zoo.title: Zoo Animals Word Cards
K:word-picture-match#p-zoo.objective: Children name zoo animals (armadillo, wolf, elephant, lion, bat, seal, bear, lemur, koala, giraffe, jaguar, panda) and tell one fact about one of them.

note.mistake: Children call the jaguar a "cheetah" or a "tiger," the lemur a "monkey" and the armadillo a "turtle"; they call the koala a "bear" (it is not, but the panda really is a bear). Name the new pictures first.
note.words: Say, "This is a jaguar. Its spots look like little rings." Ask, "Is a koala a bear? It looks like one, but it is not." Say, "A panda really is a bear. An armadillo has a hard shell, like armor."
note.watch: The first page shows an armadillo, a wolf, an elephant and a lion; the second has eight smaller cards: a bat, a seal, a bear, a lemur, a koala, a giraffe, a jaguar and a panda. Watch the names of the new animals.

K:word-picture-match#p-zoo.routine: Build a zoo in the block area with toy animals, block fences and signs with animal pictures. Children are zookeepers: they feed the animals pretend food and tell visitors about each one. Read aloud a picture book about a trip to the zoo. Show photos of a lemur, an armadillo and a jaguar, which are new to most children.
week: Block-area zoo: build fences and put each toy animal in its home.
Zoo Word Cards: armadillo, wolf, elephant and lion; name the armadillo first.
Zookeepers: feed the animals and clap their names: li-on (2), el-e-phant (3), ar-ma-dil-lo (4).
Zoo Word Cards: bat, seal, bear, lemur, koala, giraffe, jaguar and panda.
Zoo guessing game: describe an animal; friends find its card.
K:word-picture-match#p-zoo.check: Names six zoo animals and tells one fact about one

K:compare-groups#p-zoo.title: Zoo Animals: Match Them Up, More or Fewer
K:compare-groups#p-zoo.objective: Children match zoo animals one to one between two rows and find which row has more, or that they are the same.

note.mistake: Children circle the row that looks longer, even when its animals are just spread out, and draw lines from one animal to two partners; some color the star when the rows only look the same.
note.words: Say, "One line from each animal to one partner." Ask, "Does any animal have no partner? Then that row has more." Say, "If every animal has a partner, color the star."
note.watch: The page has five pairs of rows of small zoo animals (meerkats and big cats, lions and deer, koalas and monkeys, bears and hippos, a zebra and kangaroos); the child draws partner lines, then circles the row with more or colors the star when they are the same.

K:compare-groups#p-zoo.routine: Line up toy zoo animals in two rows and give each animal in the top row a partner from the bottom row. The animals left without partners show which row has more. Then play "feed the zoo": one food block for each animal, and the class says whether there is enough food.
week: Partner animals: two rows of toy animals; give each one a partner.
Feed the zoo: one food block for each animal; is there enough?
More or fewer: count two rows of animals and say which row has more.
Match Them Up page: draw partner lines, circle the row with more, color the star if the same.
Zoo train: give each animal a car; add one car when an animal has none.
K:compare-groups#p-zoo.check: Matches two rows one to one and says which row has more

K:animal-groups-homes#p-zoo.title: Zoo Animals: Farm Animals and Wild Animals
K:animal-groups-homes#p-zoo.objective: Children sort animals into farm animals and wild animals and say why zoo animals are wild animals.

note.mistake: Children say zoo animals are pets because people feed them, and put the horse with the wild animals because horses run fast; some think a tiger can live on a farm if it is friendly.
note.words: Ask, "Does this animal live on a farm or in the wild?" Say, "Zoo animals are wild animals. Zookeepers take care of them." Ask, "Why can't a tiger live on a farm?"
note.watch: The page shows a pig, a tiger, a horse and a giraffe above a Farm Animals box and a Wild Animals box; the child draws a line from each animal's dot to a box. Listen for "wild" used for zoo animals.

K:animal-groups-homes#p-zoo.routine: Compare a farm and a zoo: toy farm animals go in a toy barn and toy wild animals in the block zoo. Talk about who takes care of each animal and where wild animals live when they are not in a zoo (jungle, grassland, ocean). Look at photos of lions on the grassland and giraffes eating from tall trees.
week: Barn and zoo: put toy animals in the barn or the zoo and tell why.
Wild homes: photos of lions on the grassland and giraffes eating from trees.
Farm and Wild Animals page: lines from the pig, tiger, horse and giraffe to the boxes.
Zookeeper talk: why do wild animals need so much space?
Wild animal mural with a jungle part, a grassland part and an ocean part.
K:animal-groups-homes#p-zoo.check: Sorts four animals into farm and wild and says zoo animals are wild

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-zoo.title: Zoo Animals Tracing: A Day at the Zoo
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-zoo.objective: Children trace a zoo scene and pencil paths to zoo animals.

note.mistake: Children trace the long zoo fence as one line and skip the posts, and they miss the flamingo's thin legs; on the pencil paths they hurry past the bumps to reach the panda.
note.words: Say, "Trace every fence post, up and down." Ask, "How many legs is the flamingo standing on?" Say, "Bump, bump, bump, all the way to the panda."
note.watch: The zoo page shows a flamingo on one leg, an elephant, a kangaroo, a palm tree, a sun, a cloud and a fence; the pencil path page ends its lines at a monkey, a fox, a camel and a panda.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-zoo.routine: Move like zoo animals: stomp like an elephant, hop like a kangaroo, stand on one leg like a flamingo. Press toy animals' feet into play-dough to make tracks and trace the prints with a finger. Glue craft sticks in a row on paper to build a zoo fence.
week: Animal moves: stomp like an elephant, hop like a kangaroo, balance like a flamingo.
Play-dough tracks: press toy animals' feet and trace the prints.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the monkey, the fox, the camel and the panda.
Craft-stick zoo fence: glue sticks in a row on paper.
A Day at the Zoo page: trace the flamingo, elephant, kangaroo, palm tree and fence.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-zoo.check: Traces a zoo picture with its fence posts and thin lines

K:word-picture-match#p-ocean.title: Ocean Word Cards: Sea Animals
K:word-picture-match#p-ocean.objective: Children name sea animals (shrimp, seal, dolphin, orca, octopus, crab, seahorse, turtle) and tell one way each one moves.

note.mistake: Children call every big sea animal a "shark" or a "fish" (the orca and the dolphin are not fish), call the seal and the walrus both "seal," and think the seahorse is a horse; pufferfish and orca are new words to name first.
note.words: Say, "A dolphin breathes air, like we do. It is not a fish." Ask, "How does a crab walk? Sideways!" Say, "A seahorse is a little fish with a head shaped like a horse."
note.watch: Both pages are black-and-white cards to color: the first has a shrimp, a seal, a fish and a dolphin; the second has eight smaller cards (a pufferfish, an orca, a turtle, a penguin, a walrus, a seahorse, an octopus and a crab). Name the pufferfish and the orca first.

K:word-picture-match#p-ocean.routine: Turn the water table into an ocean with blue water, sand, big shells and toy sea animals. Children make each animal swim, crawl or float and say how it moves. Read aloud a picture book about sea animals. Show photos of real dolphins, orcas and seahorses, and start a class ocean mural where children add one sea animal each day.
week: Ocean water table: toy sea animals swim, crawl and float; say how each one moves.
Ocean Word Cards to color: shrimp, seal, fish and dolphin.
Ocean mural: add a sea animal and clap its name: crab (1), dol-phin (2), oc-to-pus (3).
Ocean Word Cards to color: pufferfish, orca, turtle, penguin, walrus, seahorse, octopus, crab.
Sea animal parade: walk like a crab, swim like a dolphin, puff up like a pufferfish.
K:word-picture-match#p-ocean.check: Names six sea animals and how one of them moves

K:heavy-light#p-ocean.title: Ocean: Which Sea Animal Is Heavier?
K:heavy-light#p-ocean.objective: Children compare two sea animals and decide which is heavier in real life.

note.mistake: Children pick the sea animal that looks scarier or more colorful, and because the pictures are the same size, the orange starfish and the octopus "look heavy." Real-life size is what counts.
note.words: Ask, "In the real ocean, which is heavier, an orca or an octopus?" Say, "The pictures are the same size, but the real animals are not." Ask, "Could you lift a starfish? Could you lift a shark?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of sea animals in equal circles (an octopus and an orca, a shark and a starfish, a whale and a clownfish); the child circles the heavier one in each pair.

K:heavy-light#p-ocean.routine: Use a balance scale with beach things: a big shell and a small shell, a cup of wet sand and a cup of dry sand. Children guess first, then watch which side goes down. Then hold a heavy beanbag "whale" in one hand and a light paper "fish" in the other. Talk about real sea animals: a whale is heavier than a school bus.
week: Balance scale: big shell and small shell, wet sand and dry sand; guess, then check.
Hold and tell: a heavy beanbag whale and a light paper fish.
Heavy or Light? page: circle the heavier sea animal in each pair.
How big is a whale? Stretch out a long rope on the playground to show it.
Heavy and light tray: sort the ocean toys into two baskets.
K:heavy-light#p-ocean.check: Chooses the heavier of two sea animals and explains why

K:land-and-water#p-ocean.title: Ocean: Land and Water on the Globe
K:land-and-water#p-ocean.objective: Children see on a globe that the earth has land and water and that there is more water than land.

note.mistake: Children color everything blue, or color the land blue because the ocean is their favorite; many think the white space is snow, and the question "more water or more land?" is hard for 3s.
note.words: Say, "Blue is water. Green is land." Ask, "Is there more blue or more green on our globe?" Say, "We live on land. The oceans are the big blue parts."
note.watch: The page shows a big round earth with land and oceans outlined, a key with a wave (water: blue) and a tree (land: green), a choice between the wave and the tree for "more water or more land," and a star to draw for the United States. Help 3s with the question.

K:land-and-water#p-ocean.routine: Toss an inflatable globe ball around the circle: each child catches it and looks where one thumb lands, on land or on water. Make a tally on the chart: water wins. Then build a sand island in a tub of blue water to show land and water side by side.
week: Globe catch: where does a thumb land, on land or water? Mark it on the chart.
Count the marks: there is more water than land.
Land and water tub: build a sand island in blue water.
Land and Water page: color the water blue and the land green (a challenge for the 5s).
Find our country on the class globe and put a star sticker on it.
K:land-and-water#p-ocean.check: Shows land and water on a globe and says there is more water

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-ocean.title: Ocean Tracing: A Turtle and Whales in the Sea
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-ocean.objective: Children trace a big sea turtle slowly, trace and count whales, and follow pencil paths to sea animals.

note.mistake: Children trace the spots on the turtle's shell and skip its outline, or go round the solid frame instead of the dashed turtle; on the whale page they count before tracing and count one whale twice.
note.words: Say, "Start at the dot and go slowly around the turtle, like a turtle walks." Ask, "Did you trace the turtle's head and its feet?" Say, "Trace a whale, then count it."
note.watch: The turtle page has one big dashed turtle with feet, inside a round frame with bubbles (the frame is not traced); the whale page has five dashed whales in the sea, a sailboat, a sun and a box for the number; the pencil path page ends at a seal, a starfish, a narwhal and a whale.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-ocean.routine: Make waves with a parachute or a long blue sheet, big and small. Draw big circles in wet sand with a finger, like a turtle's shell. Sponge-paint whales at the easel and trace their outlines with a finger once the paint is dry.
week: Parachute waves: make big and little waves with a long blue sheet.
My First Tracing page: trace the big turtle slowly, all the way round.
Wet sand drawing: finger circles and waves in the sand tray.
Whales in the Sea page: trace the five whales, count them and say how many.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the seal, the starfish, the narwhal and the whale.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-ocean.check: Traces a big shape slowly and counts five traced whales

K:story-sequencing#p-beach-summer.title: Beach and Summer: Build a Sandcastle, First to Last
K:story-sequencing#p-beach-summer.objective: Children put three pictures of building a sandcastle in order and tell the story with first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children put the picture with the most castles first because it is the "best" one, and the three pictures look alike (the same child at the same beach), so they miss the castles; some glue the strip on without cutting it apart.
note.words: Ask, "What did the beach look like first, before we built?" Say, "Next, there is one row of castles. Last, there are lots of castles." Ask, "How do you know this picture comes first?"
note.watch: The page shows three empty frames on a line (First, Next and Last) and a strip of three small pictures of the same child at the beach: with no sand castles, with one row of little bucket castles, and with many rows. The number of castles is the clue, and it is small: point to it before children cut.

K:story-sequencing#p-beach-summer.routine: Build sandcastles at the sand table or the sandbox with buckets and shovels. Take a photo at each step: smooth sand first, one row of bucket castles next, many castles last. Read aloud a picture book about a day at the beach. Children retell their castle story with the photos and act it out with a bucket and a shovel.
week: Sand table castles: fill a bucket, pat it down and flip it over.
Photo story: take a photo of each step and retell it with first, next and last.
Story Sequencing page: cut the three sandcastle pictures and glue them in order.
Mix-up game: the teacher puts the photos in the wrong order; children fix them.
Tell the sandcastle story to a friend with the glued page.
K:story-sequencing#p-beach-summer.check: Orders three pictures of building a sandcastle and tells the story

K:ordinal-position#p-beach-summer.title: Beach and Summer: Find the Place
K:ordinal-position#p-beach-summer.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of beach things and find first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children count the seagull and the starfish but skip the rock or the bottle because they are plain; others mark the picture that matches the chip's color instead of the picture in that place.
note.words: Say, "Count every picture in the row, even the rock." Ask, "Which beach thing is fifth?" Read, "This chip says third with a circle. Circle the third picture."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five beach pictures (a dolphin, a seagull, a starfish, a swimsuit, a rock, a water bottle, a snorkel mask, a crab, an umbrella, a boat, a sandcastle, a shovel) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

K:ordinal-position#p-beach-summer.routine: Line up five beach things on a towel (a bucket, a shovel, a big shell, sunglasses and a water bottle) with a paper flag at one end. Children count places from the flag and play "What is third?" Then line up for the sprinkler or water play, and each child says their place before their turn.
week: Beach towel line: five beach things in a row; count places from the flag.
What moved? Swap two beach things and say their new places.
Sprinkler line: children line up and say their places before their turn.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Shell line: set five shells in a row from the flag and find the fourth.
K:ordinal-position#p-beach-summer.check: Finds the first, third and last thing in a row of five

K:sun-warms#p-beach-summer.title: Beach and Summer: Sun or Shade?
K:sun-warms#p-beach-summer.objective: Children feel things in the sun and in the shade and find out that the sun makes them warmer.

note.mistake: Children say the shade is "wet" or colder "because it is dark," and color the circle under the picture they like; some think the sun warms things only in summer.
note.words: Ask, "Which ball feels warmer, the one in the sun or the one in the shade?" Say, "The sun warms the ground, the sand and the water." Ask, "Where can we go to cool down?"
note.watch: The page shows a soccer ball in the sun and in the shade, and a bucket of sand in the shade and in the sun, each with a circle; after feeling the real things, the child colors the circle of the warmer one red and the cooler one blue.

K:sun-warms#p-beach-summer.routine: On a sunny day, set two balls and two buckets of sand outside, one of each in the sun and one in the shade. After an hour, children feel each one and say which is warmer. The teacher touches the slide first, because a slide in the sun can burn, then children feel it and a bench in the shade. Talk about sun safety: hats, shade and drinking water.
week: Sun and shade test: a ball and a bucket of sand in the sun, and another of each in the shade.
Feel and tell: which ball is warmer? Which sand is warmer?
Sun or Shade page: color the circle of the warmer one red and the cooler one blue.
Shade hunt on the playground: find shady spots and feel the ground there.
Sun safety: put on hats, find the shade and drink water.
K:sun-warms#p-beach-summer.check: Says that things in the sun get warmer than things in the shade

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-beach-summer.title: Beach and Summer Tracing: Waves and Surf
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-beach-summer.objective: Children trace long waves from left to right and summer pictures, and follow pencil paths to beach things.

note.mistake: Children trace the long waves from right to left or start in the middle, and the waves go flat on the far side; the popsicle's dots and the watermelon's seeds get traced as scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Waves go from left to right." Ask, "Where do you start? At the left edge." Say, "Little dots on the watermelon: one at a time."
note.watch: Surf Morning has a sun, long wavy lines across the sea, a surfboard, a snorkel mask and a flipper; Ice Cream Day has a sun, waves, a popsicle, a slice of watermelon and sunglasses; the pencil paths end at a beach umbrella, a seagull, a beach hut and a sun hat.

K:pre-writing-strokes#p-beach-summer.routine: Wave a long blue ribbon up and down, slow and fast, then paint long wavy lines at the easel from left to right. Draw waves in wet sand with a stick. Cut a surfboard shape from cardboard (the teacher cuts) and trace its edge with a finger.
week: Ribbon waves: wave a long blue ribbon up and down, slow and fast.
Surf Morning page: trace the long waves left to right, then the surfboard, mask and flipper.
Wet sand waves: draw long wavy lines in the sand with a stick.
Ice Cream Day page: trace the waves, the popsicle, the watermelon and the sunglasses.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the umbrella, the seagull, the beach hut and the hat.
K:pre-writing-strokes#p-beach-summer.check: Traces long waves from left to right without lifting

K:word-picture-match#p-camping.title: Camping Word Cards: Compass, Cooler, Rope, Deer
K:word-picture-match#p-camping.objective: Children name camping things (compass, cooler, rope) and an animal campers may see (a deer), and tell how each thing is used.

note.mistake: Children call the compass a "clock" and the cooler a "toolbox" or a "lunch box"; the rope card looks like a broom to many. Some think a deer is a pet you can feed at the campsite.
note.words: Say, "A compass helps campers find their way." Ask, "What do we keep in a cooler? Cold food." Say, "We look at deer from far away. We never feed them."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a compass, a cooler, a deer and a rope with a loop at one end and a knot with a frayed tail. Watch for what each thing is used for, not only its name.

K:word-picture-match#p-camping.routine: Set up a campsite in the room: a sheet over a table for a tent, a cooler, a flashlight, a compass and a short rope kept on a hook to look at. Children pack a backpack for camping and say what each thing is for. Read aloud a picture book about camping by flashlight inside the tent.
week: Classroom campsite: a sheet tent, a cooler, a flashlight and a compass.
Camping Word Cards: compass, cooler, deer and rope; how do campers use them?
Pack the backpack and say why; clap the card words: rope (1), cool-er (2), com-pass (2).
Flashlight story time in the tent with a picture book about camping.
Compass walk: follow the teacher's compass to a hidden "campsite" on the playground.
